front_matter.purpose:
# Purpose

This Policy & Procedure Manual sets out how **[AGENCY NAME]** ("the Agency") operates as a Private Home Care Provider (PHCP) licensed by the Georgia Department of Community Health (DCH), Healthcare Facility Regulation Division, under Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. R. 111-8-65. The Agency provides, or plans to provide, the following services in clients' homes in **[GEOGRAPHIC AREA SERVED]**:

- nursing services
- personal care services
- companion or sitter services

The Agency may also take part in Georgia Medicaid home- and community-based programs: the Elderly and Disabled Waiver (CCSP/SOURCE), ICWP, and NOW/COMP community living supports. Participation in CCSP requires a current, valid DCH private home care license (DHS DAS HCBS 5300 Manual § 208).

The manual has four purposes:

1. **Define the Agency's scope of services and the clients it serves.** The Agency offers only services it can reasonably deliver and never provides a service the rules or other law prohibit (R. 111-8-65-.09(1), .09(2)).
2. **Put the written policies and procedures the rules call for in one place.** These cover service agreements, records, staffing and qualifications, training, contracted services, supervision, daily documentation, quality improvement, service planning, and client rights and complaints (R. 111-8-65-.09 through .12).
3. **Give staff clear, consistent direction** that protects the health, safety, dignity and rights of every client.
4. **Show DCH, at licensure or inspection, that the Agency's written policies meet Rule 111-8-65.** DCH may review these policies during an inspection (R. 111-8-65-.08), and a provisional license may be issued so a new provider can show its procedures comply (R. 111-8-65-.05(1)(c)).

This manual does not replace the rules. If anything here conflicts with Rule 111-8-65 or other applicable law, the rule or law controls.

# How to Use This Manual

## Who uses it

- **Governing body and Administrator:** adopt, review and approve the manual, and use it to oversee compliance.
- **Supervisors (nursing, personal care, companion/sitter):** use it for service planning, supervisory visits, competency evaluation and quality improvement.
- **Nurses, Personal Care Assistants (PCAs), companions and sitters:** use it for day-to-day direction on their duties, documentation, reporting and client rights.
- **Office and billing staff:** use it for records, confidentiality, service agreements, EVV and billing.

## How it is organized

The manual is arranged by topic and follows the structure of Rule 111-8-65, so a reviewer can find each requirement quickly. One reasonable layout is one tab per rule section:

| Topic | Rule |
|---|---|
| Governing body and licensure | .04, .05 |
| Scope of services and clients served | .09(1) |
| Service agreements and cancellation | .09(2) |
| Administrator, staffing and qualifications | .09(3), .09(5) |
| Client records, personnel records, retention, confidentiality, incident and complaint files | .09(4) |
| Orientation and annual training | .09(6) |
| Contracted services | .09(7) |
| Supervision, daily documentation, quality improvement | .10 |
| Service planning | .11 |
| Client rights, responsibilities and complaints | .12 |

**Appendix A** is the crosswalk. It lists every item in the official review document and names the policy in this manual that satisfies it. Use it to confirm nothing has been missed and to answer a reviewer's questions during an inspection or when preparing a plan of correction.

## Before the manual is put into use

1. **Customize it.** Replace every **[AGENCY NAME]** placeholder and every other bracketed field (address, license number, geographic area, names and titles, phone numbers). Remove or adapt any policy for a service the Agency does not offer. For example, a provider that does not offer nursing should say so in its scope of services. The rules require a fully licensed Georgia RN supervisor only if nursing is offered (R. 111-8-65-.10(2)(a)).
2. **Adopt it.** The governing body is empowered and responsible for determining all policies and procedures and ensuring compliance with the rules (R. 111-8-65-.04). Record adoption in the minutes, with the date and the signatures of the authorized representatives, and note the effective date on the manual.
3. **Train staff.** Each employee must be oriented to the relevant written policies before working with clients, including scope of services, client rights and complaints, duties, reporting and emergencies, and the duty to report known TB or hepatitis exposure. Annual training follows after the first year (R. 111-8-65-.09(6)). Keep signed acknowledgments and training records in each personnel file.
4. **Make it accessible.** Keep a current copy at the Agency office and make it available to staff.

## Keeping it current

- Review the manual at least annually, and whenever a rule, Medicaid program requirement, inspection finding, plan of correction or quality improvement result calls for a change.
- Have the governing body approve each revision, record the revision date and version, and retrain staff on material changes.
- Withdraw superseded versions from use, but keep them as the Agency's records require.
- Some items in this manual are flagged for verification (for example, which positions require a background check under Chapter 111-8-12, and the current status of 29 CFR § 552.109(a)). Resolve each flagged item with the responsible agency before finalizing the related policy.

# Regulatory Framework

## Governing rules

The Agency is governed by the following authorities. Cites are given as they appear in the source research.

### Licensure rule: Georgia Rules for Private Home Care Providers (adopted under O.C.G.A. § 31-7-300 et seq.)

- **Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. R. 111-8-65-.01**: Legal Authority
- **Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. R. 111-8-65-.03**: Definitions (including home management and bonding, medically frail or compromised client, medically related activities, personal care tasks, and transport and escort)
- **Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. R. 111-8-65-.04**: Governing Body

### Related rules and program requirements

- **Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. Chapter 111-8-12**: Rules and Regulations for Criminal Background Checks. The owner must comply before a new PHCP license issues (R. 111-8-65-.05(1)(b)). *Which positions beyond the owner and administrator are covered has not been verified. Confirm with HFRD.*
- **DHS DAS HCBS 5300 Manual § 208**: In-Home Services. CCSP in-home service providers must hold a current, valid DCH private home care license.
- **Social Security Act § 1915(c); CMS Waiver 0112.R08.00**: Georgia Elderly and Disabled Waiver (CCSP/SOURCE), approved 11/09/2022 to 11/08/2027. DCH handles reimbursement, enrollment and utilization review. DAS runs day-to-day CCSP operations.
- **21st Century Cures Act (2016) § 12006 — EVV; Georgia DCH EVV program**: Electronic Visit Verification is required for Medicaid-financed personal care services. Georgia's system is Netsmart Mobile Caregiver+.
- **O.C.G.A. § 30-5-4**: Reporting of need for protective services. Persons with reasonable cause to believe a disabled adult or elder person has been abused, neglected or exploited must report to DHS-DAS Adult Protective Services and to an appropriate law enforcement agency or prosecutor. Good-faith reporters are immune (§ 30-5-4(c)). The Agency's policy treats every caregiver as a reporter. *The statute's list of mandated reporters was seen only in part.*
- **29 CFR § 552.109(a)**: Third-party employers of home care workers. Per the research provided, third-party employers (agencies) may not claim the companionship exemption from overtime. *The 2026 status of this section was not confirmed. Verify before finalizing the overtime policy.*

### Version note

The Secretary of State's text of Rule 111-8-65 (rules.sos.ga.gov) controls. The Cornell LII copy of Rule .09 is an older text. For example, the current SOS text of .09(3)(a)1 also requires a satisfactory fingerprint records check determination for the administrator. Where the two differ, follow the SOS text and confirm against the current rule before adopting this manual.

## Regulators and contacts

Georgia EVV Customer Support: (833) 483-5587 (the old EVV number was retired Jan 16, 2026). |

Adult Protective Services is the designated agency for reports under O.C.G.A. § 30-5-4. | https://pamms.dhs.ga.gov/das/hcbs-5300-manual/208/ (phone not listed in source material) |
| **Area Agencies on Aging (AAAs)** | DAS administers its programs through the AAAs, the access route for in-home services and waiver intake. | https://aging.georgia.gov/programs-and-services |

| **Georgia Department of Labor** | State unemployment insurance (employer registration; $9,500 taxable wage base) | https://dol.georgia.gov/faqs-employers/employers-faqs-unemployment-insurance |

The Agency should also post the DCH address and phone number in its client notice of rights (R. 111-8-65-.12(2)) and on the service agreement (R. 111-8-65-.09(2)(a)). Insert the current DCH number, confirmed with HFRD, in **[DCH PHONE NUMBER]** wherever it appears.

## Official policy checklist and review documents

No separate DCH policy-review checklist, application packet or policy-manual template with a form number was found for the Georgia private home care license. DCH reviews the Agency's written policies against the licensure rule itself:

- **Rules and Regulations for Private Home Care Providers, Subject 111-8-65** (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-65), issued by DCH, Healthcare Facility Regulation Division, and published by the Georgia Secretary of State. The sections that set out the written-policy and plan requirements (.04 and .09 through .12, plus the transport requirement at .03(s)) are the review items for this manual.
- **DHS Division of Aging Services HCBS 5300 Manual Appendix E, Client Rights and Responsibilities** (form MAN 5300 Appendix E) is a suggested form for waiver/CCSP providers. It is a reference only and not a licensure checklist. HCBS 5300 § 208.15 requires that providers give clients a written copy of their rights and responsibilities.

**Appendix A** maps every official item, meaning each written-policy and operating requirement in Rule 111-8-65-.04 and .09 through .12 and the related .03 requirements, to the specific policy in this manual that satisfies it. Application, fee, ownership and background-check paperwork under .05 and .06 is administrative and is not part of the policy mapping.

The rules do not list separate required policies for medication, abuse reporting, emergency or disaster plans, discipline, menus, or theft and loss. This manual addresses those topics through the related rule items: incident and unusual-occurrence reports (.09(4)(d)), handling medical emergencies (.09(6)(a)3), on-call nurse consultation (.10(2)(d)), bonding (.03(g)), authorization for access to client funds or vehicle (.09(2)(a)9), and the transport waiver or insurance check (.03(s)). Abuse, neglect and exploitation reporting is additionally governed by O.C.G.A. § 30-5-4.

## Adoption, customization, currency and training

- **Customize.** This manual is a template. Every **[AGENCY NAME]** placeholder and other bracketed field must be completed, and policies must be tailored to the services the Agency actually offers.
- **Adopt.** The governing body must formally adopt the manual and its revisions (R. 111-8-65-.04).
- **Keep it current.** Review it at least annually and when rules, program requirements, inspection findings or quality improvement results change. Re-adopt each revision.
- **Train staff.** All staff must be trained on the manual. Orientation must occur before working with clients, and training continues annually (R. 111-8-65-.09(6)). Document the training in personnel files.
- **Be ready for inspection.** Application or renewal is consent to DCH entry during regular business hours, with access to premises, records, staff and consenting clients. A written plan of correction is due within ten days of receiving a written inspection report citing violations (R. 111-8-65-.08).

citations.title: Legal Authority
citations.requirement: Rules are adopted under O.C.G.A. § 31-7-300 et seq.

citations.title: Definitions
citations.requirement: Defines: applicant/licensee by entity type (.03(b)); companion or sitter tasks (.03(c)); home management, where any employee with unlimited access to client funds must be bonded through the provider (.03(g)); medically frail or compromised client (.03(j)); medically related activities, including reminding clients to take medication and assisting with self-administration, but excluding professional services (.03(k)); owner as any person with 10% or greater interest (.03(l)); personal care tasks (.03(n)); private home care provider and services (.03(o)-(p)); transport and escort, which requires a client waiver of claims or reasonable efforts to confirm motor vehicle insurance when the employee drives a vehicle not owned by the client (.03(s)).

citations.title: Governing Body
citations.requirement: Each provider must have a governing body empowered and responsible to determine all policies and procedures and to ensure compliance with the rules.

citations.title: Licenses
citations.requirement: No operation without a license or provisional license (.05(1)). Owner must comply with Chapter 111-8-12 before a new license issues (.05(1)(b)). A provisional license may be issued to a new provider for a limited time or to an existing provider with an acceptable plan of improvement (.05(1)(c)). Administrator and employees must be qualified (.05(2)). Each location is separately licensed (.05(2)(a)). The license must be displayed (.05(2)(b)). It is not assignable or transferable. It must be returned on change of name, location, ownership or governing body. DCH must get 15 days' advance notice of a location change (.05(2)(c)).

citations.title: Applications
citations.requirement: Initial application on DCH forms, with application fee, Board-set license fee, owner records check application, and description of services and geographic area (.06(1)). Periodic renewal with a description of services and area (.06(2)). Fees are reasonable and may be refunded for good cause (.06(3)). Applications must be truthful. DCH may refuse a license for false statements (.06(4)).

citations.title: Exemptions
citations.requirement: Rules do not apply to an individual who personally provides services without agents, employees, contractors or financially interested referrals (.07(1)(a)), nor to licensed home health agencies (.07(1)(d)) or personal care home staff (.07(1)(e)). No Certificate of Need is required for a PHCP-only license (.07(2)).

citations.title: Inspections and Plans of Correction
citations.requirement: Periodic inspection, with possible exemption for accredited providers (.08(1)). Application or renewal is consent to entry during regular business hours, and DCH gets access to premises, records, staff and consenting clients (.08(2)). Staff must cooperate without unreasonable delay (.08(3)). An acceptable written plan of correction is due within ten days of receiving the written report. The provider may explain or dispute findings in the plan (.08(4)).

citations.title: Administration and Organization — Services Description
citations.requirement: Written policies and procedures must define the scope of services offered and the types of clients served. No service prohibited by the rules or other law may be provided.

citations.title: Administration and Organization — Service Agreements
citations.requirement: Do not offer services you cannot reasonably deliver. Written policies are required. All services are based on a written agreement with 10 required elements (.09(2)(a)1-10), including referral and contact dates, services, frequency, charges and billing, receipt of rights notice, the provider's phone number, the DCH phone number, authorization for client funds or vehicle use, and signatures. The agreement must be completed by the 2nd visit if on a different day than the 1st, or within 7 calendar days of first service, whichever is earlier (.09(2)(b)). Good-cause delay must be documented (.09(2)(b)1). Later changes are documented in the record as agreed by the client (.09(2)(b)2). The client may cancel at any time and pays only for services rendered. Only a reasonable travel and staff-time charge is allowed if the staff member has already arrived (.09(2)(c)).

citations.title: Administration and Organization — Administrator
citations.requirement: The governing body appoints an administrator with full authority and responsibility for operations. Qualifications: no credible evidence of abuse, neglect, exploitation or deprivation; participation in required orientation and training; no material false statements. The current SOS text of (3)(a)1 also requires a satisfactory fingerprint records check determination. See the notes on version conflict.

citations.title: Record keeping — Client Records
citations.requirement: A separate file per client containing: identifying information; current service agreement; current service plan; signed nursing notes if nursing is provided; documentation of personal care and companion/sitter tasks actually performed; supervisory visit findings; material reports and communications; physician contacts; date and source of referral.

citations.title: Retention and Confidentiality of Client Records
citations.requirement: Written policies must state who supervises records, who has custody, to whom and why records are released, and how long they are retained. Minimum retention is five years from the last service. Disclosure is allowed only to appropriate staff, the client, the responsible party, the client's physician or other provider, DCH, persons authorized in writing by the client, or by subpoena.

citations.title: Personnel Records
citations.requirement: A separate record per employee containing: identifying and emergency contact information; 5-year employment history; qualifications; satisfactory TB screening at hire and annually; date of employment; job description; orientation and training documentation; at least an annual performance evaluation; bonding documentation if the employee has unlimited access to client funds (a universal bond is acceptable).

citations.title: Reports of Complaints and Incidents
citations.requirement: Keep files of all complaints under .12(2). Keep incident reports and reports of unusual occurrences (e.g., falls, accidents, significant medication errors) for at least five years. Documentation must show actions taken to resolve complaints and address incidents.

citations.title: Staffing — General and Nursing Personnel
citations.requirement: Keep sufficient qualified staff for the service agreements. On an unexpected staff shortage, advise the client and refer to another provider if the client wishes. Staff must have a written competency evaluation by direct observation or demonstration. Hires must have no credible evidence of abuse or exploitation, must complete orientation and training, and must make no false qualification statements. Nursing personnel must hold a Georgia license.

citations.title: Personal Care Assistant (PCA) Qualifications
citations.requirement: A PCA must have one of: a nurse aide program under 42 CFR Part 483 Subpart D; a DCH-recognized nurse aide competency exam; a DCH-approved health care or personal care credential; or a 40-hour provider training program covering ambulation and transfer, personal care tasks, first aid and CPR, special conditions, home management, home safety and sanitation, infection control, medically related activities and vital signs, and nutrition. The 40-hour program must be directed by an RN or an equivalent professional. 20 hours must be completed before serving clients and the other 20 within six months of starting. No PCA may be assigned a task without completed training and a competency determination. No PCA may care for a client with special conditions without training and demonstrated competency.

citations.title: Companions or Sitters
citations.requirement: Companions or sitters may perform only companion or sitter tasks unless also qualified as a nurse or PCA. They must read, write, follow instructions and complete reports. They must be trained or competent in the needs of elderly, handicapped or convalescing persons, meal preparation, transport and escort, housekeeping and sanitation, home safety, handling medical emergencies, and infection control.

citations.title: Staff Training
citations.requirement: Orientation before working with clients must cover: written policies on scope of services and client types; client rights and complaints (.12); the employee's duties; reporting client progress and problems and handling medical emergencies and incidents; and the duty to report known exposure to TB or hepatitis. Each employee must receive at least 8 clock hours of training annually after the first year of employment, in subjects relating to their duties.

citations.title: Contracted Services
citations.requirement: Contractor arrangements must be in writing and detail the services. The provider must ensure the contractor follows the rules and is qualified. The services must be supervised under .10(2) by a supervisor of the licensed provider.

citations.title: Categories of Services
citations.requirement: Nursing services are delivered by an RN or LPN under a supervisor. Personal care tasks are performed by a qualified PCA (or nurse) per the service plan. Companion or sitter tasks are performed by a qualified companion or sitter per the service plan. PCAs, companions and sitters must report client needs, changes in condition and observed problems.

citations.title: Supervision of Services; Nursing Supervision
citations.requirement: Qualified staff must supervise all services. Each staff member must be evaluated in writing at least annually by direct observation or demonstration. No supervisor may knowingly permit an employee who has been exposed to or diagnosed with TB or hepatitis to serve clients until the employee is determined not to be contagious. A provider offering nursing must employ a fully licensed Georgia RN supervisor.

citations.title: Supervision of Personal Care Tasks
citations.requirement: Supervisors must be qualified by education, training and experience. A licensed RN or LPN must supervise personal care for medically frail or compromised clients. An RN must complete the initial service plan for those clients. A supervisory home visit to the client's residence is due at least every 92 days from the date of initial service, or sooner as the level of care requires. The visit assesses general condition and vital signs, progress, problems, client satisfaction and appropriateness of services, and is documented in the client file or plan.

citations.title: Supervision of Companion or Sitter Tasks
citations.requirement: A qualified supervisor (RN, LPN, the administrator or another assigned staff member) completes the service plan. A supervisory home visit is due at least every 122 days from initial service, or when a complaint raises a serious question about services. The visit assesses condition, progress, problems, satisfaction and appropriateness of services, is made in the residence, and is documented.

citations.title: On-call Representative for Medically Frail Clients
citations.requirement: When staff perform personal care for medically frail or compromised clients in their homes, a provider representative must be on call and able to reach a nurse supervisor by phone or other means to consult with staff on the clients' medical needs.

citations.title: Documentation of Home Care Services Provided
citations.requirement: Written policies must provide for documenting the services actually performed each day. The documentation goes into the client file under .09(4)(a).

citations.title: Quality Improvement Program
citations.requirement: Maintain documentation of an effective quality improvement program that continuously monitors program performance and client outcomes against standards of care and the rules. At minimum, document receipt and resolution of complaints, problems with care identified, and corrective actions.

citations.title: Service Plans
citations.requirement: Written policies are required. The plan is developed with the client, the responsible party, and the physician if nursing is provided. Content: functional limitations, services, times and frequency, duration, goals and objectives, and discharge plans. Where applicable it also covers diagnoses, medications and treatments, equipment, and diet. The service supervisor completes the plan within seven working days after services start. Nursing plans are reviewed and updated at least every 62 days. Other plans are reviewed at each supervisory visit and revised when the content items change.

citations.title: Client Rights, Responsibilities, and Complaints
citations.requirement: A written notice of rights and responsibilities must be given when the service agreement is completed. It covers 11 items (.12(2)(a)-(k)): participation in planning, being informed of changes, accepting or refusing services, charges, the supervisor's name and contact, complaint procedures and non-retaliation, confidentiality, respect for property and residence, DCH address and phone, a copy of the most recent inspection report on written request (after the plan of correction is filed, with a reasonable copying charge), and the client's duty to report changes in condition. Also required: oral or written complaint procedures with timely resolution (.12(3)), and giving the provider's phone number for information, questions and complaints (.12(4)).

citations.title: Enforcement and Penalties
citations.requirement: After notice and an opportunity for hearing, DCH may refuse, limit, restrict, suspend, revoke or refuse to renew a license, issue a public reprimand, or impose a fine.

citations.title: Rules and Regulations for Criminal Background Checks
citations.requirement: The owner must comply before a new PHCP license is issued (per .05(1)(b)). Which positions beyond the owner and administrator are covered was not verified; confirm with HFRD.

citations.title: In-Home Services
citations.requirement: CCSP in-home service providers must hold a current, valid DCH private home care license.

citations.title: Georgia Elderly and Disabled Waiver (CCSP/SOURCE)
citations.requirement: 1915(c) waiver approved 11/09/2022 to 11/08/2027. DCH handles reimbursement, enrollment and utilization review, and DAS runs day-to-day CCSP operations.

citations.cite: 21st Century Cures Act (2016) § 12006 — EVV; Georgia DCH EVV program
citations.title: Electronic Visit Verification
citations.requirement: EVV is required for Medicaid-financed personal care services. Georgia's system is Netsmart Mobile Caregiver+. Each visit records service type, recipient, provider, date, location and start/end times. Waiver billing: CCSP/SOURCE (IDs 590/930) T1019 with TF/UC; ICWP (660) and NOW/COMP (680/681) T2025.

citations.title: Reporting of need for protective services
citations.requirement: Persons with reasonable cause to believe a disabled adult or elder person has been abused, neglected or exploited must report to the designated adult protection agency (DHS-DAS Adult Protective Services) and to an appropriate law enforcement agency or prosecutor. A staff member of a hospital, social agency, financial institution or similar facility must notify the person in charge, who reports or causes the report. Any other person may report. Good-faith reporters are immune (§ 30-5-4(c)). The statute's list of mandated reporters was seen only in part; the agency's policy treats every caregiver as a reporter.

citations.title: Third-party employers of home care workers
citations.requirement: Per the provided research: third-party employers (agencies) may not claim the companionship exemption from overtime. The 2026 status of this section was not confirmed, so verify before finalizing the overtime policy.

policies.title: Governing Body Authority, Policy Approval and Annual Review
policies.applies_to: Governing body members, Administrator, and all employees and contractors who follow the policy manual
policies.purpose: To establish that [AGENCY NAME] has a governing body with the authority and responsibility to set all policies and procedures and to ensure compliance with Georgia Rule 111-8-65, adopted under O.C.G.A. § 31-7-300 et seq. (Rule 111-8-65-.01).
policies.policy: This policy meets Rule 111-8-65-.04 (Governing Body). [AGENCY NAME] has a governing body that is empowered and responsible to determine all policies and procedures and to ensure compliance with Rule 111-8-65. Where the provider is owned by a corporation or LLC, that entity is the applicant/licensee and its governing body acts for the agency. The governing body appoints the Administrator, who has full authority and responsibility for daily operations under Rule .09(3) (see ADM-04). No policy takes effect until the governing body approves it. Each policy carries an approval date and version number. The governing body reviews the whole manual at least once a year. It also reviews the manual whenever DCH amends Rule 111-8-65, including the 2026 revision, and whenever the independent contractor law change (HB 183) affects how the agency engages workers.

definitions.definition: The owner(s), board, or managers of the licensee who hold final authority over [AGENCY NAME], determine its policies, and are accountable for compliance with Rule 111-8-65.
The person or entity (sole proprietor, partnership, corporation, or LLC) to which DCH issues the private home care provider license.
The person appointed by the governing body with full authority and responsibility for operating the agency.
The written policies and procedures adopted by the governing body to operate the agency in compliance with Rule 111-8-65.

procedures: The owner(s) sign a governing body resolution or operating document naming the governing body members and stating its authority to determine all policies and procedures. The document is kept in the corporate records at [ADDRESS].

If the licensee is a corporation or LLC, the document states that the entity is the licensee and that its governing body acts for the agency. The governing body keeps formation and annual registration records current with the Secretary of State.
The governing body meets at least once a year, and more often as needed. The secretary or designee records the date, attendees, and decisions in written minutes.
The governing body approves each new policy and each revision by recorded vote. The policy header shows the approval date, version number, and the approving signature of [GOVERNING BODY CHAIR NAME].
The governing body appoints the Administrator in writing and gives the Administrator written authority over operations. It names a back-up designee for the Administrator's absences (see ADM-04).
The Administrator reports to the governing body at least [QUARTERLY] on census, staffing, complaints, incidents, quality improvement results, inspection findings, and any open corrective actions.
The Administrator keeps a policy index showing each policy ID, title, version, approval date, and next review date.

The annual review is scheduled in the same month each year. Before it, the Administrator compares the manual with the current text of Rule 111-8-65 as published by the Georgia Secretary of State, with any DCH notices, and with any recent change in law affecting independent contractors.

The governing body records in the minutes that the annual review was done, which policies were changed, and the new approval dates. Policies found compliant are re-signed or noted as reviewed without change.

If DCH amends Rule 111-8-65 between annual reviews, the Administrator brings a gap analysis to the governing body within [30] days of the effective date. The governing body approves revisions before the effective date where possible.

After approval, the Administrator distributes revised policies to affected staff within [10] days. Staff sign an acknowledgment that they received and understand the change. Superseded versions are archived and not destroyed.
The Administrator makes the current policy manual available to all staff, to DCH surveyors on request, and to clients on request for the policies that affect them.
The governing body reviews the results of the Quality Improvement Program (SVC-10) and any DCH inspection report or plan of correction (LIC-03). It directs policy changes where needed.

Any employee or contractor who identifies a conflict between a policy and Rule 111-8-65 reports it to the Administrator at once. The Administrator corrects it through the governing body approval process.

responsibilities.duty: Determine all policies and procedures, approve them with a date and version, appoint the Administrator, review the manual annually, and ensure compliance with Rule 111-8-65.
Sign approvals and minutes and call the annual review.
Implement approved policies, maintain the policy index, report to the governing body, and prepare the annual and rule-change reviews.
Follow current policies, sign acknowledgments, and report conflicts or gaps.

documentation: Governing body resolution or operating document and member list
Signed minutes of each meeting, including annual policy review
Signed Administrator appointment
Policy index with version, approval date, and next review date
Archived superseded policy versions
Staff acknowledgment of policy changes

policies.title: Scope of Services, Types of Clients Served and Acceptance of Clients
policies.applies_to: Administrator, intake staff, RN Supervisor, supervisors, schedulers, and all caregivers
policies.purpose: To define in writing the services [AGENCY NAME] offers and the clients it serves, to prevent prohibited services, and to ensure it accepts only clients it can reasonably serve under Rule 111-8-65.
policies.policy: This policy meets Rule 111-8-65-.09(1) (Services Description) and Rule 111-8-65-.09(2) (Service Agreements, first sentence of the rule: no offering of services that cannot reasonably be delivered). [AGENCY NAME] offers: (a) personal care tasks, and (b) companion or sitter tasks, each as defined in Rule .03(n) and .03(c). The agency offers nursing services only while it employs an RN supervisor (see SVC-01). Home management, medically related activities (medication reminders and self-administration assistance, without professional services), and transport and escort are offered only as described in the service plan and agreement. The agency serves [DESCRIBE CLIENT TYPES, e.g., older adults and adults with disabilities living in their own homes in [SERVICE AREA]] and [DOES / DOES NOT] accept medically frail or compromised clients as defined in Rule .03(j). Accepting those clients requires the added supervision and on-call coverage in SVC-05 and SVC-08. The agency never provides a service prohibited by Rule 111-8-65, the legal authority it operates under, or other law. It never accepts a client whose needs, schedule, or location it cannot reasonably meet with current staffing. Staff may perform only the tasks listed in the client's service plan.

definitions.definition: The hands-on and related personal assistance tasks defined in Rule 111-8-65-.03(n) and listed in SVC-02.
The non-hands-on companionship and supervision tasks defined in Rule 111-8-65-.03(c) and listed in SVC-03.
A client who meets the definition in Rule 111-8-65-.03(j) and is subject to the added supervision requirements in SVC-05 and SVC-08.
Activities such as reminding clients to take medication and assisting with self-administration. They exclude professional services (Rule .03(k)).
Household support tasks as defined in Rule .03(g). Any employee with unlimited access to client funds must be bonded through the provider.

procedures: The governing body approves the written scope of services and client types. The Administrator reviews it at the annual policy review (GB-01) and whenever services change.

The scope statement lists each service offered (personal care, companion or sitter, and nursing only if an RN supervisor is employed). It also lists the service area, the hours of service, and any categories of client that the agency does not serve.
Intake staff screen every referral against the scope statement using the intake checklist (OPS-01). They record the date and source of referral on the intake form.

Before accepting a referral, the Administrator or designee confirms that (a) the requested services are within the scope, (b) the services are not prohibited by Rule 111-8-65 or other law, (c) qualified staff are available for the requested days and hours, and (d) supervision, including the on-call requirement for medically frail clients, can be provided (ADM-08, SVC-05, SVC-08).

If a referral needs services outside scope, such as skilled nursing without an RN supervisor, the Administrator declines it and documents the reason. Intake staff offer the referral source or client information on other resources.

If the client appears medically frail or compromised and the agency has decided to serve that group, the RN Supervisor or qualified supervisor reviews the referral before acceptance. The review is documented in the intake record.
Intake staff never promise a service, start date, or schedule that scheduling has not confirmed as deliverable.
The Administrator documents each acceptance or denial, with the date, reason, and who decided, on the intake log.
If a client is accepted, the service plan (PLN-01) and service agreement (ADM-02, ADM-03) list only the tasks the agency has agreed to perform.
Caregivers receive a copy of the service plan or task list before the first visit. They are trained in orientation (ADM-13) that they may not perform tasks outside the plan.

If a client or family asks a caregiver to perform an unlisted or prohibited task, the caregiver politely declines, continues authorized tasks, and reports the request to the supervisor the same day. The supervisor decides whether to amend the plan within the scope or to decline.
Staff report any task they think may be prohibited to the Administrator immediately. The Administrator investigates and corrects the practice and records the action.
If a client's needs change so that the agency can no longer reasonably meet them, the supervisor notifies the Administrator, who follows the discharge and transfer process (OPS-03).
The Administrator reviews the intake log quarterly for denials, missed starts, and unmet requests. The results are reported through the Quality Improvement Program (SVC-10).

responsibilities.duty: Approve the scope of services and client types.
Make acceptance decisions, keep the scope current, and prevent prohibited services.
Review referrals for medically frail or compromised clients and confirm that supervision can be delivered.
Screen referrals against the scope, confirm staff availability, and document the outcome.
Perform only tasks in the service plan and report requests for unlisted tasks.

documentation: Written scope of services and client types, with approval date
Intake log and referral forms showing date and source of referral
Acceptance and denial records with reasons
Supervisor review of medically frail or compromised referrals
Service plans and task lists
Records of out-of-scope requests and the response

policies.title: Service Agreement Content (10 Required Elements)
policies.applies_to: Administrator, intake staff, supervisors, and any staff who prepare or sign service agreements
policies.purpose: To ensure every client receives services under a written service agreement that contains all ten elements required by Rule 111-8-65-.09(2)(a).
policies.policy: This policy meets Rule 111-8-65-.09(2)(a) (service agreement policies and procedures). All services are based on a written service agreement between [AGENCY NAME] and the client or the client's responsible party, if applicable. The agreement form includes each of the following required elements. Item .09(2)(a)1: the date the agency first contacted the client. Item .09(2)(a)2: the date of referral, meaning the date the agency received a specific request to provide services to that client. Item .09(2)(a)3: a description of the services needed as stated by the client or responsible party. Item .09(2)(a)4: a description of the services to be provided and the expected frequency and duration. Item .09(2)(a)5: the charges and the mechanisms for billing and payment. Item .09(2)(a)6: the client's acknowledgment of receipt of a copy of the rights and responsibilities required by Rule .12 (see CR-01). Item .09(2)(a)7: the agency's telephone number for information, questions, or complaints about services. Item .09(2)(a)8: the telephone number of the state licensing authority (DCH) for information or questions about a licensing violation not resolved to the client's satisfaction by complaining to the agency. Item .09(2)(a)9: written authorization from the client or responsible party for access to personal funds when home management includes bill paying or shopping, and for use of the client's motor vehicle when transport and escort services will use it. Item .09(2)(a)10: signatures and dates of the agency's representative and the client or responsible party. If the client or responsible party refuses to sign, the refusal is noted on the agreement with an explanation from the agency's representative.

definitions.definition: The written agreement signed by the agency and the client or responsible party that sets out the services, schedule, charges, and required notices.
The date on which the agency received a specific request to deliver private home care services to a particular client.
A person legally authorized or designated to act for the client in arranging services, where applicable.
The Georgia Department of Community Health (DCH), Healthcare Facility Regulation Division.

procedures: The governing body approves the standard service agreement form. The Administrator checks it against all ten elements of Rule .09(2)(a)1-10, using the checklist in this policy, at each annual policy review.

The form has a labeled field or section for each element: initial contact date (1), referral date (2), services needed as stated by client (3), services to be provided with frequency and duration (4), charges and billing and payment mechanisms (5), rights acknowledgment (6), agency phone (7), DCH phone (8), funds and vehicle authorizations (9), and signature blocks (10).
Intake staff enter the date of first contact and the date of referral from the intake record (OPS-01). The two dates are not combined or assumed to be the same.

The supervisor or intake staff meet the client or responsible party and record the services the client says they need, in the client's own words where possible, before describing what the agency will provide.

The supervisor lists the services the agency will provide, consistent with the scope in ADM-01, and the expected frequency and duration (days, hours per visit, and expected length of service). These match the service plan (PLN-01).

The supervisor states the hourly or visit rate, any minimums allowed by policy, the billing cycle, payment methods, and who is billed (client, responsible party, payer, or Medicaid waiver program). The terms follow ADM-03 on cancellation and charges.

The agency representative gives the client or responsible party the written notice of rights and responsibilities (CR-01) and reviews it. The client initials or signs the acknowledgment on the agreement.

The agreement shows the agency's telephone number, [PHONE], as the number to call for information, questions, or complaints. It also shows the DCH telephone number, [DCH HFRD PHONE], stated as the number to call about a licensing violation not resolved by complaining to the agency.

If the services include bill paying or shopping or other activities involving the client's personal funds, the client or responsible party signs the funds authorization. Staff handle funds only as in CR-04. Employees with unlimited access to client funds are bonded through the agency. If no home management is planned, the agreement states "not applicable."

If transport and escort will use the client's car, the client or responsible party signs the vehicle authorization. If the employee will drive a vehicle not owned by the client, staff follow SAF-06 (client waiver of claims or reasonable efforts to confirm motor vehicle insurance). If not applicable, the agreement states so.
The client or responsible party signs and dates the agreement. The agency representative signs and dates it. Both parties receive a complete copy.

If the client or responsible party refuses to sign, the agency representative writes the refusal on the agreement with a dated explanation and signs it. The Administrator is notified the same day and decides whether services may continue.

Before filing, the Administrator or designee audits each new agreement against the ten-element checklist. Missing elements are corrected with the client within [2] business days and the correction is dated.
The original agreement is placed in the client record (ADM-05). The Administrator audits a sample of agreements quarterly and reports results through the Quality Improvement Program (SVC-10).

responsibilities.duty: Approve the agreement form.
Ensure the form contains all ten elements, audit agreements, and decide on continuation when a client refuses to sign.
Complete each element accurately with the client, obtain signatures, and give copies.
Review, sign, and keep a copy of the agreement.

documentation: Approved service agreement form with ten-element checklist
Signed and dated service agreement in each client record
Rights and responsibilities acknowledgment
Funds and vehicle authorizations, where applicable
Refusal-to-sign notation with explanation, where applicable
Quarterly audit results

policies.title: Service Agreement Timing, Revisions and Client Cancellation
policies.applies_to: Administrator, intake staff, supervisors, schedulers, billing staff
policies.purpose: To make sure service agreements are completed on time, changes are properly documented and agreed to, and clients may cancel at any time and pay only as the rule allows.
policies.policy: This policy meets Rule 111-8-65-.09(2)(b), .09(2)(b)1, .09(2)(b)2, and .09(2)(c). Timing (.09(2)(b)): for each new client, the initial service agreement is completed no later than the second visit to the client's residence, if the second visit is on a different day from the first, or no later than seven calendar days after services are first provided in the residence, whichever is earlier. Good cause (.09(2)(b)1): if the agency cannot complete the agreement for good cause, it documents the reason in the client's file. Revisions (.09(2)(b)2): later changes to the agreement, such as adding or removing a service or changing frequency, duration, or charge, are handled by noting in the client's record the specific change and that it was discussed with and agreed to by the client or responsible party who signed the initial agreement, before the change takes effect. Cancellation (.09(2)(c)): the client may cancel any service agreement at any time and is charged only for services actually rendered before the agency was notified. The agency may charge a reasonable amount for travel and staff time only if the cancellation notice came too late to stop the caregiver from arriving at the client's home. The agency does not use minimum-hour terms, non-cancellable terms, or penalty fees.

definitions.definition: The first written service agreement with a new client, containing the elements in ADM-02.

A reason outside the agency's reasonable control, such as the client or responsible party being unavailable or hospitalized, that prevents signing within the required time. Convenience or workload is not good cause.
A documented change to services, frequency, duration, or charges after the initial agreement is signed.
The client's or responsible party's notice, oral or written, ending a service agreement or a scheduled service.

procedures: At scheduling, the scheduler records the date of the first visit. The agreement due date is calculated as the earlier of (a) the second visit, if on a different day from the first, or (b) seven calendar days after the first service. The due date is entered on the intake tracking log and given to the supervisor.
Whenever possible, the supervisor completes and signs the agreement before or at the first visit, following ADM-02.
The Administrator checks the tracking log each business day for agreements due within the next two days or overdue. The supervisor is told the same day of any that are open.

If the agreement cannot be completed by the due date for good cause, the supervisor records in the client file, on the date it becomes known, the reason, the steps taken to complete it, and the new target date. The Administrator reviews and initials the note.
Where good cause exists, the supervisor completes the agreement as soon as the cause ends, with no more delay than needed. Services continue only as agreed with the client during the delay.

If the delay is not for good cause, the Administrator treats it as a compliance error. The Administrator completes the agreement at once, documents corrective action, and reports the instance through the Quality Improvement Program (SVC-10).

For a change in service, frequency, duration, or charge, the supervisor first discusses the change with the client or responsible party who signed the initial agreement. The supervisor does not make the change until the client or responsible party agrees.

The supervisor writes a dated note in the client record that states the specific change (what is added, removed, or changed, and the new frequency, duration, or charge), that it was discussed with and agreed to by the client or responsible party (named), and the effective date. The supervisor signs the note.

The supervisor updates the service plan (PLN-01), the schedule (OPS-02), and the billing record to match the change before the effective date. A copy of the change note is given to the client on request.
Staff accept a cancellation by phone, in person, or in writing, at any time. The person receiving it records the date, time, and caller and tells the scheduler and supervisor at once.
The scheduler stops scheduled visits as soon as notice is received. The scheduler contacts the caregiver immediately to prevent a trip, using a phone call or text to the caregiver.
Billing staff bill only for services actually rendered before the agency was notified. No charge is made for visits that did not take place, and no minimum-hour charge is made.

A travel and staff-time charge applies only if the caregiver had already arrived at the home before the agency could stop the visit. Billing staff calculate the charge from the agency's written rate for travel and staff time, which must be reasonable and stated in the service agreement. The Administrator approves each charge, which is recorded in the client record.

If the client cancels all services, the supervisor follows the discharge process in OPS-03, including a final bill that shows only services rendered, and the Administrator reviews it before it is sent.
The Administrator audits agreement timing, change notes, and cancellation charges quarterly and reports results under SVC-10.

responsibilities.duty: Monitor agreement due dates, approve good-cause notes and any cancellation charge, and correct late agreements.
Complete agreements on time, document good cause, and record agreed changes before they take effect.
Calculate due dates, update schedules on changes, and stop visits on cancellation.
Bill only for services rendered and apply a travel and staff-time charge only as allowed.

documentation: Intake tracking log with agreement due dates
Signed initial service agreement
Good-cause documentation in the client file
Dated change notes showing the specific change and client or responsible party agreement
Cancellation record (date, time, and person who gave notice)
Billing records showing only services rendered and any approved travel and staff-time charge

policies.title: Administrator Appointment and Qualifications
policies.applies_to: Governing body, Administrator, and back-up designee
policies.purpose: To ensure [AGENCY NAME] is run by a qualified administrator appointed by the governing body, with full authority and responsibility for operations.
policies.policy: This policy meets Rule 111-8-65-.09(3) (Administrator) and Rule 111-8-65-.09(3)(a) (minimum qualifications). The governing body appoints an Administrator, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], who has full authority and responsibility for the operation of the agency. Any administrator employed by the agency must: (1) obtain a satisfactory fingerprint records check determination in compliance with the Rules and Regulations for Criminal Background Checks, Chapter 111-8-12 (item .09(3)(a)1); (2) participate in the orientation and training required by Rule 111-8-65 (item .09(3)(a)2); and (3) not have made any material false statement about qualifications to DCH or to the agency (item .09(3)(a)3). The agency also requires that there be no credible evidence of abuse, neglect, exploitation, or deprivation by the Administrator. The current Georgia Secretary of State text of Rule .09(3)(a)1 includes the fingerprint requirement. Some older versions of the rule do not include it, and the agency follows the current text. The agency names a back-up person to act when the Administrator is absent.

definitions.definition: The person appointed by the governing body with full authority and responsibility for the operation of the agency.
A determination issued under the Rules and Regulations for Criminal Background Checks, Chapter 111-8-12, that the individual may work in the position.
A qualified person named in writing to carry out administrator duties when the Administrator is absent.

procedures: The governing body selects the Administrator after reviewing the candidate's application, references, and evidence of qualifications. It records the decision in its minutes (GB-01).

Before the start date, the governing body obtains a signed statement from the candidate that all statements about qualifications, education, and experience given to the agency and to DCH are true, and checks references and employment history.

The governing body issues a written appointment letter giving the Administrator full authority and responsibility for operations. It states the Administrator's duties, including compliance with Rule 111-8-65, hiring, supervision, finance, and reporting to the governing body.

The agency starts the fingerprint records check under Chapter 111-8-12 before the Administrator begins duties, following PER-01. The Administrator's file contains the satisfactory determination before the Administrator functions in the role.

For a new license, the owner also complies with Chapter 111-8-12 before the license is issued. The agency confirms with DCH's Healthcare Facility Regulation Division which other positions are covered. That list has not been verified, and the confirmation, with date and source, is placed in the personnel file (PER-01).

The agency screens the candidate for any credible evidence of abuse, neglect, exploitation, or deprivation, using the background and registry checks in PER-01. Any such evidence disqualifies the person from serving as Administrator.

The Administrator completes the agency's orientation (ADM-13) and any orientation and training required by Rule 111-8-65 and documents the dates and content. The Administrator takes the annual in-service training (ADM-14) in later years.
The Administrator signs an acknowledgment of the duty to make no false or misleading statement to DCH or the agency about qualifications or operations (LIC-02).

The governing body names a back-up designee in writing who meets the same qualifications, and records the designee's contact information. The Administrator tells staff, and the designee's name is posted for staff use.
When the Administrator is absent more than [3] consecutive days, the back-up designee acts. The Administrator notifies the governing body and keeps a log of the dates.
The Administrator's contact information is on file with DCH, and the agency notifies DCH of an Administrator change as required by LIC-01 and LIC-06.

If the Administrator resigns, is removed, or becomes disqualified, the governing body appoints a replacement or interim in writing without delay. The new Administrator must satisfy this policy before acting.
The governing body evaluates the Administrator in writing at least once a year and keeps the evaluation in the personnel file.
The personnel file for the Administrator contains the appointment letter, qualification statement, fingerprint determination, registry results, orientation and training records, and evaluations.

responsibilities.duty: Appoint the Administrator and a back-up designee, verify qualifications, and evaluate performance.
Operate the agency, ensure compliance with Rule 111-8-65, complete required orientation and training, and answer to the governing body.
Perform administrator duties during absences.

documentation: Governing body minutes and written appointment letter
Signed qualification and truthful-statement attestation
Satisfactory fingerprint records check determination
Registry and abuse, neglect, exploitation check results
Orientation and training records
Back-up designee appointment
Annual evaluation
Record of HFRD confirmation on covered positions

policies.title: Client Record Contents
policies.applies_to: Administrator, RN Supervisor, supervisors, schedulers, caregivers, and office staff who create or file client records
policies.purpose: To ensure [AGENCY NAME] keeps a separate, complete record for each client containing the nine items required by Rule 111-8-65-.09(4)(a).
policies.policy: This policy meets Rule 111-8-65-.09(4)(a) (Client Records). [AGENCY NAME] keeps a separate file containing all written records about the services provided to each client. Each file contains: item 1, identifying information including name, address, telephone number, and responsible party, if any; item 2, the current service agreement under Rule .09(2) (ADM-02, ADM-03); item 3, the current service plan under Rule .11 (PLN-01); item 4, clinical or progress notes, signed and dated by the staff providing direct care, if the client receives nursing services; item 5, documentation of personal care tasks and companion or sitter tasks actually performed for the client (SVC-09); item 6, documentation of findings of home supervisory visits by the supervisor unless entered in the service plan (SVC-06, SVC-07); item 7, any material reports from or about the client relating to care, including progress notes and problems reported by employees, communications with personal physicians or other health care providers, and communications with family members or responsible parties; item 8, the names, addresses, and telephone numbers of the client's personal physicians, if any; and item 9, the date and source of referral. Security, retention, confidentiality, and release of records are governed by ADM-06.

definitions.definition: The separate file, paper or electronic, of all written records about services provided to one client.
Any report or communication about the client that bears on the care provided, including employee-reported problems and communications with physicians, family, or responsible parties.
The caregiver's record of each personal care or companion/sitter task actually performed at each visit (SVC-09).

procedures: The Administrator designates a record custodian, [RECORD CUSTODIAN NAME]. The custodian creates one separate file for each client when the referral is accepted, with a unique client identifier. Clients are never combined in one file.
The custodian uses a record checklist listing the nine required items. The checklist is kept at the front of each file, with the date each item was added.

Item 1: at intake, staff record the client's name, address, telephone number, and responsible party (name, relationship, and phone) on the face sheet (OPS-01). Staff update it within [2] business days of any change.
Item 9: intake staff record the date of referral and the source of referral (person or organization) on the intake form, and file it on the day the referral is accepted.
Item 8: intake staff ask the client for the names, addresses, and telephone numbers of personal physicians and other health care providers and record them. If the client has none, staff write "none."
Item 2: the signed service agreement is filed under ADM-02 and ADM-03. Each change note under ADM-03 is filed behind it so the current agreement is always apparent.
Item 3: the supervisor files the current service plan (PLN-01) and replaces it at each revision. The earlier version is retained and marked superseded.

Item 4: if the agency provides nursing services, the nurse writes clinical or progress notes for each nursing visit and signs and dates each note. The RN Supervisor reviews notes at the interval in SVC-01. Unsigned notes are not accepted.

Item 5: caregivers record, at each visit, the tasks actually performed, as in SVC-09, and submit the record to the office by [DEADLINE, e.g., end of the pay period or 48 hours]. The custodian files them in the record. Tasks not performed are noted with the reason.

Item 6: the supervisor documents the findings of each supervisory home visit, with date, observations, client feedback, and actions, either on the visit form or in the service plan. The form is filed in the client record (SVC-06, SVC-07).

Item 7: staff file material reports within [2] business days. These include problems reported by caregivers, change-in-condition reports (SAF-07), incident reports (SAF-02), and notes of communications with physicians, other providers, family members, and responsible parties, each with date, person contacted, and content.

Every entry is dated and shows the author's name and title. Late entries are marked as late with the date written. Corrections are made by a single line and initials, never by erasing or removing a record.

The custodian audits a sample of active client files each [QUARTER] against the checklist. The audit records the missing items and the date they were corrected. Missing items are corrected within [5] business days.
The Administrator reviews audit results and reports them under the Quality Improvement Program (SVC-10).
Staff keep client records at [ADDRESS] or in the agency's secure electronic system and protect them under ADM-06 and CR-03.

responsibilities.duty: Ensure a separate, complete record exists for each client and review audit results.
Create files, maintain the checklist, file documents, and run the quarterly audit.
Document supervisory visits, keep the service plan current, and review nursing notes.
Document services and tasks actually performed, sign and date entries, and report problems to the office.
Record identifying information, physicians, and the date and source of referral.

documentation: Separate client file with record checklist
Face sheet with identifying information and responsible party
Intake record with date and source of referral
Current service agreement and change notes
Current service plan and superseded versions
Signed and dated nursing or progress notes, if nursing is provided
Task documentation for personal care and companion/sitter tasks performed
Supervisory visit findings
Material reports and communications
Physician names, addresses, and telephone numbers
Quarterly record audit results

policies.title: Client Record Security, Retention, Confidentiality and Release
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors and volunteers who create, handle, store, or have access to client records; Administrator; Records Custodian
policies.purpose: To protect the privacy and security of client records, state who is responsible for them, define when and to whom they may be released, and set how long they are kept, as required of a Georgia Private Home Care Provider.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains written, implemented procedures for the maintenance and security of client records. This policy meets Rule 111-8-65-.09(4)(b) (Retention and Confidentiality of Client Records) by stating: (1) WHO SUPERVISES records: the Administrator, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], supervises the maintenance of all client records; (2) WHO HAS CUSTODY: the Administrator holds ultimate custody, and day-to-day custody is delegated to the Records Custodian, [RECORDS CUSTODIAN NAME/TITLE], at [ADDRESS]; (3) TO WHOM AND WHY records may be released: only to the categories and for the purposes listed in this policy; and (4) HOW LONG records are retained: at least five years from the date of last service. This policy meets Rule 111-8-65-.09(4)(b)1 (retention of at least five years from the date of last service, and maintenance of confidentiality). It meets Rule 111-8-65-.09(4)(b)2 by prohibiting any employee from disclosing, or knowingly permitting disclosure of, information in a client record except to appropriate provider staff, the client, the responsible party (if applicable), the client's physician or other health care provider, the Department of Community Health (DCH), other individuals authorized by the client in writing, or by subpoena. Any other disclosure is prohibited. To the extent the agency is a HIPAA covered entity (for example, because it bills Medicaid electronically), it also follows 45 CFR 164.530 (administrative requirements, including safeguards, workforce training, sanctions and complaints) and 45 CFR 164.312 (technical safeguards for electronic records).

definitions.definition: All paper and electronic information about a client held by the agency, including the service agreement, service plan, assessments, daily service documentation, supervisory visit notes, incident reports, correspondence and release authorizations.
The person legally authorized to act for the client, or the person the client has designated to receive information and act for the client, as documented in the client record.
Agency employees and contractors who need the information to deliver, supervise, schedule, bill for or review the client's services.
The date on which the agency last provided a service to the client. The five-year retention period starts on this date.
The person designated by the Administrator to control storage, access, release logs and retention tracking.

procedures: The Administrator supervises the maintenance of client records and designates in writing a Records Custodian and one back-up custodian. The designation is kept in the Administrator's policy file and updated within 7 days of any change.

The Records Custodian keeps an access list that names each position with access to client records and the level of access (read, add entries, release). Access is limited to what each person needs for their duties. The Administrator approves the list and reviews it at least quarterly.
Paper records are kept in locked cabinets at [ADDRESS], in a room that is locked when unattended. Keys or codes are issued only to the Administrator, the Records Custodian and the back-up custodian.

Electronic records are kept only in agency-approved systems that use unique user IDs, strong passwords (with multi-factor authentication where available), automatic log-off, encryption of stored and transmitted data, audit logs and regular backups. These are the technical safeguards the agency applies under 45 CFR 164.312. Shared log-ins are prohibited.

Caregivers may keep a client's service plan and daily service documentation in the client's home. They may not copy, photograph, text, email or post client information outside agency-approved systems. Completed daily documentation is returned or uploaded to the agency by the date set in the schedule, and the Records Custodian files it in the client record.
Records may not leave the office except for client care, a supervisory visit, or a documented release. Any record removed is signed out on a log and returned by the end of the next business day.

Before releasing any information, the person handling the request confirms the requester's identity and checks the request against the allowed categories in this policy (the client; the responsible party; appropriate provider staff; the client's physician or other health care provider; DCH; a person authorized by the client in writing; or a subpoena). If the requester does not fit a category, the request is declined and referred to the Administrator.

Written client authorizations must identify the client, the person or organization to receive the information, the specific information to be released, the purpose, an expiration date or event, the client's or responsible party's signature and the date. Clients are told they may revoke an authorization in writing at any time. Authorizations are kept in the client record.

Disclosures to Medicaid waiver case managers or agencies other than DCH (such as the Division of Aging Services or an Area Agency on Aging) are made only with the client's written authorization signed at intake or another authorization on file, or as another allowed category permits. Staff ask the Administrator if unsure.

The Records Custodian records each release outside the agency in a release log: date, client, recipient, information released, purpose, authority (category or authorization) and the staff member who released it. Routine use within the agency for care, supervision and scheduling is not logged.

For a subpoena, the person receiving it gives it to the Administrator the same day. The Administrator confirms that it is valid and properly served, consults legal counsel as needed, releases only the records the subpoena requires, notifies the client when appropriate, and documents the release in the log.
When DCH surveyors request records during an inspection, the Administrator or designee provides them promptly (see LIC-03). The release is logged.

Records of all clients are kept for at least five years from the date of last service. The Records Custodian records the last-service date in the closed-record index when the client is discharged (OPS-03) and calculates the earliest destruction date.

Closed records are stored securely and remain retrievable for the entire retention period. Records are not destroyed while a complaint, audit, investigation, claim or legal proceeding involving the client is open, or a longer period is required by a payer or program contract. The Administrator decides when a longer period applies.

After the retention period ends and the Administrator approves in writing, the Records Custodian destroys paper records by cross-cut shredding or secure shredding service and permanently erases electronic records. A destruction log with dates, client identifiers and method is kept permanently.

If the agency closes or changes ownership, the Administrator arranges in writing for continued custody, security and availability of all client records for the remaining retention period, and notifies HFRD and clients as directed by HFRD (see LIC-06).

All employees sign a confidentiality statement at hire and receive training on this policy at orientation (ADM-13) and annually (ADM-14). Violations result in discipline up to termination under PER-03. Suspected unauthorized disclosures are reported to the Administrator at once, who investigates, takes corrective action, notifies affected clients and applicable authorities as required, and documents the outcome.
The Administrator reviews this policy at least annually as part of the Governing Body review (GB-01).

responsibilities.duty: Supervises the maintenance of records; approves access; decides on non-routine releases, subpoenas and retention holds; investigates breaches; approves destruction.
Has day-to-day custody; controls storage and access; keeps the release log, closed-record index and destruction log.
Use records only as needed for their job; follow security rules; never disclose information outside the allowed categories; report suspected breaches immediately.
Reviews and approves this policy annually.

documentation: Records Custodian designation and access list
Client authorizations for release
Release log
Record sign-out log
Closed-record index with last-service dates
Destruction log
Signed employee confidentiality statements
Breach investigation notes

policies.title: Personnel Records and Employee Health Screening
policies.applies_to: Administrator, supervisors, human resources staff, all employees and contractors who interact with clients or conduct activities with environmental impact
policies.purpose: To keep a complete, separate personnel record for each employee and to run a health screening program that protects clients and staff from infection, injury and improper care.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a separate written personnel record for every employee. This policy meets Rule 111-8-65-.09(4)(c) (Personnel Records), items 1 through 9: (1) identifying information (name, address, telephone number and emergency contact person(s)); (2) a five-year employment history, or a complete history if the person has worked fewer than five years; (3) records of qualifications; (4) records of health screenings, including the health screening program and TB screening described below; (5) date of employment; (6) job description or statement of duties and responsibilities; (7) documentation of the orientation and training required by the rules; (8) documentation of at least an annual performance evaluation; and (9) documentation of bonding if the employee performs home management services that permit unlimited access to a client's personal funds (evidence of a universal bond need not be kept separately in each personnel file). The agency's health screening program is designed to identify conditions that may place clients at risk for infection, injury or improper care, and includes initial, routine and targeted health screenings of employees and contractors who interact with clients or conduct other activities with environmental impact. All employees are screened for tuberculosis (TB) before starting work in accordance with CDC guidance for baseline screening and testing of health care personnel. As an additional agency practice, the agency re-screens employees annually. Employees must report known exposure to, or diagnosis of, TB or hepatitis. Under Rule 111-8-65-.10(2), no supervisor may knowingly permit an employee who has been exposed to or diagnosed with TB or hepatitis to serve clients until the employee is determined not to be contagious.

definitions.definition: The agency's written process for initial (pre-work), routine (periodic) and targeted (event- or risk-based) screening of employees and contractors.
A screening prompted by a specific event or risk, such as a reported exposure, symptoms of a communicable disease, an outbreak, or a direction from a public health authority.
Screening and testing for TB infection done before the person starts work, in line with CDC guidance for health care personnel.
A single bond that covers all employees, so that proof of bonding is not required in each personnel file.

procedures: The Administrator or designee opens a separate personnel file for each employee when the offer is accepted. Files are never combined for several employees.
The file includes a face sheet with name, address, telephone number and at least one emergency contact. The employee updates this within 7 days of any change.
The hiring supervisor obtains and files a five-year employment history (or the full history if under five years) on the application and verifies it as part of reference checks.

The file includes copies and verification of qualifications for the position: nursing license verification (ADM-10), PCA credential or 40-hour training records (ADM-11), the written competency evaluation (ADM-09) and any other required credentials.
The file contains the date of employment and the signed job description or statement of duties, which the employee acknowledges in writing before starting work.

The Administrator arranges baseline TB screening, in line with CDC guidance for health care personnel, for every employee before the first day of work. Results go in the health section of the file. Employees may not start work until a satisfactory result is on file.

Each year, within the month of the hire anniversary, the employee completes TB re-screening under the agency's annual practice. The Administrator tracks due dates on a screening tracker and removes from the schedule, with documentation, any employee who is overdue until the screening is complete.
Health records are kept in a confidential section of the personnel file, separate from general personnel information, accessible only to the Administrator and designated human resources staff.

The Administrator extends the health screening program to contractors who interact with clients or whose activities affect the client environment (for example, contract nurses). Contract terms require equivalent screening (ADM-15).

For targeted screenings, the Administrator decides when a screening is needed, such as after a reported exposure or symptoms or when a public health authority recommends it. The employee is referred to a health care provider, and the date, reason and result are filed.

Employees must report to the Administrator immediately, before their next shift, any known exposure to, or diagnosis of, TB or hepatitis. They are told this at orientation (ADM-13) and sign an acknowledgment.

On a report of exposure or diagnosis, the Administrator removes the employee from client contact. The employee does not return to serving clients until a health care provider's written statement that the employee is not contagious is in the file. No supervisor may knowingly permit an exposed or diagnosed employee to serve clients before then (see SVC-04).

For employees with occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials, the agency follows 29 CFR 1910.1030: exposure determination, training, hepatitis B vaccination offered at no cost where required, and post-exposure evaluation. Records are kept in the confidential health section (see SAF-03).
The Administrator files documentation of orientation (ADM-13) and training (ADM-11 and ADM-14), including dates, hours, topics and trainer.

The employee's direct supervisor completes and files a performance evaluation at least annually. This is separate from the written competency evaluation by observation in SVC-04, though both may be done at the same visit.

For any employee who performs home management services with unlimited access to a client's personal funds, the Administrator confirms bonding before the employee is assigned and files proof, or a statement that the employee is covered by the agency's universal bond, with a copy of the bond (CR-04).

Before each employee anniversary and before each annual license renewal inspection, the Administrator audits a sample of personnel files against the nine required items and corrects deficiencies within 14 days.

Personnel records are kept in locked storage or access-controlled electronic systems and retained for the length of employment and at least five years after separation. Files are available to DCH on inspection.
