Supervises personal care for medically frail or compromised clients when assigned, reports to the RN, and documents revisions for RN review.
Completes the frailty screening and refers every screen to the RN before service begins.
Follows the service plan and reports changes in condition and problems to the supervisor.

documentation: Supervisor qualification file with the basis for qualification
Medical frailty screening and RN determination in the client record
RN-signed initial service plan for medically frail or compromised clients
LPN revision notes with the RN's review signature and date
PCA plan acknowledgement
Quarterly record audit results

policies.category: Rule .10 Private Home Care Provider Services
policies.title: Supervisory Home Visits — Personal Care Clients (Every 92 Days)
policies.applies_to: Supervisors, RNs, LPNs and the Administrator for every client receiving personal care tasks
policies.purpose: To make sure each personal care client receives a supervisory visit in the residence at least every 92 days, or sooner when the level of care requires, with the assessment elements the rule requires, and that each visit is documented.
policies.policy: This policy meets Rule 111-8-65-.10(2)(b)2 — Supervisory Home Visits for Personal Care Clients. The appropriate supervisor makes a supervisory home visit to each personal care client's residence at least every 92 days, counting from the date of initial service in the residence, or sooner as the client's level of care requires to make sure the client's needs are met. The visit includes an assessment of the client's general condition and vital signs, a review of progress being made, the problems the client has encountered, and the client's satisfaction with the services delivered by agency staff. The supervisor also records observations about the appropriateness of the level of services offered. Routine quarterly supervisory visits are made in the client's residence and are documented in the client's file or service plan. For medically frail or compromised clients the visit is made by a licensed RN or LPN under SVC-05. A client who receives any personal care task follows this 92-day schedule, even if the client also receives companion or sitter tasks.

definitions.definition: The first date an agency employee provides service to the client in the residence. The 92-day clock starts on this date.
An in-person visit by the qualified supervisor to the client's residence, not a phone call or telehealth contact, to assess the client and the services.
At minimum, temperature, pulse, respirations and blood pressure, taken and recorded by a supervisor competent to do so.
The routine supervisory visit due at least every 92 days.

procedures: On the day of initial service, the scheduler enters the date in the supervisory visit tracking log and calculates the due date: no later than 92 days after initial service. The target is a visit within 80 days to leave room for rescheduling.

After each visit, the next due date is set no later than 92 days from the date of that visit, and never later than the date the previous cycle allows. The tracker shows a 30-day advance alert, a 14-day alert and an overdue flag.
The Administrator reviews the tracking log weekly and assigns visits to a qualified supervisor. Visits to medically frail or compromised clients are assigned to a licensed RN or LPN (SVC-05).
The scheduler calls the client or representative at least 3 days ahead to arrange a convenient time. The PCA is invited to participate, or the supervisor speaks with the PCA separately.

The supervisor visits the residence and assesses the client's general condition. This includes appearance, skin, mobility, cognition and mood, nutrition and hydration, safety hazards in the home, and any signs of abuse, neglect or exploitation (reported under SAF-01).

The supervisor takes and records the client's vital signs. If the client refuses, or a reading is outside the client's normal range, the supervisor records this and notifies the RN the same day. An RN or LPN takes the vital signs for medically frail or compromised clients.

The supervisor reviews progress against the goals and tasks on the service plan, and asks the client (and representative) about problems encountered and satisfaction with the PCA and the services, including punctuality and dignity and respect.
The supervisor records observations about whether the level of services is appropriate: more care is needed, less care is needed, or the services are right for the client.
The supervisor observes the PCA performing at least one service plan task, if the PCA is present. Any concern is addressed with the PCA immediately and documented under SVC-04.
The supervisor reviews the daily service records (SVC-09) for the period and compares them with the service plan.

The supervisor documents the visit on the Supervisory Home Visit Report in the client file or service plan on the day of the visit, including date, time in and out, who was present, vital signs, findings on each required element, and actions taken. The supervisor signs the report.

If the level of care is inappropriate or the condition has changed, the supervisor revises the service plan (RN approval where required under SVC-05) within 3 business days and informs the client, PCA and, where applicable, the payer or case manager (OPS-04).

The supervisor makes visits sooner than 92 days when the level of care requires it. Triggers include hospital discharge, a fall or injury, a significant change in condition, a complaint, a PCA change, new high-risk tasks or an RN request. The reason is documented.

If a visit cannot be made on time (for example, a client hospitalized or declining the visit), the supervisor makes and records at least three attempts on different days, notifies the Administrator, and completes the visit within 7 days of the client's return or consent. The visit is not skipped. The Administrator approves and documents any extension.
The Administrator reports on timeliness of supervisory visits, with any late visits, root causes and corrections, to the quality improvement program every quarter (SVC-10).

responsibilities.duty: Reviews the tracking log weekly, assigns qualified supervisors and approves any extension.

responsibilities.role: Supervisor (RN, LPN or other qualified supervisor)
responsibilities.duty: Makes the in-person visit, takes vital signs, assesses all required elements, documents the visit and revises the plan.
Maintains the tracking log, sets due dates and alerts, and arranges visit times with clients.
Cooperates with the visit and reports concerns to the supervisor.

documentation: Supervisory visit tracking log with initial service date and due dates
Supervisory Home Visit Report in the client file or service plan (condition, vital signs, progress, problems, satisfaction, appropriateness of services)
Documentation of attempts to schedule and any approved extension
Service plan revisions resulting from the visit
Quarterly timeliness report to the quality improvement program

policies.category: Rule .10 Private Home Care Provider Services
policies.title: Supervision of Companion or Sitter Services and 122-Day Home Visits
policies.applies_to: Supervisors, the Administrator, companions and sitters, and clients who receive only companion or sitter tasks
policies.purpose: To make sure companion or sitter services are supervised by a qualified supervisor, service plans are completed by the appropriate supervisor, and in-home supervisory visits occur at least every 122 days or sooner when a complaint raises a serious question about services.
policies.policy: This policy meets Rule 111-8-65-.10(2)(c) — Supervision of Companion or Sitter Tasks; Rule 111-8-65-.10(2)(c)1 — Service Plan Completion; and Rule 111-8-65-.10(2)(c)2 — Supervisory Home Visits. [AGENCY NAME] supervises companion or sitter tasks through a qualified supervisor: a registered nurse, a licensed practical nurse, the Administrator, or another staff member assigned responsibility for supervising the delivery of care. The appropriate supervisor completes the client's service plan under PLN-01, in coordination with the staff who will provide the services. The supervisor makes a supervisory home visit to each client's residence at least every 122 days, starting from the date of initial service in the residence, or when the agency receives a complaint that raises a serious question about the services being delivered. The visit includes an assessment of the client's general condition, a review of progress, the problems the client has encountered, and the client's satisfaction with services. It also includes observations about the appropriateness of the level of services. Routine supervisory visits are made in the client's residence, and every supervisory visit is documented in the client's file or service plan. A client who receives any personal care task is supervised under SVC-05 and SVC-06, and the 92-day schedule applies instead.

definitions.definition: A client who receives only companion or sitter tasks and no personal care or nursing services.
The first date a companion or sitter provides service in the client's residence. The 122-day clock begins on this date.
A complaint alleging possible harm, neglect, abuse, exploitation, unsafe practice, theft, or a failure to deliver the services on the plan.
The staff member the Administrator designates in writing to supervise companion or sitter services.

procedures: The Administrator designates in writing the qualified supervisor (RN, LPN, the Administrator or another assigned staff member) for companion or sitter services. The designation is dated and filed in the supervisor file.

At intake, the supervisor confirms that the client needs companion or sitter tasks only. If any personal care task is needed, the client is placed on the personal care schedule under SVC-05 and SVC-06.
The assigned supervisor completes the service plan in coordination with the companion or sitter before service begins, following PLN-01, and signs and dates it.

On the day of initial service the scheduler enters the date in the supervisory visit tracking log and sets the due date: no later than 122 days from initial service. The target is a visit within 110 days.
After each visit, the next due date is set no later than 122 days from that visit. The tracker shows alerts at 30 and 14 days and an overdue flag.
The supervisor contacts the client or representative at least 3 days ahead to arrange a time in the residence. Routine visits are made in the home, not by phone or at the office.

During the visit the supervisor assesses the client's general condition, including appearance, mobility, nutrition, mood, safety of the home and any signs of abuse, neglect or exploitation (reported under SAF-01).
The supervisor reviews progress against the service plan, and asks the client or representative about problems encountered and satisfaction with the companion or sitter and the services.

The supervisor makes observations on whether the level of services is appropriate and whether the client now needs more care. If the client needs any personal care or nursing task, the supervisor notifies the Administrator, and the client is moved to the correct level of supervision and a qualified provider is assigned.
The supervisor reviews daily service records (SVC-09) and, if the companion or sitter is present, observes tasks being performed. Concerns are addressed with the employee and documented under SVC-04.

The supervisor documents the visit in the client file or service plan on the day of the visit, including date, time in and out, persons present, findings on each element and actions taken, and signs the entry.
If the visit shows a need to change the plan, the supervisor revises the service plan within 3 business days and informs the client and the employee (PLN-01, ADM-03).

When the agency receives a complaint that raises a serious question about services, the Administrator logs it under CR-02 and assigns a supervisor to make a home visit within 2 business days. This visit is in addition to the routine 122-day visit, and the 122-day cycle is then reset from the date of the complaint visit.

If a routine visit cannot be made on time because the client is hospitalized, away or declines the visit, the supervisor makes and documents at least three attempts on different days, notifies the Administrator, and completes the visit within 7 days after the client is available. The Administrator documents any extension.
The Administrator reports visit timeliness and complaint-triggered visits to the quality improvement program every quarter (SVC-10).

responsibilities.duty: Designates the supervisor, reviews the tracking log weekly, and assigns complaint-triggered visits.
Completes service plans, makes and documents home visits, and moves clients to the correct level of supervision when personal care is needed.
Maintains the tracking log with due dates and alerts, and arranges visit times.
Coordinates with the supervisor on the plan, cooperates with visits and reports concerns promptly.

documentation: Written designation of the assigned supervisor
Service plan completed and signed by the supervisor
Supervisory visit tracking log
Supervisory visit documentation in the client file or service plan
Complaint log entry and complaint-triggered visit documentation
Records of scheduling attempts and any approved extension

policies.category: Rule .10 Private Home Care Provider Services
policies.title: On-Call Representative for Medically Frail or Compromised Clients
policies.applies_to: On-call representatives, nurse supervisors, PCAs, subcontractors and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To make sure that whenever personal care is being delivered in the home to a medically frail or compromised client, an agency representative is on call and accessible and able to reach a nurse supervisor to consult with staff on the client's medical needs.
policies.policy: This policy meets Rule 111-8-65-.10(2)(d) — On-Call Representative for Medically Frail or Medically Compromised Clients. When employees or subcontractors are performing personal care tasks in the residences of clients who are medically frail or medically compromised, [AGENCY NAME] has a representative on call and accessible. That representative is able to contact a nurse supervisor by telephone or other means to provide appropriate consultation to the employees or subcontractors on responding to the clients' medical needs. Coverage applies during every hour that such care is scheduled, including nights, weekends and holidays. Emergencies are handled by calling 911 first.

definitions.definition: An agency staff member designated on the on-call roster who answers the after-hours line and can reach a nurse supervisor.
The agency's RN, or an LPN reporting to the RN, who provides clinical consultation.
Answers calls or returns messages within the response time in this policy, and has the means to reach the nurse supervisor.
A client identified as such by the RN under SVC-05.

procedures: The Administrator prepares a weekly on-call roster listing, for every hour in which personal care is scheduled for medically frail or compromised clients, the on-call representative and a named nurse supervisor with a backup nurse. Each person is listed with a working phone number.

The Administrator publishes the roster and the after-hours number, [PHONE], to all PCAs and subcontractors serving medically frail or compromised clients. The number is printed on the employee ID badge card and on the service plan in the home. The roster is updated whenever coverage changes.

Before accepting a shift on the on-call roster, the representative confirms that he or she has a charged phone, the roster and nurse supervisor contact numbers, and the client list with medical frailty status.

The scheduler marks each visit for a medically frail or compromised client on the schedule. The schedule must never have a visit for such a client during a time with no assigned on-call representative.

At orientation and before the first visit for such a client, the PCA is told how to reach the on-call representative and when to call. Reasons to call include any change in condition, a concern about the client's medical needs, a problem with equipment, an unexpected event or uncertainty about what the service plan allows.

A PCA who has a medical concern calls the on-call representative. In an emergency, such as unresponsiveness, chest pain, difficulty breathing, stroke signs or serious injury, the PCA calls 911 first and then the on-call representative (SAF-07).
The on-call representative answers the call or returns it within 15 minutes. If the call is not answered, the PCA calls the backup number on the roster and then the Administrator.

The on-call representative gathers the facts (client name, symptoms, vital signs if available, what the PCA saw and did) and contacts the nurse supervisor immediately by phone or other means. The representative then relays the nurse's direction to the PCA, or connects the nurse and the PCA directly.

Consultation is for guidance within the PCA's scope and the service plan. The PCA does not perform nursing tasks on advice from the phone. The nurse may direct the PCA to monitor and report, call the client's physician, call 911, or remain until relief arrives. The nurse may also make a visit.

If the on-call representative cannot reach the nurse supervisor within 15 minutes, the representative tries the backup nurse and the Administrator, and advises the PCA to call 911 if the situation is urgent. The failure to connect is reported to the Administrator the next business day.

The on-call representative logs each call on the On-Call Consultation Log, noting date, time, caller, client, issue, nurse contacted, advice given and outcome. The representative gives the log to the Administrator by the next business day.

The nurse supervisor follows up by the next business day, reviews the client's service plan, makes revisions if needed and arranges an earlier supervisory visit when indicated (SVC-06). Incidents are reported under SAF-02.
The Administrator tests the on-call system by placing a test call at least quarterly at varied times, including a weekend or night, and documents the result. Any failure is corrected within 7 days.
The Administrator reviews the on-call logs quarterly for patterns and response times and reports to the quality improvement program (SVC-10).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the on-call roster, ensures coverage for all scheduled hours, tests the system and reviews logs.
Stays accessible, responds within 15 minutes, reaches the nurse supervisor, relays direction and logs each call.
Provides clinical consultation, directs the next steps and follows up on the client's needs.
Calls 911 in emergencies, calls the on-call representative with medical concerns and follows the direction given.
Checks that visits for medically frail or compromised clients are scheduled only when on-call coverage is in place.

documentation: Weekly on-call roster and published after-hours number
On-Call Consultation Log
Nurse supervisor follow-up notes in the client record
Quarterly on-call test call results
Quarterly review of on-call logs for the quality improvement program

policies.category: Rule .10 Private Home Care Provider Services
policies.title: Daily Documentation of Services Performed
policies.applies_to: All caregivers (nurses, personal care assistants, companions and sitters), service supervisors, the Administrator and office staff who handle client records or billing.
policies.purpose: To make sure the services actually performed for each client each day are documented, kept in the client's file, and available for supervisors, DCH surveyors and, for Medicaid clients, billing and EVV reconciliation.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] documents the services actually performed for each client each day. This policy meets Rule 111-8-65-.10(3) (Documentation of Home Care Services Provided), which requires written policies and procedures for documenting the services actually performed for clients each day, and for incorporating that documentation into the client's file in accordance with Rule .09(4)(a). Caregivers document the tasks they actually performed, not only the scheduled visit. Daily documentation is placed in the client's separate file as required by Rule .09(4)(a). Nursing notes are signed by the nurse who provided the service. Service supervisors review the daily notes at each supervisory visit. For Medicaid clients, the electronic visit verification (EVV) record must match the daily note.

definitions.definition: A written or electronic record, made for each visit or shift, of the services and tasks actually performed for the client that day.
A note listing each personal care, companion/sitter or nursing task performed. A statement such as "services provided" or a copy of the schedule is not a task-level note.
Electronic visit verification, the system used for Medicaid-funded visits to record the date, time, location and caregiver for each visit (see OPS-05).
The separate file kept for each client under Rule 111-8-65-.09(4)(a) (see ADM-05).

procedures: At orientation (ADM-13) and before a caregiver's first assignment, the service supervisor trains the caregiver on this policy, the agency's daily note form and how to complete it. The training is recorded in the personnel file.
For each visit or shift, the caregiver completes a daily service note on the agency form [FORM NAME] or in the agency's electronic system.
The note must show the client's name, the date, the caregiver's name and title, and the actual start and stop times.

The note must list each task actually performed, using the tasks in the client's service plan (PLN-01) as the checklist. For example: bathing, dressing, meal preparation, medication reminder, companionship or supervision.
The caregiver records any scheduled or planned task that was not performed, the reason (such as client refusal, client unavailable, or lack of supplies), and who was told.

The caregiver records relevant observations, such as a change in condition, a fall, a refusal of care, or a concern for safety. Any change in condition, incident or complaint is also reported immediately by phone to the supervisor under SAF-07 and SAF-02. The daily note does not replace that report.
The caregiver completes the note during or immediately after the visit, before leaving the home or at the end of the shift. Caregivers must not fill in notes ahead of time or from memory days later.

The caregiver signs and dates each note. Where the client or responsible party is asked to verify the visit, the client's signature or electronic confirmation is requested but is not a substitute for the caregiver's task documentation.
Nursing services are documented in nursing notes that are signed by the nurse who performed the service, with the date, time and credentials.
If a caregiver makes a mistake, they draw a single line through it, write the correction, and initial and date it. Caregivers may not use correction fluid, erase or destroy a note.

Caregivers deliver or upload completed notes to the office by [DEADLINE, e.g., end of each work week]. The office checks for missing notes weekly, and the supervisor follows up with the caregiver on any gaps.
Office staff file each note in the client's separate file under Rule .09(4)(a), and the notes are kept with the client record for the retention period in ADM-06.

For Medicaid-funded clients, the office compares each daily note against the EVV record (date, start and stop times, caregiver) before billing. Any mismatch is resolved and documented with a dated explanation, and no claim is submitted for a visit that is not supported by both a daily note and an EVV record (see OPS-05 and LIC-05).

At each supervisory visit, the service supervisor reviews the daily notes since the last visit. The supervisor checks that tasks match the service plan, that notes are complete, and that any care concerns are followed up. The supervisor records the review in the supervisory visit documentation (SVC-06, SVC-07).

If notes show tasks that are not in the service plan, or planned tasks that are repeatedly not performed, the supervisor reviews the plan with the client and updates it under PLN-01, or coaches the caregiver.
The Administrator includes a sample of daily notes in the quality improvement audits under SVC-10, and reports missing or inadequate notes as problems with care to be corrected.
Caregivers who fail to document, or who falsify documentation, are subject to corrective action up to termination under PER-03, and falsified documentation tied to billing is handled under LIC-05.

responsibilities.duty: Completes a task-level, signed daily note for every visit, on time, records tasks not performed and why, and reports changes in condition to the supervisor.
Trains caregivers on documentation, reviews daily notes at each supervisory visit, and follows up on gaps or inconsistencies.
Collects and files notes in the client file, tracks missing notes weekly, and reconciles notes with EVV before Medicaid billing.
Ensures this policy is implemented, audits documentation through the QI program, and applies corrective action.

documentation: Daily service notes for each visit, filed in the client file
Signed nursing notes where nursing is provided
Documentation training records in personnel files
Supervisor review entries in supervisory visit records
EVV-to-note reconciliation records for Medicaid clients
Corrections and corrective action records, and QI audit results

policies.category: Rule .10 Private Home Care Provider Services
policies.title: Quality Improvement Program
policies.applies_to: The governing body, Administrator, service supervisors, nurses and all staff whose work affects care and client outcomes.
policies.purpose: To keep documentation showing an effective quality improvement (QI) program that continuously monitors the agency's performance and client outcomes against acceptable standards of care and the licensure rules, and that finds and corrects problems.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written quality improvement program and documentation that it is effective. This policy meets Rule 111-8-65-.10(4) (Quality Improvement Program). The program continuously monitors the performance of the agency itself and client outcomes to make sure that care meets acceptable standards of care and complies with the minimum requirements of Rule 111-8-65. At a minimum, the QI documentation records (1) the receipt and, if possible, the resolution of client complaints, (2) problems with care that are identified, and (3) the corrective actions taken. The Administrator reviews the QI log with the governing body at least quarterly. The program includes audits of supervisory visit timeliness, service agreement timing and personnel file completeness.

definitions.definition: The running record of complaints received and resolved, problems with care identified, corrective actions taken and follow-up results.

Any finding that care did not meet the service plan, the standard of care, or a rule requirement (for example a missed supervisory visit, a missed task, an unreported change in condition, or a medication-related error).
A specific, assigned and dated step taken to fix a problem and keep it from happening again.
The result of services for the client, such as falls, hospitalizations, complaints, goal progress and client satisfaction.

procedures: The governing body designates the Administrator [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] as the QI program lead. The Administrator may assign a QI coordinator in writing, but remains accountable to the governing body.

The Administrator sets up and maintains the QI log on the agency form [FORM NAME] or electronic system. Entries are dated and identify the source, the problem, the person responsible, the action taken and the result.
Complaints: every client complaint, oral or written, is entered into the QI log within [2] business days of receipt, with how it was resolved or why it could not be resolved (see CR-02).
Problems with care: staff report problems with care, incidents and unusual occurrences to the supervisor. The Administrator enters them into the QI log (see SAF-02 and SAF-07).
Monthly, the Administrator or QI coordinator audits a sample of client files and personnel files, and records the results in the QI log.

Supervisory visit timeliness: the audit compares the date of each client's last supervisory home visit with the required interval for that client's type of service (see SVC-06 and SVC-07) and lists any overdue or missed visits.
Service agreement timing: the audit checks that each new client's signed service agreement was completed within the required time, and that revisions were documented (see ADM-03).

Personnel file completeness: the audit checks that each employee's file contains all required items (see ADM-07, ADM-09, ADM-11, PER-01) and that orientation and annual in-service training are on time (see ADM-13, ADM-14).
The audit also reviews service plan timeliness and reviews (PLN-01), completeness of daily service documentation (SVC-09), and missed visits (OPS-02).

The Administrator reviews client outcome indicators, including falls, emergency department visits, hospitalizations, discharges, goal progress and client feedback, and looks for trends by caregiver, client or time period.

For each problem found, the Administrator assigns a corrective action, a responsible person and a due date, and records them in the QI log. Examples are retraining, a revised procedure, scheduling changes or disciplinary action.

The responsible person reports completion. The Administrator verifies the correction, for example with a re-audit within [30] days, and records the result. A problem is not closed until it is verified.

At least quarterly, the Administrator presents the QI log, audit results, trends and open corrective actions to the governing body. The governing body's review, its comments and any decisions are recorded in the meeting minutes (see GB-01).
The governing body directs changes in policies, staffing or resources where QI results show a need, and the Administrator updates the affected policies.
The Administrator shares relevant QI findings with staff at meetings or training, without identifying clients unnecessarily.
The Administrator keeps QI records, audits and meeting minutes for at least five years, so that they are available to DCH surveyors on request (see LIC-03).

responsibilities.duty: Reviews the QI log at least quarterly, directs corrective changes and records its review.
Leads the QI program, maintains the QI log, conducts audits, assigns and verifies corrective actions, and reports to the governing body.
Report complaints and problems with care promptly, carry out assigned corrective actions and supply supervisory visit data for audits.
Report complaints, incidents and care problems, and take part in corrective actions and training.

documentation: QI log recording complaints, problems with care and corrective actions
Monthly audit worksheets and results, including supervisory visit timeliness, service agreement timing and personnel file completeness
Corrective action plans with owners, due dates and verification of completion
Governing body quarterly review minutes
Complaint files and incident reports referenced in the log

policies.title: Service Plan Development, Content and Review
policies.applies_to: Service supervisors, nurses, caregivers, the Administrator, and clients and responsible parties taking part in planning.
policies.purpose: To make sure that each client has a written service plan developed with the client, completed on time, matched to the client's needs and kept current.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] develops a written service plan for every client and carries it out as written. This policy meets Rule 111-8-65-.11(1) (Service Plan Content): the written plan of service is established in collaboration with the client and the responsible party, if applicable, and with the client's personal physician if the services to be provided are nursing services and the client has a personal physician. This policy also meets Rule 111-8-65-.11(2): the service supervisor completes the service plan within seven working days after services are initially provided in the residence. Service plans for nursing services are reviewed and updated at least every 62 days. Other service plans are reviewed at each supervisory visit and revised when the plan content changes. Each plan includes the client's functional limitations, the services to be provided, the times and frequency, the duration, goals and objectives, and discharge plans. Where applicable, the plan also covers diagnoses, medications and treatments, equipment and diet.

definitions.definition: The written plan that sets out what services the agency will provide to the client and how, based on the client's needs.
The agency employee designated to supervise services, complete the service plan and make supervisory visits (see SVC-04 to SVC-07).
A person legally or otherwise authorized to act for the client, where applicable.
A weekday that is not a legal holiday. The seven-working-day period starts the day after services are first provided in the home.

procedures: At intake, the agency obtains the client's functional needs, preferences and any physician orders (see OPS-01), and gives them to the service supervisor who will develop the plan.

The service supervisor sets up a planning discussion with the client and the responsible party (if applicable). It is held in the home or by phone or video, at the client's choice, and is scheduled so that the plan can be finished within the deadline.

If the client will receive nursing services and has a personal physician, the supervisor or RN consults that physician about the plan, obtains orders as required, and records the contact (date, name, content) in the client file.
The supervisor records the date services first began in the residence, and calculates the seventh working day. The due date is entered in the agency's tracking system.

The supervisor writes the plan on the agency form [FORM NAME]. It includes: (a) the client's functional limitations; (b) each service to be provided; (c) the times and frequency of services; (d) the expected duration of services; (e) goals and objectives; and (f) discharge plans.
Where applicable, the supervisor also records diagnoses, medications and treatments, equipment in use and diet or dietary restrictions. If an item does not apply, the plan says "not applicable."

Task descriptions are written to match what the caregiver may lawfully do under the agency's scope of services (see SVC-01 to SVC-03, SAF-08). The plan must not assign tasks that the caregiver's role or training does not allow.

For clients with Medicaid waiver services, the supervisor makes sure the agency plan is consistent with the care plan or authorization issued by the waiver program and with the hours and tasks authorized (see OPS-04).
The supervisor reviews the finished plan with the client and the responsible party, explains it in plain language, and answers questions. The client may accept or refuse any service (see CR-01).

The supervisor completes the plan within seven working days after services first begin in the residence and files it in the client file (see ADM-05). If a plan cannot be completed on time, the supervisor tells the Administrator on the day the delay is known and documents the reason. The delay is entered in the QI log (SVC-10).

The agency gives the client or responsible party a copy of the plan, and tells the caregivers about the plan and any changes before their next visit. Caregivers keep or can access the current plan in the home or electronically.

Nursing plans: the RN supervisor reviews and updates each nursing service plan at least every 62 days. The review is dated and signed, and the physician is contacted when changes affect the physician's orders.

Other plans (personal care, companion/sitter): the service supervisor reviews and updates the plan at every supervisory visit (see SVC-06 and SVC-07), including a review of the daily service notes (SVC-09) and an update on the goals.

The supervisor revises the plan whenever the content changes, such as a change in functional limitations, services, times or frequency, duration, goals, diagnoses, medications, equipment, diet or discharge plan. Reasons include a client request, a change in condition, hospitalization, or a physician's order.

The client and responsible party are promptly informed of every change in the plan (see CR-01). The revision date, reason and the person informed are recorded, and caregivers are told of the change before their next visit.
When a client is being discharged or services are ending, the supervisor uses the discharge plan in the service plan to arrange the transition (see OPS-03).
The Administrator checks service plan timeliness and review dates monthly through the QI audits (SVC-10).

responsibilities.duty: Develops the plan with the client, responsible party and physician (nursing), completes it within seven working days, reviews it at each supervisory visit and revises it when needed.
Reviews and updates nursing plans at least every 62 days and keeps the physician informed.
Perform the tasks in the current plan, document them, and report any needed changes to the supervisor.
Audits plan timeliness and reviews, and takes corrective action when deadlines are missed.
Take part in planning, accept or refuse services, and report changes in condition.

documentation: Signed and dated service plan in the client file
Record of the date services started and the plan completion date
Physician contact notes for nursing clients
62-day nursing plan review records
Plan reviews and revisions recorded at supervisory visits
Records showing the client and caregivers were told of changes

policies.category: Rule .12 Client Rights, Responsibilities, and Complaints
policies.title: Client Rights and Responsibilities and Written Notice
policies.applies_to: All clients and responsible parties, the staff who complete service agreements and intake, service supervisors and caregivers.
policies.purpose: To make sure every client knows, in writing and at the right time, their rights and responsibilities, and that staff respect those rights in every visit.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] respects the rights of its clients and gives each client a written notice of rights and responsibilities. This policy meets Rule 111-8-65-.12(1): the agency has written policies and procedures on client rights and responsibilities, and on the handling and resolution of complaints (complaints are covered in CR-02). It also meets Rule 111-8-65-.12(2): a written notice of rights and responsibilities is provided to each client or responsible party, if applicable, when the service agreement described in Rule .09(2) is completed. The notice includes, among its items: (a) Rule .12(2)(a), the right to be informed about the plan of service and to participate in the planning; (b) Rule .12(2)(b), the right to be promptly and fully informed of any changes in the plan of service; (c) Rule .12(2)(c), the right to accept or refuse services; and (d) Rule .12(2)(d), the right to be fully informed of the charges for services. The notice also states the client's responsibility to report changes in condition. The remaining notice items are covered in CR-02 (supervisor and complaint contacts), CR-03 (confidentiality), CR-04 (respect for property and residence) and CR-05 (DCH contact information and inspection report). The client acknowledges receipt of the notice in the service agreement. Medicaid home and community-based services clients also receive the rights notices of their waiver program, and the agency follows the person-centered service planning requirements of 42 CFR 441.301(c).

definitions.definition: The written document, given to each client or responsible party when the service agreement is completed, that lists the client's rights and responsibilities required by Rule 111-8-65-.12(2).
A person legally or otherwise authorized to act for the client, where applicable.
A client who receives services paid through a Medicaid home and community-based waiver program (CCSP/SOURCE, ICWP, NOW/COMP).

procedures: The Administrator keeps one current written Notice of Rights and Responsibilities on the agency form [FORM NAME]. It states every item required by Rule .12(2), including those in (a) to (d) above and the items covered in CR-02 to CR-05, and states the client's duty to report changes in condition.
The notice is written in plain language, in a format and language the client can understand (see CR-06). Large-print copies, translated copies or an interpreter are provided when needed.

The staff member who completes the service agreement (see ADM-02 and ADM-03) gives the notice to each client or responsible party at the time the service agreement is completed. It is not delayed until after services start.

The staff member reviews the notice with the client or responsible party, explains each right in plain words and answers questions. In particular, the staff member explains the right to take part in planning (PLN-01), to be promptly told of plan changes, to accept or refuse services, and to be fully told of charges.

Plan participation: the service supervisor invites the client and responsible party to take part in developing and reviewing the service plan (PLN-01). The client's preferences are recorded in the plan.

Plan changes: when a service plan is changed, the service supervisor tells the client and responsible party promptly, before the change takes effect where possible, and records the date, how they were told, and who was told.

Accepting or refusing services: the client may accept or refuse any service or task at any time. A caregiver who is refused must not argue or pressure the client. The caregiver records the refusal in the daily note (SVC-09) and tells the supervisor the same day. The supervisor reviews the effect of the refusal on the client's safety with the client, and changes the plan if appropriate.

Charges: before services start, the client or responsible party is told in writing all charges for services, including rates, billing, minimum hours and any other fees, as set out in the service agreement. Changes in charges are given in writing before they apply.

The client or responsible party signs the acknowledgment of receipt in the service agreement. The signed acknowledgment, and a copy of the notice given, are put in the client file (ADM-05). If the client cannot or will not sign, the staff member documents this and the reason.
The client or responsible party is given a copy of the notice to keep. For clients who are not able to read it, staff read it aloud and document that they did so.

For Medicaid waiver clients, staff confirm that the client has received the waiver program's rights notices from the program or support coordinator. The agency gives a copy of its own notice and honors the rights described in both (see OPS-04). The service plan is developed in a person-centered way consistent with 42 CFR 441.301(c).
Caregivers receive training on client rights at orientation and in annual in-service (ADM-13, ADM-14). Caregivers must honor client rights in every visit.
A client who says a right has been violated is directed to the complaint procedure (CR-02). Staff may not retaliate against a client for raising a concern.

The Administrator checks that the signed notice is in each new client file as part of the monthly QI audit (SVC-10), and reviews the notice at least annually with the governing body review of policies (GB-01) to make sure it is current.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the current notice, makes sure it contains every item required by Rule .12(2), and audits delivery.
Give and explain the notice when the service agreement is completed and get the acknowledgment.
Involves the client in planning, informs the client promptly of plan changes, and responds to refusals of service.
Respect client rights, honor refusals, and document and report them.
Take part in planning and report changes in the client's condition.

documentation: Current Notice of Rights and Responsibilities form
Signed acknowledgment of receipt in the service agreement, filed in the client file
Records of plan changes and of who was told, and when
Documentation of service refusals in daily notes and supervisor follow-up
Written disclosure of charges
Records of waiver program rights notices received by waiver clients

policies.category: Rule .12 Client Rights, Responsibilities, and Complaints
policies.title: Complaints and Grievances; Supervisor Contact Information
policies.applies_to: All clients and responsible parties, the Administrator, the designated complaint handler, service supervisors and all staff.
policies.purpose: To make sure clients know who supervises their care and how to reach that person, and that every complaint is received, investigated within a reasonable time, resolved if possible, recorded and used to improve services, without retaliation.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] tells every client who supervises their services and how to reach that person, and accepts and investigates complaints promptly and fairly. This policy meets Rule 111-8-65-.12(2)(e): the client has the right to be informed of the name, business telephone number and business address of the person supervising the services and how to contact that person. This policy also meets Rule 111-8-65-.12(2)(f): the client has the right to be informed of the complaint procedures, to submit complaints without fear of discrimination or retaliation, and to have them investigated by the provider within a reasonable period of time. The complaint procedure in the client notice includes the name, business address and telephone number of the person designated by the agency to handle complaints and questions. Complaints may be oral or written. The agency gives the client the agency telephone number for information, questions and complaints. Every complaint and its resolution is recorded, kept as required by Rule .09(4)(d), and entered into the quality improvement program (SVC-10). Clients are also told that unresolved licensing complaints may be directed to DCH.

definitions.definition: Any expression of dissatisfaction or concern about the agency, its services or its staff, made orally or in writing by a client, responsible party, family member or other person.
The person designated by the agency to receive and handle complaints and questions: [COMPLAINT HANDLER NAME AND TITLE], [ADDRESS], [PHONE].
The person who supervises the client's services: the service supervisor or RN supervisor assigned to that client.
Any adverse action, such as reduced service, threats, rudeness, schedule changes or discharge, taken because a person made a complaint.

procedures: The Administrator designates in writing the complaint handler, with business address and telephone number, and records the designation in the policy manual. Any change is made in writing, and clients are informed of the change.

At the time the service agreement is completed, the staff member gives the client or responsible party the written notice of rights (CR-01). The notice must show: the name, business telephone number and business address of the person supervising the client's services, and how to contact that person.

The same notice includes the complaint procedure and the name, business address and telephone number of the complaint handler, and the agency's general telephone number for information, questions and complaints.

The staff member reviews this information with the client, including that complaints may be made orally or in writing and that the client will not suffer discrimination or retaliation for making a complaint.

If the supervisor assigned to a client changes, the agency informs the client of the new supervisor's name, telephone number and address before or at the time of the change, and records the notification in the client file.

The notice tells clients that if they are not satisfied with the agency's response, or if they believe the agency has violated licensing rules, they can contact the Georgia Department of Community Health, Healthcare Facility Regulation Division. The DCH address and telephone number are shown in the client notice (see CR-05).

Any staff member who receives a complaint, orally or in writing, writes it down on the complaint form [FORM NAME] the same day (what happened, who is involved, date, how the person can be contacted) and gives it to the complaint handler within one business day. Staff must not discourage, dismiss or argue with the person.
If the complaint involves suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, or a client in immediate danger, staff follow SAF-01 and SAF-07 right away, in addition to this policy.
The complaint handler acknowledges the complaint to the person who made it within [2] business days, and explains how it will be investigated.

The complaint handler investigates within a reasonable period of time. As the agency's internal standard, the investigation is completed within [14] calendar days unless the complaint is complex, in which case the person is told of the delay and the reason. The investigation includes talking with the complainant, the staff involved and others with knowledge, and reviewing the client file and daily notes.

The complaint handler may remove staff from the client's home during the investigation if needed for the client's safety or to prevent retaliation. The agency never retaliates or discriminates against a client, family member or staff member who makes a complaint in good faith.

The complaint handler tells the complainant the result and any action taken, orally or in writing as the person prefers, and records the date and how the person was informed. If the complaint cannot be resolved, the file records why and what the person was told about other options, including contacting DCH.

The complaint handler records in the complaint file the complaint, the investigation, the resolution (or reason it could not be resolved), actions taken and the dates. The complaint file is kept for at least five years, in line with Rule .09(4)(d).

The complaint handler enters each complaint and its resolution in the QI log within [2] business days of receipt, and notes any problem with care that was identified and any corrective action (SVC-10).
The Administrator reviews complaint trends monthly, and reports them to the governing body at least quarterly with the QI log. The Administrator uses findings to retrain staff or revise policies.

At each supervisory visit, the service supervisor asks the client or responsible party whether they have any concerns or complaints and whether they know how to reach the supervisor and the complaint handler, and records the answer.

responsibilities.duty: Designates the complaint handler, makes sure complaints are investigated and resolved, prevents retaliation, and reports trends to the governing body.
Receives, acknowledges, investigates and resolves complaints, records them and enters them in the QI log.
Is available to clients, tells clients how to reach them, and asks about concerns at each supervisory visit.
Accept and forward every complaint the same day without retaliation or discouragement.

documentation: Client notice showing the supervisor's name, business telephone and address, the complaint procedure and the complaint handler's name, address and telephone
Written designation of the complaint handler
Complaint forms and the complaint file, including investigation notes and resolution, kept at least five years
QI log entries for complaints and corrective actions
Records of supervisor changes communicated to clients
Supervisory visit notes on client concerns

policies.category: Rule .12 Client Rights, Responsibilities, and Complaints
policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, volunteers and students, and the Administrator and privacy officer. All client information in any form.
policies.purpose: To protect the confidentiality of client records and information, tell clients about that right, and limit disclosure to the people and purposes allowed by Georgia rules and, where it applies, HIPAA.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps each client's record and personal information confidential. This policy meets Rule 111-8-65-.12(2)(g): the client has the right of confidentiality of the client record, and the written notice of rights states this right. Disclosure of client records is limited to the persons permitted by Rule .09(4)(b): appropriate agency staff, the client, the responsible party, the client's physician or other provider, the Department of Community Health, persons authorized in writing by the client, or a subpoena. The agency names a privacy officer and trains all staff on privacy at hire. Caregivers do not discuss clients on social media or with people who are not agency staff. Where the agency is a covered entity under HIPAA (for example because it bills Medicaid electronically), it also follows 45 CFR Part 160 and 45 CFR Part 164, including the privacy practices notice (45 CFR 164.520), administrative requirements (45 CFR 164.530) and breach response and notification under 45 CFR Part 164, Subpart D.

definitions.definition: All information in the client file kept under Rule 111-8-65-.09(4)(a), in paper or electronic form (see ADM-05).
Individually identifiable health information about a client, in any form, that is held by the agency.
The person designated by the agency to develop and carry out privacy practices and receive privacy complaints: [PRIVACY OFFICER NAME], [PHONE].
A health care provider that electronically transmits health information in connection with covered transactions, such as Medicaid billing, and so is subject to HIPAA.
An unauthorized acquisition, access, use or disclosure of PHI that compromises its security or privacy, unless an exception applies under 45 CFR Part 164, Subpart D.

procedures: The governing body designates a privacy officer in writing. The Administrator [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] acts as privacy officer unless another person is named.

At the time the service agreement is completed, staff give the client or responsible party the written notice of rights, which states the right of confidentiality of the client record (CR-01). Staff explain it and record that they did.

If the agency is a HIPAA covered entity, it also gives each client its Notice of Privacy Practices in line with 45 CFR 164.520 at the first service delivery, makes a good-faith effort to get a written acknowledgment of receipt, and posts the notice in the office and on any agency website.

Every employee, contractor and volunteer signs a confidentiality agreement and is trained on this policy at hire, before first contact with client information, and again at annual in-service (ADM-13, ADM-14). Training is recorded in the personnel file.
Staff may use or see client information only as needed to do their jobs (minimum necessary). Caregivers see only the information on their assigned clients.

Disclosure of the client's record is limited to the following, as allowed by Rule .09(4)(b): appropriate agency staff; the client; the responsible party; the client's physician or other provider; the Department of Community Health; persons authorized in writing by the client; and persons who present a subpoena.

For a release to a person authorized by the client, staff get a signed, dated written authorization that names the person, the information to be released, the purpose and an expiration date. The authorization is kept in the client file, and the release is logged.

For a subpoena, staff do not release records at once. They send the subpoena to the Administrator, who verifies it and, if needed, consults legal counsel, and then releases only what is required. The date, requestor and records released are logged (see ADM-06).

Staff do not discuss clients, or post, photograph or describe them, on social media, in text messages on personal apps, or in public places. Staff do not discuss clients with anyone who is not agency staff or an authorized person, including family members who are not the responsible party.

Caregivers keep any paper records, such as daily notes and schedules, in their possession and out of view, and turn them in at the end of the work week or as directed. Phones and devices used for client information are password protected, and lost devices are reported at once.
Paper records are kept in locked cabinets and electronic records are protected by passwords, access limited by job role, and backups (see ADM-06). Staff do not leave records unattended in vehicles.
Staff report any suspected unauthorized access, use or disclosure of client information to the privacy officer immediately, and no later than the end of the same workday.

The privacy officer investigates, contains the problem, and decides if a breach has occurred. If the agency is a covered entity, the privacy officer follows 45 CFR Part 164, Subpart D, in notifying affected clients, the federal Department of Health and Human Services and, where required, the media, within the required times. The incident is recorded under SAF-02.
Clients with privacy questions or complaints are directed to the privacy officer or the complaint procedure (CR-02). No client is retaliated against for raising a privacy concern.

Staff who violate this policy are subject to corrective action up to and including termination (PER-03). The privacy officer keeps records of privacy training, disclosures, breach evaluations and sanctions for the retention period in ADM-06.

responsibilities.duty: Oversees privacy practices, trains staff, approves non-routine disclosures, investigates breaches and handles privacy complaints.
Makes sure records are kept secure and disclosed only as allowed, and applies sanctions for violations.
Give the client the notice of rights, and the Notice of Privacy Practices where applicable, and record that they did.
Keep client information confidential, access it only as needed for their job, avoid social media or other non-staff discussions, and report any unauthorized disclosure at once.

documentation: Signed confidentiality agreements and privacy training records in personnel files
Written designation of the privacy officer
Client acknowledgment of the notice of rights and, where applicable, of the Notice of Privacy Practices
Signed client authorizations for release of information, and a disclosure log
Subpoena handling records
Breach evaluation and notification records, and incident reports

policies.category: Rule .12 Client Rights, Responsibilities, and Complaints
policies.title: Respect for Property, Client Funds, Gifts, Bonding and Exploitation Prevention
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, supervisors, the Administrator and owners of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect each client's property, home and money, to make sure anyone with unlimited access to a client's personal funds is bonded, and to prevent financial exploitation of clients.
policies.policy: This policy meets Rule 111-8-65-.12(2)(h) (right to have property and residence treated with respect) and Rule 111-8-65-.03(g) (home management: any employee authorized unlimited access to a client's personal funds for home management must be bonded through the provider). [AGENCY NAME] treats every client's residence and belongings with respect and tells each client of this right in the written notice of rights and responsibilities (CR-01). No employee may have unlimited access to a client's personal funds unless the employee is bonded through [AGENCY NAME]. A universal (blanket) bond covering all such employees is acceptable. Access to client funds is allowed only when the client has authorized it in writing in the service agreement. No caregiver may accept gifts, loans or bequests from a client or a client's family, or add themselves to a client's bank or other accounts. Every caregiver is a mandated reporter of suspected financial exploitation and follows SAF-01 and O.C.G.A. § 30-5-4.

definitions.definition: Household tasks that may include handling a client's personal funds, for example shopping or paying a bill on the client's behalf, as defined in Rule 111-8-65-.03(g).
Authority to use a client's cash, bank or debit cards, checks or accounts without a specific per-transaction limit or the client's approval of each transaction.
Covered by a fidelity (surety) bond purchased and maintained by [AGENCY NAME] that protects clients against employee dishonesty. A universal bond covering all employees meets this requirement.
Improper use of a client's money, property or resources for another person's benefit, including theft, undue influence, forged signatures and coerced gifts or loans.

procedures: The Administrator buys and maintains a fidelity bond or universal bond through [AGENCY NAME] that covers every employee who may have unlimited access to client funds. The Administrator keeps the bond certificate in the administrative file and checks the bond's limits and expiration date at each annual policy review (GB-01).

During intake, the Intake Coordinator asks whether the client wants help with money-related home management. The default is no access to client funds. Access is offered only if the client or the client's legal representative requests it.

If the client requests access to funds, the RN Supervisor or Administrator writes the scope into the service agreement (ADM-02): who may handle funds, for what purposes, any dollar limit, and how receipts are returned. The client or legal representative signs it. No staff member may handle client funds before this written authorization is in the file.

Before an employee is assigned to a client with unlimited access to funds, the Administrator confirms the employee is covered by the bond, has a completed background determination (PER-01) and has completed orientation (ADM-13), including this policy.

If a client's needs change so that a caregiver would handle funds beyond what the agreement authorizes, the RN Supervisor revises the service agreement in writing before the caregiver does so (ADM-03).

When handling funds, the caregiver keeps the client's money separate from all personal money. The caregiver gets an itemized receipt for each purchase, returns change and receipts to the client, and records the amount in and out on the agency Client Funds Log, which the client signs when able.
Caregivers never use a client's debit or credit card, PIN, checks or online account passwords for their own purposes, and never keep those items beyond the errand.
Caregivers do not borrow money or items from a client, lend money to a client, sell items to or buy items from a client, or ask a client to give them or their family money or property.

Caregivers decline gifts, loans and bequests from clients and their families. A caregiver who is offered one tells the supervisor the same day. The supervisor documents the offer and arranges to return or decline any item already given.

No caregiver may add themselves or a family member to a client's bank account, credit card, deed, vehicle title, insurance policy or will, or act as the client's agent, representative payee or power of attorney, unless the Administrator has reviewed the arrangement in writing and confirmed it is lawful and not a conflict of interest.

Caregivers treat the client's home and property with respect. They do not use the client's phone, computer, vehicle, food or supplies for personal use. They do not enter areas of the home the client has asked them to avoid. They do not move or discard belongings without the client's permission.

If a caregiver damages or loses client property, they report it to the supervisor the same day. The supervisor documents the incident on the incident report form (SAF-02), tells the client, and the Administrator handles any resolution.

If a client or family reports missing money or property, the supervisor documents the report, tells the Administrator the same day, reviews the Client Funds Log and receipts, and does not accuse anyone before the facts are reviewed. If theft or exploitation is suspected, the Administrator follows SAF-01.

Any employee who has reasonable cause to believe a client has been financially exploited tells the Administrator immediately. The Administrator reports, or causes a report to be made, to Adult Protective Services at [APS HOTLINE] and to law enforcement as required by O.C.G.A. § 30-5-4. Any employee may also report directly, and reports made in good faith are protected by § 30-5-4(c). Retaliation against a reporter is prohibited.

The RN Supervisor reviews the Client Funds Log and receipts for each client with fund access at each supervisory home visit (SVC-06, SVC-07) and signs the log. Any discrepancy is referred to the Administrator the same day.
Violations of this policy lead to discipline up to and including termination and referral to law enforcement. The Administrator documents the action in the personnel record (ADM-07).

responsibilities.duty: Approve this policy and make sure the bond is funded and kept in force.
Maintain the bond, confirm bonded status before assignment, receive and act on reports, and make required reports to APS and law enforcement.
Document fund authorizations in the service agreement, review the Client Funds Log at supervisory visits, and investigate property complaints.
Handle funds only as authorized in writing, keep receipts and logs, decline gifts, respect property, and report suspected exploitation.
Decide whether to authorize fund access, review receipts and logs, and report concerns to the agency, DCH or APS.

documentation: Bond or universal bond certificate
Written fund-access authorization in the signed service agreement
Client Funds Log and itemized receipts
Gift, loan or bequest offer notes and supervisor follow-up
Property damage or loss incident reports
Exploitation report records (APS and law enforcement)
Orientation sign-off on this policy

policies.category: Rule .12 Client Rights, Responsibilities, and Complaints
policies.title: DCH Contact Notice and Copy of Inspection Report
policies.applies_to: Administrator, RN Supervisor, intake and office staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure every client knows how to reach the Georgia Department of Community Health (DCH) and can obtain the agency's most recent licensure inspection report.
policies.policy: This policy meets Rule 111-8-65-.12(2)(i) (right to receive written notice of the address and telephone number of the state licensing authority, with an explanation that DCH is responsible for licensing the provider and investigating client complaints that appear to violate licensing regulations) and Rule 111-8-65-.12(2)(j) (right to obtain a copy of the provider's most recent completed report of licensure inspection on written request). [AGENCY NAME] gives each client the DCH notice in writing when the service agreement is completed, as part of the notice of rights and responsibilities (CR-01). The DCH phone number is also in the service agreement (ADM-02). On a client's written request, [AGENCY NAME] provides a copy of its most recent completed inspection report after the plan of correction has been filed, and may charge a reasonable copying fee. The Administrator checks the full text of Rule .12(2)(j) and any later items in .12(2) against the live rule at each annual policy review, because the excerpt used to prepare this policy was cut off.

definitions.definition: The Georgia Department of Community Health, Healthcare Facility Regulation Division, which licenses and inspects private home care providers.
The written report of the latest DCH licensure inspection of [AGENCY NAME] for which the plan of correction has been filed.
The written plan [AGENCY NAME] submits to DCH within ten days of receiving an inspection report (LIC-03).

procedures: The Administrator keeps one approved DCH Contact Notice. It gives the DCH Healthcare Facility Regulation Division address [DCH ADDRESS] and telephone number [DCH PHONE], and states that DCH licenses private home care providers and investigates client complaints that appear to violate licensing regulations. The Administrator checks the address and phone number against the DCH website at each annual review and whenever DCH announces a change.

The RN Supervisor or intake staff gives the DCH Contact Notice to each client or legal representative at the time the service agreement is completed, with the notice of rights and responsibilities (CR-01), and explains it in plain language or in the client's language (CR-06).

The client or representative signs an acknowledgment of receipt of the notice. A copy of the notice and the signed acknowledgment go in the client record (ADM-05). If the client declines to sign, the staff member notes the refusal, date and time in the record.
The DCH phone number is entered in the service agreement form (ADM-02) so that it appears in two places: the agreement and the rights notice.
The Administrator posts the DCH Contact Notice in the office reception area and includes it in the client information packet.

Clients may request the inspection report orally or in writing, but [AGENCY NAME] provides the report on written request. If a client requests it orally, staff offer to help the client write the request and do not refuse the request.
Staff who receive a request send it to the Administrator the same business day. The Administrator logs the date received, requester and date provided on the Inspection Report Request Log.

The Administrator confirms the plan of correction for that inspection has been filed with DCH before releasing the report. If it has not been filed, the Administrator tells the client when it will be available and provides the report as soon as the plan is filed.

The Administrator provides a complete copy of the most recent completed inspection report within a reasonable time, normally within 5 business days of the written request or of filing the plan of correction, whichever is later.

The Administrator may charge a reasonable copying fee set out in a written fee schedule approved by the Governing Body. The fee does not exceed the actual cost of copying. The fee schedule is given to the client before copying, and no client is denied a copy for inability to pay a reasonable fee without Administrator review.
The Administrator keeps a complete copy of the most recent inspection report and the filed plan of correction in the office where staff can retrieve it quickly (LIC-03).

At each annual policy review (GB-01), the Administrator checks the text of Rule 111-8-65-.12(2)(i), (j) and any later paragraph of .12(2) against the published rule. If the rule has changed or lists additional items, the Administrator revises the notice and this policy and submits them to the Governing Body for approval.
The RN Supervisor reminds clients of the DCH notice and their right to contact DCH at each supervisory home visit (SVC-06, SVC-07) and answers questions about the notice.
No employee may discourage or retaliate against a client who contacts DCH or requests an inspection report (CR-02).

responsibilities.duty: Maintain the DCH Contact Notice, process report requests, set the copy fee schedule, and verify the rule text annually.
Deliver the notice and obtain the signed acknowledgment at service agreement completion, and forward report requests the same day.
Approve the notice, the fee schedule and annual revisions.
Contact DCH with concerns, and request the inspection report in writing if wanted.

documentation: DCH Contact Notice (current approved version)
Signed acknowledgment of receipt in the client record
Service agreement showing the DCH phone number
Inspection Report Request Log
Copy of the most recent inspection report and filed plan of correction
Copy-fee schedule
Annual rule-text verification note

policies.category: Rule .12 Client Rights, Responsibilities, and Complaints
policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Language Access
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, supervisors, applicants and owners of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] serves clients and employs staff without discrimination, and that clients with limited English proficiency or disabilities can understand and use the agency's notices, agreements and complaint procedures.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate in accepting or serving clients, or in hiring, assigning, promoting or disciplining staff, on the basis of race, color, national origin, language, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, age, disability, genetic information, marital status or any other protected basis. [AGENCY NAME] provides interpreters and translated notices at no charge to clients with limited English proficiency. It offers the written notice of rights and responsibilities, the service agreement and the complaint procedures required by Rule 111-8-65-.12 in accessible formats. It makes reasonable accommodations for clients and employees with disabilities. This policy follows Title VI of the Civil Rights Act (42 USC 2000d), the Americans with Disabilities Act (42 USC 12101 et seq.) and Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act (45 CFR 92), to the extent each applies to [AGENCY NAME].

definitions.definition: Having a limited ability to read, speak, write or understand English well enough to take part in services without language help.

A person who is competent in both languages and trained in interpreting. A client's minor child is not used as an interpreter, and an adult family member is used only if the client requests it and the agency has offered a qualified interpreter.

A change to a process, format or practice that allows a person with a disability an equal opportunity to receive services or perform a job, unless it causes undue hardship or fundamentally alters the service.
A format a person can use, such as large print, Braille, audio, plain-language summary, or reading aloud.

procedures: The Administrator posts a nondiscrimination statement in the office and includes it in the client information packet and on the agency website, if any. The statement says services and employment are provided without discrimination and tells clients how to file a complaint with the Administrator (CR-02) and with DCH (CR-05).

At intake, the Intake Coordinator asks each client or representative what language they prefer to speak and read, whether they need an interpreter or an accessible format, and whether they need any accommodation. The answers are recorded in the client record (ADM-05 and OPS-01).

Services are never refused, limited or conditioned because of a protected characteristic. Acceptance decisions are based only on the criteria in ADM-01, including whether the agency can safely meet the client's needs within its licensed scope and staffing.

If a client needs language help, the Intake Coordinator arranges a qualified interpreter (in person, by telephone or video service) at no charge to the client for the intake, the service agreement signing, the rights notice review, the service plan and any complaint. The Administrator keeps a list of available interpreter services and phone numbers.

Staff do not use a minor child as an interpreter except in an emergency when no qualified interpreter is available. Staff use an adult family member or friend only at the client's informed request, and the RN Supervisor documents that the client was offered a free interpreter.

The Administrator has the notice of rights and responsibilities, the DCH contact notice and the complaint procedure translated into the languages most commonly encountered in the agency's service area, and offers a verbal interpreter for any language not translated. The Administrator keeps translated forms in the client record forms binder.

For clients with vision, hearing, cognitive or literacy limitations, the RN Supervisor offers large print, reading aloud, written-note communication, a sign language interpreter or a plain-language summary. The RN Supervisor confirms that the client understands the notice of rights and the service agreement before signing, and documents how this was done.

Reasonable accommodations are requested by the client or employee orally or in writing. The RN Supervisor (for clients) or Administrator (for employees) responds within 5 business days, documents the request, the decision and any alternative offered, and reviews the accommodation periodically.

Caregivers are assigned without regard to protected characteristics. A client's request for a caregiver of a particular gender for personal care tasks is handled under OPS-02 as a privacy and dignity preference, and the RN Supervisor documents it.

Job postings, interviews, hiring and promotion decisions use only job-related qualifications under ADM-09, ADM-10 and ADM-11. The Administrator does not ask applicants about protected characteristics.
All employees are trained on this policy at orientation (ADM-13) and in annual in-service (ADM-14), including how to arrange an interpreter and how to report discrimination.

Any client, employee or applicant who believes discrimination occurred may complain to the Administrator or the Governing Body orally or in writing without fear of retaliation. If the complaint is about the Administrator, the complaint goes directly to the Governing Body. The complaint is handled under CR-02 and resolved promptly.
The Administrator reviews complaints, interpreter use and accommodation requests annually as part of the quality improvement program (SVC-10) and reports trends to the Governing Body.

responsibilities.duty: Approve this policy, fund interpreter and translation services, and hear complaints about the Administrator.
Maintain the nondiscrimination statement, interpreter resources and translated forms, handle accommodation and discrimination complaints, and train staff.
Identify language and accommodation needs at intake, arrange interpreters and accessible formats, and confirm client understanding.
Treat all clients with respect, tell the supervisor when a client cannot understand or communicate, and do not act as interpreter unless approved.

documentation: Nondiscrimination statement as posted
Intake language and accommodation record
Interpreter use log (date, language, interpreter, purpose)
Translated rights notice, service agreement and complaint procedure
Accommodation request and decision records
Discrimination complaint records
Orientation and in-service sign-in sheets

policies.title: Licensure, Location, License Display, Advertising and Notice of Changes
policies.applies_to: Owners, Governing Body, Administrator and all staff of [AGENCY NAME] who advertise or describe the agency's services
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] operates only with a valid Georgia DCH private home care provider license, displays it, advertises only what it is licensed to do, and gives DCH timely notice of changes.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is licensed under the Georgia private home care provider rules, Rule 111-8-65, adopted under O.C.G.A. § 31-7-300 et seq. (Rule .01).
