[AGENCY NAME] does not operate, accept clients or provide services until DCH has issued a license or a provisional license (Rule .05(1)). Before a new license is issued, the owner complies with Chapter 111-8-12 (Rule .05(1)(b)). A Certificate of Need is not required for a license limited to private home care services (Rule .07(2)). [AGENCY NAME] does not rely on the exemptions in Rule .07, which cover an individual who personally provides services without agents, employees, contractors or financially interested referrals, licensed home health agencies and personal care home staff. Each office location is separately licensed, and the license is displayed at that location (Rule .05(2)(a)-(b)). The license is not assignable or transferable. It is returned to DCH on a change of name, location, ownership or governing body, and DCH receives 15 days' advance written notice of a location change (Rule .05(2)(c)). All advertising is truthful and describes only the services licensed and offered and the service area stated in the application.

definitions.definition: An entity licensed by DCH under Rule 111-8-65 to provide nursing services, personal care services or companion/sitter services in a client's residence, as defined in Rule .03(o)-(p).
A license DCH may issue to a new provider for a limited time or to an existing provider with an acceptable plan of improvement (Rule .05(1)(c)).
Any person with a 10% or greater interest in [AGENCY NAME] (Rule .03(l)).
The office address named on the license. Each office is licensed separately.

procedures: The Governing Body does not authorize operations to start, and no employee accepts a client, schedules a visit or collects payment, until the Administrator confirms in writing that the license or provisional license has been issued by DCH and records the license number and effective dates in the administrative file.

Before the initial application is submitted, the Administrator confirms that each owner (10% or greater interest) has met the requirements of Chapter 111-8-12 and that the owner records check application is complete (LIC-02).

If DCH issues a provisional license, the Administrator records the end date and any conditions or plan of improvement, assigns each condition to a named person with a due date, and reports progress to the Governing Body at each meeting.

The Administrator displays the original license in a conspicuous place at the licensed office location where clients and visitors can see it. The Administrator keeps a copy in the licensure file and gives a copy to a client on request.

The Administrator does not use or display the license at any other address. If the agency plans to open an additional office, the Governing Body files a separate application for that location and the new office does not operate until its own license is issued.

The Administrator submits written notice to DCH at least 15 days before moving the licensed location, and does not move or begin services at the new location until DCH approves, if the location change requires a new license or an updated license from DCH. The Administrator confirms the DCH requirement in writing with HFRD before the move.

Before any change of agency name, ownership or governing body, the Administrator contacts DCH HFRD in writing, asks what filing is required, and returns the existing license to DCH as the rule requires. The agency does not treat the license as transferable to a new owner, a new entity or a buyer.

The Administrator updates DCH within 15 days (agency standard) of any change in the Administrator, mailing address, telephone or other contact information in the license file, and notes the date in the licensure file. See LIC-06 for other state notices.

Before any ad, website, brochure, social media post, business card, directory listing or marketing script is used, the Administrator reviews and approves it. It states only services actually offered and licensed: nursing services, personal care and companion/sitter services as stated in the application and in ADM-01.

The agency advertises nursing services only while the Administrator has confirmed a Georgia-licensed registered nurse is employed or contracted as RN Supervisor (SVC-01). If the RN Supervisor position becomes vacant, the Administrator removes or suspends nursing advertising until the position is filled.

All advertising states the service area stated in the application and does not promise services outside it. It does not make claims about outcomes, state approval or Medicaid enrollment that the agency cannot document.
The Administrator keeps a dated copy of each advertisement and a list of where it ran in the licensure file for at least 5 years.
Staff who answer inquiries use the approved services script and do not offer services outside the license. They refer questions about licensure to the Administrator.

The Administrator reviews licensure status, displayed license, advertising and location information at each annual policy review (GB-01) and reports any gap to the Governing Body, which corrects it within 10 days.

responsibilities.duty: Decide on new locations, name, ownership and governing body changes, and make sure DCH is notified and the license is returned as required.
Keep the license current and displayed, approve all advertising, file notices with DCH and maintain the licensure file.
Confirm nursing services are offered only when the RN supervision requirement is met.
Describe services accurately and refer licensure questions to the Administrator.

documentation: License or provisional license with number and dates
Chapter 111-8-12 compliance record for each owner
Provisional license conditions and progress tracker
15-day location change notice and DCH response
Name, ownership and governing body change filings and license return receipts
Approved advertising file with dates
Annual licensure compliance check

policies.title: Applications, Renewal, Fees and Truthful Statements
policies.applies_to: Owners, Governing Body and Administrator of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure all applications, renewals and fee payments to DCH are complete, timely, accurate and truthful.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] files its initial application and each renewal on DCH forms. The initial application includes the application fee, the license fee set by the Board of Community Health, the owner records check application, and a description of the services to be provided and the geographic area to be served (Rule 111-8-65-.06(1)). Renewals are filed periodically with an updated description of services and area (Rule .06(2)). All licensure fees are paid in full before the license is issued. DCH's checklist lists a $300 application processing fee that is non-refundable; the Administrator confirms the current amount on the DCH form before payment. Fees are reasonable and may be refunded for good cause (Rule .06(3)). Every statement in an application, renewal or supporting document is truthful, because DCH may refuse a license for false statements (Rule .06(4)). Each owner (10% or greater interest) must satisfy Chapter 111-8-12 before a new license issues (Rule .05(1)(b)).

definitions.definition: The fee due when the application is submitted. The DCH checklist lists $300, non-refundable; the amount on the current DCH form controls.
The fee set by the Board of Community Health that must be paid in full before the license is issued.
The records check application for each owner that must accompany the initial application.
The counties or other area in which [AGENCY NAME] states it will provide services.

procedures: The Administrator downloads the current application forms and checklist from the DCH HFRD Private Home Care Program page and does not use forms from consultants or older files. The Administrator confirms the current application fee and license fee amounts with DCH before payment and records the source and date.

The Administrator identifies every owner with 10% or greater interest and obtains each owner's legal name, address and ownership percentage in writing. Each owner completes the owner records check application and the Chapter 111-8-12 requirements before the application is submitted.

The Administrator prepares the written description of services and geographic area. It lists only the services the agency will provide (nursing, personal care and/or companion/sitter) and only counties the agency can staff and supervise within the 92-day and 122-day visit schedules (SVC-06, SVC-07) and in accordance with ADM-08.

A second person (an owner or Governing Body member) reviews each completed application against the DCH checklist and against source documents (business registration, ownership records, resumes, qualifications). The reviewer initials the checklist.

The responsible owner signs the application only after the signer has read it and confirmed that each statement is true and complete. No statement is estimated, exaggerated or filled in without proof. If information is unknown, the Administrator asks DCH rather than guessing.

The Administrator submits the application with all required fees and attachments by a trackable method and keeps a complete copy of the filed application, proof of payment and proof of delivery in the licensure file.

The Administrator pays all fees in full before the license is issued and does not begin services until the license or provisional license is in hand (LIC-01). The Administrator tracks DCH correspondence and replies to requests for more information within the deadline DCH gives, or within 10 days if no deadline is given.

If DCH denies or delays the application, the Administrator informs the Governing Body immediately. The agency does not operate while the application is pending. Hearing and appeal rights are handled under LIC-04.

The Administrator asks DCH in writing for a refund when a fee was paid in error or there is another good cause (Rule .06(3)), keeps the request and response, and does not assume a refund is available for the non-refundable application processing fee.

The Administrator enters the license expiration date and the renewal due date in the agency compliance calendar with reminders at 120, 90 and 60 days before expiration, and confirms the renewal date and process with HFRD.

At least 90 days before renewal, the Administrator updates the description of services and area to match actual operations (current services, counties served, any changes) and has the Governing Body review it.

The renewal form is checked and signed using the same truthfulness review described in steps 4 and 5. The Administrator submits it with the renewal fee at least 30 days before the due date, keeps proof of filing and confirms receipt with DCH.

If the agency finds that a prior application, renewal or other statement to DCH was inaccurate, the Administrator tells the Governing Body within 2 business days and corrects it in writing with DCH promptly.

Anyone who knowingly makes a false statement to DCH is subject to discipline up to and including removal from the agency's governing or management role. The Governing Body also takes corrective action, since DCH may refuse a license for false statements.

responsibilities.duty: Provide accurate ownership information, review and sign applications and renewals, and fund fees.
Prepare and submit applications and renewals, confirm fee amounts, manage the compliance calendar and respond to DCH requests.
Verify the application against the checklist and source documents before signature.

documentation: Complete copy of filed application and renewal packets
DCH checklist with reviewer initials
Fee payment records and refund requests
Owner records check applications and Chapter 111-8-12 compliance records
Description of services and geographic area (each version)
Compliance calendar with renewal dates
DCH correspondence log

policies.title: DCH Inspections and Plans of Correction
policies.applies_to: Administrator, RN Supervisor, office staff and all employees of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] cooperates fully with DCH inspections and submits an acceptable written plan of correction on time.
policies.policy: DCH inspects private home care providers periodically (Rule 111-8-65-.08(1)). Accredited providers may be exempt from some inspections, but [AGENCY NAME] does not assume an exemption and prepares for inspection at all times. Submitting an application or renewal is consent to entry by DCH during regular business hours, and [AGENCY NAME] gives DCH access to its premises, records, staff and consenting clients (Rule .08(2)). All staff cooperate without unreasonable delay (Rule .08(3)). [AGENCY NAME] submits an acceptable written plan of correction within ten days of receiving the written inspection report, and may explain or dispute findings in the plan (Rule .08(4)). The Governing Body and Administrator treat the inspection report as a priority document and correct each cited deficiency.

definitions.definition: The hours [AGENCY NAME] posts at its licensed office, [OFFICE HOURS], during which DCH may enter without prior notice.
The report DCH sends to the provider listing the findings of the inspection.
The provider's written response stating how and when each cited deficiency will be corrected, and any explanation or dispute of a finding.

procedures: The Administrator posts the office's regular business hours at the entrance and keeps the office staffed by the Administrator or a designated manager during those hours. The designee is named in writing, and staff know to call the Administrator immediately when DCH arrives.

The Administrator assigns one person (and a backup) to receive all DCH mail, e-mail and fax. That person logs the date of receipt of any inspection report or notice on the day it arrives and gives it to the Administrator the same day.

Maintain an inspection-ready binder or file, updated monthly by the Administrator, containing: the license and renewal; the policy manual; personnel files with background, health screening, licensure and training records; the client list; sample service agreements and service plans; supervisory visit records; training records; complaint log; incident reports; and the last inspection report and plan of correction.

When surveyors arrive, the staff member on duty asks for identification, notes the time and names, and notifies the Administrator immediately. The Administrator or designee meets surveyors promptly, conducts the entrance conference, and provides workspace.

The Administrator gives DCH access to the premises and to requested records, including client and personnel records (Rule .08(2)), and keeps a list of documents provided. The Administrator makes copies for DCH when requested and keeps a duplicate set of anything provided.

Staff interviewed by DCH answer truthfully and without unreasonable delay. Staff are not coached to give false answers and are not retaliated against for what they tell surveyors. A manager may be present during staff interviews unless the surveyor or the employee objects.

For client interviews or home visits, the RN Supervisor asks the client's consent in advance and does not require a client to take part. DCH has access to consenting clients only. The Administrator does not discourage a client from speaking with surveyors.
At the exit conference, the Administrator takes notes, asks for clarification of any cited deficiency, and tells the Governing Body of the preliminary findings within 1 business day.

On the day the written report is received, the Administrator writes the receipt date on the report, calendars the due date (10 days from receipt) and an internal target of day 7, and gives a copy to the Governing Body.

Within 3 days of receipt, the Administrator and RN Supervisor review each cited deficiency and prepare a draft POC that states, for each: the corrective action; the person responsible; the completion date; how it will be monitored to prevent recurrence; and any evidence available.

If the agency believes a finding is inaccurate, the plan of correction includes a written explanation or dispute of that finding with supporting documents (Rule .08(4)). The agency still addresses any related practice that can be improved.
The Governing Body or its designated owner reviews and signs the POC. The Administrator submits it to DCH by a trackable method before the 10-day deadline and keeps proof of delivery.

The Administrator carries out each corrective action by the date in the POC, documents completion, and reviews progress at each Governing Body meeting until all items are closed. If DCH requests proof or a revised plan, the Administrator responds promptly within the date DCH sets.

After the POC is filed, the Administrator files the report and POC in the licensure file and makes the report available to clients who ask in writing (CR-05). Findings are entered into the quality improvement program (SVC-10) for trend review.
If DCH proposes a sanction or other enforcement action, the Administrator follows LIC-04 and tells the Governing Body immediately.

responsibilities.duty: Review and sign the POC, support corrective action and monitor completion.
Receive surveyors, produce records, log and calendar the report, prepare and submit the POC within 10 days, and track correction.
Help draft clinical corrections, ask client consent for DCH contact and keep clinical records current.
Cooperate with DCH without unreasonable delay, answer truthfully and notify the Administrator when surveyors arrive.

documentation: Inspection-ready binder checklist and monthly update log
Surveyor sign-in and documents-provided list
Inspection report with date-received stamp
Plan of correction with Governing Body signature and proof of delivery
Corrective action tracking log
Any written explanation or dispute of findings
Quality improvement review of inspection findings

policies.title: Enforcement Actions, Sanctions and Hearing Rights
policies.applies_to: Administrator, governing body, compliance officer and all staff who receive or handle correspondence from DCH
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] responds promptly and lawfully to any enforcement action by the Georgia Department of Community Health (DCH), protects its hearing rights, and keeps clients' services safe and uninterrupted while a matter is pending.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] recognizes that, after notice and an opportunity for hearing, DCH may refuse, limit, restrict, suspend, revoke or refuse to renew a license, issue a public reprimand, or impose a fine (Rule 111-8-65-.13). The administrator must notify the governing body within one business day of receiving any DCH notice of sanction. The agency follows the hearing request deadline stated on the DCH notice, without exception. All enforcement correspondence is logged and retained. The agency complies with every limit or restriction placed on its license while a matter is pending. No staff member may ignore, discard or delay a DCH notice.

definitions.definition: Any DCH notice proposing or imposing refusal, limitation, restriction, suspension, revocation or non-renewal of a license, a public reprimand, or a fine.
The written notice from DCH that states the proposed or final action, the basis for it, and the deadline and method for requesting a hearing.
The agency's running record of every enforcement notice, response, deadline and outcome.

procedures: Any employee who receives mail, email, fax, a courier delivery or a phone call from DCH about a sanction, proposed sanction or fine gives it to the administrator the same day, unopened if it is addressed to the administrator.
The administrator date-stamps the notice, records how and when it was received, and scans a copy into the enforcement log file.
Within one business day of receipt, the administrator notifies the governing body in writing (email with read confirmation is acceptable) and attaches a copy of the notice.

The administrator identifies the action proposed (refusal, limitation, restriction, suspension, revocation, non-renewal, public reprimand or fine), the stated reasons, and the hearing request deadline printed on the DCH notice.
The administrator enters the hearing request deadline and every other response date in the compliance log, with reminders set 10, 5 and 2 days ahead.

Within three business days, the administrator and governing body chair meet, in person or by phone, to review the notice and the underlying findings, and to decide whether to request a hearing. The agency may consult legal counsel [LEGAL COUNSEL NAME] at this step.
If the agency decides to request a hearing, the administrator submits the written request in the manner and by the deadline stated on the DCH notice, and keeps proof of delivery.
If the agency decides not to contest, the governing body records its decision and reasons in the minutes, and the administrator responds to DCH as the notice directs.

The administrator gathers relevant records for the hearing, including client records, personnel records, training and supervision records, incident and complaint files and inspection reports. Records are kept intact and are not altered.

While the matter is pending, the administrator complies with any limit, restriction or suspension in effect. If the action limits the services or the geographic area the agency may offer, the administrator stops those services as of the effective date and arranges referrals for affected clients in line with OPS-03.

If a suspension or revocation will interrupt client care, the administrator notifies each affected client and the supervising staff promptly, helps clients move to another licensed provider, and documents each transfer.
If a fine is imposed, the governing body approves payment or contest, and the administrator keeps the payment record or the dispute documentation.
If DCH issues a public reprimand, the administrator gives the governing body a copy. All public or media inquiries go to the governing body chair or a person the chair designates.

The governing body requires a written corrective action plan addressing the root cause of the violation. The administrator assigns owners and due dates, and verifies completion. Results are reported through the Quality Improvement Program (SVC-10).

The administrator updates the enforcement log whenever any development occurs (hearing date, decision, payment, closure) and reports the status at each governing body meeting until the matter is closed.
Enforcement files are kept in the administrative records for at least five years after closure, or longer if a dispute is pending.

responsibilities.duty: Receives and logs notices, notifies the governing body within one business day, calendars deadlines, files timely hearing requests, carries out corrective actions and keeps the enforcement log.
Decides whether to contest an action, approves corrective action plans and fines, and oversees closure.
Confirms deadlines are calendared and works with the administrator on root-cause review and trending.
Route any DCH communication to the administrator the same day and never discard or ignore it.

documentation: Enforcement log (date received, type of action, hearing deadline, responses, outcome)
Copy of each DCH notice with date stamp
Written governing body notification and meeting minutes
Hearing request and proof of delivery
Corrective action plan and verification of completion
Client transfer or notification records, if services were limited or suspended

policies.title: Corporate Compliance, Fraud and Billing Integrity
policies.applies_to: Governing body, administrator, compliance officer, billing and scheduling staff, supervisors, and all caregivers and contractors
policies.purpose: To prevent fraud, waste and abuse and to make sure every claim [AGENCY NAME] submits, whether to Medicaid or a private payer, reflects services that were actually delivered, documented and authorized.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] bills only for services actually delivered and documented, and for Medicaid, only where the EVV record matches the visit. The agency screens every employee and contractor against the OIG exclusion list before hire and monthly afterward. Referral arrangements must follow federal anti-kickback rules, and the agency does not treat a person with a financial interest in referrals as exempt from them. Staff may report compliance concerns without retaliation, and the compliance officer investigates every report. As a Medicaid waiver provider, the agency must hold a current, valid DCH private home care license (DAS HCBS 5300 Manual § 208), and it participates in the Georgia Elderly and Disabled Waiver (CCSP/SOURCE) and related waiver programs under the 1915(c) authority (Social Security Act § 1915(c); CMS Waiver 0112.R08.00). The agency follows the Georgia Medicaid EVV requirement for personal care services, using Netsmart Mobile Caregiver+.

definitions.definition: A claim for payment for services not delivered, not documented, not authorized, delivered by an unqualified or excluded person, or otherwise misrepresented (31 USC 3729).
Offering, paying, soliciting or receiving anything of value to induce or reward referrals of federally funded program business (42 USC 1320a-7b).
Exclusion of a person or entity from federal health care programs under 42 CFR 1001. Federal programs may not pay for items or services furnished by an excluded person.
Electronic Visit Verification: the record of service type, recipient, provider, date, location and start and end times for each Medicaid personal care visit.
The person designated by the governing body, [COMPLIANCE OFFICER NAME], who runs this policy.

procedures: The governing body designates a compliance officer in writing. The compliance officer reports directly to the governing body on compliance matters and may bypass the administrator when needed.

Before every claim is submitted, billing staff compare each billed visit with the caregiver's daily service documentation (SVC-09), the service agreement or authorized service plan, and for Medicaid, the EVV record (OPS-05).

Billing staff bill Medicaid personal support using the codes for the program: T1019 with TF/UC modifiers for CCSP/SOURCE (waiver IDs 590/930), and T2025 for ICWP (660) and NOW/COMP (680/681). Any code or modifier question goes to the compliance officer before submission.

Billing staff do not submit a claim when the documentation, EVV data and authorization do not match. They return it to the supervisor to resolve, and corrections to EVV records are made only through the system's approved correction process with a documented reason.

Before hire or contracting, the administrator checks every candidate against the OIG List of Excluded Individuals/Entities and any other exclusion list Georgia Medicaid requires. The result is printed or saved to the personnel file (ADM-07, PER-01).
The compliance officer repeats the exclusion check for all current employees and contractors every month, and records the date, the person who ran the check and the results.

If any person appears on an exclusion list, the administrator removes that person from all duties tied to federally funded programs immediately. The compliance officer reviews every claim for that person's services and arranges to refund any payments that should not have been billed.

The agency does not pay or accept anything of value in exchange for client referrals. Staff may not receive gifts, commissions or bonuses tied to referrals. The compliance officer reviews any marketing, referral-source or discharge-planner arrangement before it begins, and the governing body approves it in writing.
The compliance officer reviews every proposed arrangement with a person who has a financial interest in referrals, and documents why it complies with anti-kickback rules.

The agency keeps its DCH private home care license current as a condition of Medicaid waiver participation (DAS HCBS 5300 Manual § 208). The administrator notifies the compliance officer immediately of any lapse, suspension or restriction on the license, and no waiver services are billed during any period when the license is not valid.

Any employee or contractor who suspects a billing error, falsified timekeeping, kickback or other violation reports it to the compliance officer, the administrator or the governing body chair, verbally or in writing, anonymously if preferred, via [COMPLIANCE REPORTING PHONE/EMAIL].
The agency does not retaliate against anyone who reports a concern in good faith. Retaliation by any employee is grounds for discipline up to termination.

The compliance officer opens a written investigation file within two business days of a report, interviews involved staff, reviews records, and gives findings and recommendations to the governing body.

When an overpayment or erroneous claim is found, the compliance officer promptly reports it to the payer, returns the money and corrects the underlying process. Staff who knowingly falsify documentation or EVV data are subject to discipline, up to termination, and may be reported to the appropriate authorities.

Every year, the compliance officer trains all billing, scheduling and supervisory staff on the False Claims Act, anti-kickback rules, exclusion screening, EVV and documentation integrity, and records attendance.
The compliance officer presents a summary of audits, reports, exclusion screening and corrective actions to the governing body at least annually, as part of the policy review in GB-01.

responsibilities.duty: Designates the compliance officer, approves referral arrangements and reviews the annual compliance report.
Runs monthly exclusion screening, investigates reports, reviews referral arrangements, audits claims and trains staff.
Makes sure claims match documentation and EVV, keeps the license current and removes excluded persons.
Verify documentation, authorization and EVV before billing and use the correct codes.
Record services truthfully, use EVV correctly and report concerns without fear of retaliation.

documentation: Pre-billing verification checklists or audit logs
Monthly OIG exclusion screening records for each person screened
Compliance reports, investigation files and corrective actions
Referral arrangement reviews and governing body approvals
Overpayment refund records
Annual compliance training sign-in sheets
EVV correction logs with reasons

policies.title: Required Reports and Notices to the State
policies.applies_to: Administrator, compliance officer, governing body, supervisors and all staff who prepare or send reports
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] sends every required report and notice to Georgia DCH, Adult Protective Services, law enforcement and Medicaid programs accurately and on time, and keeps proof of each.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] gives DCH 15 days' advance notice of any location change (Rule 111-8-65-.05(2)(c)). The agency returns its license when its name, location, ownership or governing body changes, because the license is not assignable or transferable (Rule 111-8-65-.05(2)). The agency files its renewal application with a description of services and geographic area (Rule 111-8-65-.06(2)), and all information in applications and reports is truthful (Rule 111-8-65-.06(4)). The agency sends DCH an acceptable written plan of correction within ten days of receiving the written inspection report (Rule 111-8-65-.08(4)). Reports of abuse, neglect and exploitation go to DHS-DAS Adult Protective Services and to law enforcement (O.C.G.A. § 30-5-4). The agency keeps incident, unusual occurrence and complaint files for at least five years (Rule 111-8-65-.09(4)(d)). Medicaid program reports and incident reporting follow each waiver program's requirements. Every due date is calendared in a compliance log.

definitions.definition: The calendar and tracking record the administrator keeps of every report, notice, renewal and deadline owed to a regulator or payer.
The agency's written response to a DCH inspection report that addresses each finding and may explain or dispute a finding.
A change in the agency's name, location, ownership or governing body.

procedures: The administrator keeps a compliance log, with entries for: license renewal, plan-of-correction deadlines, change-event notices, waiver program reporting dates and annual policy review. Each entry names an owner and a due date, with reminders set 30, 14 and 7 days ahead.

Location change: before moving any office, the administrator sends written notice to DCH at least 15 days before the move date. The notice gives the new address and effective date. The administrator keeps proof of delivery and does not begin operating at the new location until DCH requirements for the new location are met.

Change of name, ownership or governing body: the administrator notifies DCH in writing before the change takes effect. The agency returns the license to DCH, as it is not assignable or transferable, and does not operate under the new name, ownership or governing body until DCH has issued the appropriate license.

Renewal: at least 60 days before the license expiry date shown on the license, the administrator starts the renewal application on the DCH form, with an updated description of services and geographic area and the fees DCH requires. A second person reviews the application for accuracy before it is signed.

Truthfulness: the administrator and any signer verify every statement in an application, renewal or report against source records. The agency does not make a false statement to DCH, because DCH may refuse a license for false statements.
Inspection reports: the administrator date-stamps every written inspection report on receipt and enters the ten-day plan-of-correction due date in the compliance log the same day.

Within ten days of receiving the written report, the administrator submits an acceptable written plan of correction to DCH, with owners and completion dates for each finding. Where the agency disagrees with a finding, the plan explains or disputes it. Proof of delivery is kept.

Abuse, neglect or exploitation: any employee with reasonable cause to believe a disabled adult or elder has been abused, neglected or exploited reports immediately to DHS-DAS Adult Protective Services at [APS INTAKE PHONE] and to law enforcement or a prosecutor, as set out in SAF-01. The agency standard is to make the report before the end of the same shift.

The employee also notifies the administrator or supervisor. This notice does not replace the employee's own duty to report. The administrator documents the report, who made it, the time and the agency or person contacted.

Incidents and unusual occurrences (falls, accidents, significant medication errors): caregivers report to the supervisor immediately and complete the written report the same day (SAF-02). The supervisor records the actions taken, and the report is filed in the incident file.
Complaints: every complaint is logged and filed under the complaints process (CR-02) with the actions taken to resolve it.
Incident reports, unusual occurrence reports and complaint files are kept at least five years, and the documentation shows what actions, if any, the agency took.

Medicaid waiver programs: before serving each waiver client, the administrator confirms the reporting and incident notification requirements of that program (CCSP/SOURCE, ICWP, NOW/COMP) with the program contact or case manager. The administrator adds those requirements to the compliance log and follows them (OPS-04).

The administrator reviews the compliance log weekly, and the compliance officer reviews it monthly. The administrator reports any missed or at-risk deadline to the governing body the same day it is found.
If a report is found to be late or inaccurate, the administrator sends the corrected or late report right away, records why it happened, and takes corrective action.
The governing body reviews the compliance log summary at each meeting and during the annual policy review (GB-01).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the compliance log, sends all notices and applications to DCH on time and files the plan of correction.
Reviews the log monthly, checks accuracy of filings and tracks Medicaid program reporting.
Make sure incident and complaint reports are complete and filed, and that abuse, neglect and exploitation reports are made.
Report suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation and incidents immediately.
Approves change events, reviews compliance reports and oversees timeliness.

documentation: Compliance log
Copies of DCH notices, applications and renewals with proof of delivery
Plans of correction with date of submission
Returned license receipt after a change event
APS and law enforcement report records
Incident, unusual occurrence and complaint files (five-year retention)
Medicaid program report copies

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, volunteers, supervisors, administrator and governing body
policies.purpose: To protect clients from abuse, neglect and exploitation, and to make sure every suspected case is reported to the right authorities without delay.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has zero tolerance for abuse, neglect and exploitation of clients. Every employee is treated as a reporter. Anyone with reasonable cause to believe a disabled adult or elder has been abused, neglected or exploited must report to DHS-DAS Adult Protective Services and to law enforcement or a prosecutor (O.C.G.A. § 30-5-4). The employee also reports to the person in charge, but that does not replace the individual's own duty to report. Good-faith reporters are immune from liability, and the agency does not retaliate against anyone who reports. The agency does not hire a person against whom there is credible evidence of abuse or exploitation (Rule 111-8-65-.09(5)), and staff must not make false statements about qualifications. An accused employee is removed from contact with the client while the matter is investigated. The agency's approach to protecting people receiving Medicaid home and community-based services is consistent with 42 CFR 441.301(c).

definitions.definition: Willful infliction of physical pain, injury or mental anguish, or willful deprivation of services or care necessary to maintain a client's health or welfare.
Failure to provide the care, supervision or services necessary to maintain a client's physical and mental health, including failure to perform assigned tasks.
Illegal or improper use of a client, or of a client's funds, property or resources, for another person's profit or advantage.
The administrator, or the supervisor on duty or on call when the administrator is unavailable.
A belief that a reasonable person would hold based on what the reporter saw, heard or was told. Proof is not required.

procedures: At hire and orientation, every employee receives this policy, signs that they understand they are personally a reporter, and receives the APS intake number, which the agency posts in the office and gives to each caregiver on a wallet card: [APS INTAKE PHONE].

Before hire, the administrator reviews the candidate for credible evidence of abuse or exploitation through background checks and registry checks (PER-01, ADM-09) and records the results in the personnel file.
Training: abuse, neglect and exploitation recognition and reporting is covered in orientation (ADM-13) and refreshed during annual in-service training (ADM-14).

Any employee who has reasonable cause to believe a client has been abused, neglected or exploited immediately makes a report to DHS-DAS Adult Protective Services at [APS INTAKE PHONE] and to local law enforcement or the prosecutor. The agency standard is to report immediately and no later than the end of the same shift.
If a client is in immediate danger or needs medical care, the employee first calls 911 and follows SAF-07.
The employee also notifies the person in charge, who must report or cause the report to be made. If the person in charge does not act, the employee's own report still stands.
No employee may be told, expected or pressured to wait, to investigate first, or to get permission before reporting. No supervisor may discourage a report.

The person in charge records the report on an incident report the same day: who reported, what was seen or said, the date and time, the agencies contacted, the name of any intake worker, and any reference number.

The administrator removes an accused employee from contact with the client right away, pending the investigation, and reassigns that employee away from all clients if the allegation is credible or the investigation needs it. Removal is not a finding of guilt.

The administrator offers the client a safe alternative caregiver, notifies the client's representative or emergency contact unless doing so would put the client at risk, and notifies the Medicaid case manager or program contact for waiver clients (OPS-04).

The agency cooperates fully with APS, law enforcement and DCH investigations, including by giving access to records and staff, and keeps its own internal review separate from, and secondary to, those investigations.

After the investigation, the administrator takes corrective action, which can include discipline, retraining, termination, and where applicable a report to the nursing licensing board or the employee registry (PER-01).

The agency does not retaliate against any reporter. An employee who believes they were retaliated against reports to the administrator or governing body chair. Retaliation is grounds for discipline up to termination.

Prevention: supervisors watch for warning signs during home visits (SVC-06, SVC-07), including unexplained injuries, changes in finances, missing property, fear of a caregiver or poor hygiene, and report them as above. Staff follow the property and funds rules in CR-04 and the boundaries in PER-03.
Incident reports and any related files are kept at least five years (SAF-02), and the governing body reviews trends through the Quality Improvement Program (SVC-10).

responsibilities.duty: Reports reasonable cause to believe abuse, neglect or exploitation to APS and law enforcement, and also to the person in charge.
Makes or confirms the report, documents it, protects the client and removes the accused employee from the client.
Posts the APS number, runs training, oversees internal review and corrective action, and prevents retaliation.
Watch for warning signs on home visits and make sure no one delays a report.
Reviews reports and trends and supports a no-retaliation culture.

documentation: Signed employee acknowledgment of reporter duty
Posted APS number and wallet card distribution record
Incident report for each suspected case, with APS and law enforcement contact details
Record of removal of accused employee and reassignment
Investigation file and corrective action
Orientation and in-service training records
Background and registry check results

policies.title: Incident and Unusual Occurrence Reporting
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, nursing personnel, supervisors, administrator and records staff
policies.purpose: To make sure every incident and unusual occurrence affecting a client's health, safety or welfare is reported, acted on, documented and retained, and to meet Rule 111-8-65-.09(4)(d).
policies.policy: This policy meets Rule 111-8-65-.09(4)(d) — Reports of Complaints and Incidents. [AGENCY NAME] documents all incident reports and reports of unusual occurrences, such as falls, accidents and significant medication errors, that affect the health, safety and welfare of its clients, and keeps them on file for a minimum of five years. The documentation shows what actions, if any, the agency took to address each incident or unusual occurrence. The agency also maintains files of all documentation of complaints submitted under Rule .12(2), together with the actions taken to resolve each complaint. Caregivers report incidents to the supervisor immediately and complete the written report the same day.

definitions.definition: Any event that affects or could affect a client's health, safety or welfare, such as a fall, accident, injury, property loss or conflict.
An out-of-the-ordinary event such as a fall, accident or significant medication error that affects a client's health, safety or welfare.

A medication-related error, such as a wrong person, wrong drug, missed dose or wrong time reported to the supervisor, that could harm or has harmed the client. Caregivers do not give medications beyond reminders and self-administration assistance (SAF-08), so most errors will be reminder, record or missed-dose events.
The record of a complaint submitted under Rule .12(2) and the actions taken to resolve it.

procedures: The caregiver first makes sure the client is safe, calls 911 for emergencies and follows SAF-07.
The caregiver reports the incident or unusual occurrence verbally to the supervisor [SUPERVISOR PHONE] or on-call representative immediately.

The caregiver completes the written incident report the same day, before leaving the shift where possible. The report states the client, date, time, place, what happened, who was present, injuries or damage, and what the caregiver did.
The supervisor reviews the report on the day of receipt, confirms the client's condition, makes sure follow-up care is arranged, and notifies the client's representative or emergency contact.
For waiver clients, the supervisor also notifies the Medicaid case manager or program contact in line with that program's incident reporting rules (OPS-04, LIC-06).
If the incident involves suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, the supervisor makes sure the report is made to APS and law enforcement as required by SAF-01.
The supervisor documents the actions taken: for example, medical care sought, service plan changed, equipment replaced, staff retrained, disciplinary action or client referral.
The supervisor sends the completed report to the administrator within one business day. The administrator reviews it, assigns any follow-up and signs it.
Where an incident involves a staff member's performance, the administrator arranges retraining and supervisory evaluation (SVC-04).

Complaints submitted under Rule .12(2) are filed in the complaint file with the actions taken to resolve them (CR-02). Entries show the date received, the complainant, the substance, the investigation, the resolution and the date the complainant was told.
Records staff file each incident report in the agency's incident file and in the client record (ADM-05) in a secure location (ADM-06).
The agency retains incident reports and reports of unusual occurrences for a minimum of five years, and complaint files for at least the same period.

The compliance officer or administrator reviews the incident file each month for trends such as repeated falls, repeated errors or one caregiver involved in multiple events, and reports the findings to the Quality Improvement Program (SVC-10).
The governing body receives a quarterly summary of incident numbers, types and corrective actions.
During a DCH inspection, the administrator gives inspectors access to the incident and complaint files on request (LIC-03).

responsibilities.duty: Protects the client, reports verbally at once and completes the written report the same day.
Reviews each report, makes sure care and notifications happen, records the actions taken and forwards the report to the administrator.
Signs off on reports, assigns corrective actions, retains files at least five years and reports trends.
File reports securely in the incident file and client record.
Reviews quarterly summaries.

documentation: Incident / unusual occurrence report form for each event
Record of actions taken on each report
Complaint files under Rule .12(2), with resolution actions
Incident log and monthly trend review
Five-year retention schedule entry
Quarterly governing body summary

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, nursing personnel, companions and sitters, supervisors and the administrator
policies.purpose: To prevent the spread of infection among clients and staff, and to make sure employees exposed to or diagnosed with tuberculosis (TB) or hepatitis do not serve clients while contagious.
policies.policy: Infection control in the home is part of the Personal Care Assistant training program (Rule 111-8-65-.09(5)(c)), and of the competency required for companions and sitters. All staff must report known exposure to TB or hepatitis, which is covered in orientation (Rule 111-8-65-.09(6)). No supervisor may knowingly permit an employee who has been exposed to or diagnosed with TB or hepatitis to serve clients until the employee is determined not to be contagious (Rule 111-8-65-.10(2)). [AGENCY NAME] provides gloves and personal protective equipment at no cost to employees. Employee screening follows CDC-based guidance (see ADM-07). Where the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard (29 CFR 1910.1030) applies, the agency offers hepatitis B vaccination.

definitions.definition: Infection control practices applied to all clients, including hand hygiene, gloves, safe handling of soiled items, and respiratory etiquette.
Items such as gloves, masks and gowns that protect staff and clients from contact with infectious material.
Contact with a person known or suspected to have TB or hepatitis, or contact with blood or body fluids, in a way that may transmit infection.
A finding by a licensed health care provider, documented in writing, that the employee may safely return to client care.

procedures: The administrator makes sure infection control is a taught component of the 40-hour PCA training program and of companion and sitter competency, and records it in the training and competency records (ADM-11, ADM-12).

During orientation, before the employee works with any client, the trainer reviews standard precautions, hand hygiene, PPE use, cleaning and disinfecting of surfaces, handling of soiled laundry and waste, and the employee's duty to report known exposure to TB or hepatitis (ADM-13). The employee signs that the topic was covered.

The agency supplies gloves and PPE in sufficient quantities, and caregivers pick up supplies at [ADDRESS] or by delivery. Caregivers tell the supervisor when supplies are low, and the supervisor restocks within one business day.

Caregivers wash hands before and after each client contact, before and after glove use, before preparing food, and after toileting care, using soap and water or alcohol-based sanitizer as appropriate. Gloves are worn for contact with blood, body fluids, broken skin or soiled items, and are changed between tasks and clients.
Caregivers do not come to work with symptoms of contagious illness, such as fever, persistent cough, vomiting or diarrhea. They call the supervisor, who arranges coverage under OPS-02 and ADM-08.
Any employee who has been exposed to or diagnosed with TB or hepatitis must tell the supervisor or administrator immediately, before the next shift.
The supervisor or administrator removes the employee from client care immediately on learning of known exposure or diagnosis, and does not knowingly permit that employee to serve any client.

The administrator refers the employee to a licensed health care provider for evaluation. The employee returns to client care only when a written determination that the employee is not contagious is received and placed in the personnel file (ADM-07). The administrator keeps health information confidential and in a separate medical file.
The administrator arranges replacement staffing so that clients still receive care, or tells the client and refers to another provider if the client prefers (ADM-08).

If a client is known to have TB, hepatitis or another transmissible infection, the supervisor makes sure the service plan and caregiver instructions include the precautions needed (PLN-01), and shares information only with those who need it for care or safety (CR-03).

Staff who have a needlestick, or contact with blood or body fluids, wash the area immediately, report to the supervisor the same day, complete an incident report (SAF-02) and are referred for medical evaluation.

Where OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard applies to the agency's work, the administrator offers the hepatitis B vaccination series at no cost to eligible employees within the required timeframe, or documents a signed declination, and keeps an exposure control plan up to date.
Employee TB and health screening is done per ADM-07, using CDC-based guidance.
Supervisors observe infection control practice during annual written evaluations by direct observation (SVC-04) and during supervisory home visits, and correct problems on the spot with retraining.
The administrator reviews infection-related incidents, exposures and supply shortages each quarter and reports to the Quality Improvement Program (SVC-10).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures PPE supply, training content, exposure removal, return-to-work documentation and vaccination offers.
Enforce precautions, exclude exposed employees, observe practice and restock supplies.
Use standard precautions and PPE, stay home when symptomatic and report known TB or hepatitis exposure immediately.
Teach infection control in orientation and the 40-hour program and verify competency.

documentation: Orientation checklist showing infection control and exposure-reporting duty covered
40-hour training and competency records including infection control
Exclusion and return-to-work records with written determination of non-contagious status
PPE supply log
Hepatitis B vaccination or declination records, where applicable
Exposure incident reports
Annual written evaluation showing infection control observation

policies.title: Client Emergency and Disaster Plans
policies.applies_to: All employees, supervisors, the on-call representative and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To make sure each client's emergency and evacuation needs are identified before services begin, that staff know how to respond to medical emergencies and disasters, and that clients are contacted before and after severe events.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] assesses every client's emergency and evacuation needs at intake and records them in the service plan. Employees are trained during orientation, before working with clients, in handling medical emergencies and incidents (Rule 111-8-65-.09(6)). For clients who are medically frail or compromised, [AGENCY NAME] keeps a provider representative on call who can reach a nurse supervisor by phone or other means to consult with staff (Rule 111-8-65-.10(2)(d); see SVC-08). The agency prepares for severe weather, power loss and hurricane evacuation, and calls clients before and after such events. The agency does not promise rescue, sheltering or evacuation transport that it cannot reasonably deliver. Clients and their responsible parties remain responsible for their own evacuation decisions.

definitions.definition: A client identified under the agency's screening (see OPS-01 and SVC-05) as having medical needs that call for nurse supervisor access when personal care is provided.
A hurricane, tropical storm, tornado, ice or winter storm, flood, extended power or water outage, fire or other event that disrupts the safety of clients or the agency's ability to deliver services.
The agency representative reachable during service hours who can contact a nurse supervisor to consult with staff on a client's medical needs.

procedures: At intake, the intake coordinator or nurse supervisor asks each client and responsible party about emergency needs: mobility limits, oxygen or other power-dependent equipment, ability to evacuate alone, hearing, vision or cognitive limits, pets, nearby helpers, a planned shelter or relative's home, and emergency contacts. The answers are recorded in the intake record.
The service supervisor enters the client's emergency and evacuation needs and any special instructions in the service plan (see PLN-01).

The service supervisor flags clients who are medically frail or compromised on the client roster and confirms that the on-call representative and nurse supervisor contact process in SVC-08 covers each of them.

The Administrator keeps a current roster of active clients showing risk level, responsible party phone number, physician contact, and whether power-dependent equipment is in use. The roster is updated whenever a client is admitted, discharged or changes condition.

During orientation, before the employee works alone with clients, the trainer teaches handling of medical emergencies and incidents, including calling 911 and reaching the supervisor or on-call representative. Attendance is documented in the personnel record (see ADM-13).
The Administrator monitors National Weather Service alerts and local emergency management announcements and decides when to activate the emergency steps below.

When a severe event is forecast, the scheduler or a designated supervisor calls clients, starting with medically frail or compromised clients and those on power-dependent equipment. The caller confirms the client's plan (stay, relocate or evacuate), verifies the responsible party's number, and reviews medication and supply needs. Each call is logged with date, time, caller and outcome.

Clients who plan to evacuate are asked to tell the agency where they are going. The agency does not provide evacuation transport unless it is part of the client's written scope of services and the requirements in SAF-06 are met.

If an event begins while an employee is in a client's home, the employee stays with the client only while it is safe, follows the client's plan, and calls the supervisor. Employees are not required to drive in dangerous conditions. They tell the supervisor when they cannot travel safely, and the supervisor handles the missed visit under OPS-02.

During a power or equipment failure, the employee does not make medical decisions. The employee calls 911 for any emergency, then the supervisor, and helps the client call the utility, equipment supplier or physician as directed. The supervisor notifies the responsible party.

After an event, once it is safe, the supervisors call every affected client, again starting with the highest-risk clients, and in any case within 24 hours of the event ending. They confirm the client's safety and needs, and resume or reschedule visits. Any client who cannot be reached is escalated to the responsible party and, if needed, to local authorities for a welfare check.
The nurse supervisor updates the service plan if the event changed the client's needs, and reports any changes in condition under SAF-07.
Injuries, missed care, or other unusual events caused by the disaster are reported under SAF-02. Waiver clients' case managers are told of service interruptions under OPS-04.

After each activation, the Administrator reviews what worked and what did not, and records improvements in the quality improvement file (SVC-10). Emergency procedures are reviewed at least annually with the policy review in GB-01.

responsibilities.duty: Activates emergency steps, maintains the client roster and emergency contact list, and reviews the response after each event.
Assesses emergency needs, documents them in the service plan, calls high-risk clients, and consults with staff on medical needs.
Is reachable to staff and can contact a nurse supervisor for medically frail or compromised clients.
Complete emergency training, follow each client's plan, call 911 for emergencies, and report problems and changes in condition.
Make and share their own evacuation decisions and report changes in condition or contact information.

documentation: Intake emergency and evacuation assessment
Service plan entries on emergency needs
Client roster with risk flags
Pre-event and post-event call logs
Orientation records showing medical emergency training
Incident reports and post-event review notes

policies.title: Caregiver Safety in the Home and Workplace Violence
policies.applies_to: All employees, supervisors and contractors who work in clients' homes or the agency office
policies.purpose: To protect employees from injury, violence, harassment and exposure to infectious hazards while working in clients' homes and at the office, and to identify home hazards before they harm anyone.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides a workplace free of recognized hazards, consistent with the OSHA General Duty Clause (29 USC 654), and protects employees from occupational exposure to blood and other potentially infectious materials (29 CFR 1910.1030; see SAF-03). Home safety is taught in orientation, and subjects related to employees' duties, including safe lifting and transfers, are covered in annual in-service training (Rule 111-8-65-.09(6)). Any employee may leave an unsafe home and call a supervisor. The agency does not retaliate against anyone who reports workplace violence, harassment or a hazard.

definitions.definition: Any threat or act of physical violence, intimidation, stalking, or verbal or sexual harassment against an employee by a client, family member, visitor, co-worker or other person.

A home where there is an immediate threat to the employee's safety, such as violence, weapons used in a threatening manner, impaired or aggressive persons, fire or structural hazards, gas odors, or infestations.
Any condition in the home or workplace that could injure an employee or client, including clutter, poor lighting, pets, unsafe equipment or unsafe lifting situations.

procedures: Orientation, before the employee works with clients, includes home safety, personal safety, how to leave an unsafe situation, and how to report. The trainer documents completion in the personnel record (see ADM-13).

The intake nurse or supervisor screens for known safety concerns at intake (aggressive behavior, firearms, pets, smoking with oxygen, stairs, pests and household members' behavior). The findings are recorded and shared with assigned staff before the first visit.

Employees receive training on body mechanics, safe lifting and transfers, and use of client equipment and gait belts. Competency is demonstrated and documented before the employee performs transfers, and refreshed in annual in-service (ADM-14).
Employees follow standard precautions and use personal protective equipment supplied by the agency, as described in SAF-03, to meet 29 CFR 1910.1030.

An employee who feels threatened or finds an unsafe condition may stop work, leave the home, go to a safe place and call the supervisor or on-call representative. If there is an immediate danger, the employee calls 911 first.

The supervisor responds immediately, confirms the employee is safe, decides whether the visit is rescheduled, and, if the client needs care, arranges a safe alternative such as a different staff member, a welfare check or notice to the responsible party. The client is not abandoned. See OPS-03.
The employee reports the incident to the supervisor the same day and completes an incident report by the end of the next business day (see SAF-02).

The Administrator reviews each report of violence or harassment, takes action such as reassigning staff, requiring two-person visits, changing the plan, notifying police, or discharging the client under OPS-03, and records the outcome.
An employee injured on the job tells the supervisor immediately, gets medical treatment, and the Administrator documents the injury and handles workers' compensation and required OSHA recordkeeping.

Supervisors check for hazards at each supervisory home visit (SVC-06 and SVC-07). Hazards found are documented in the visit note with the action taken, and the supervisor tells the client or responsible party in writing what needs correcting.

Employees may report harassment or violence to any supervisor or directly to the Administrator, orally or in writing. If the Administrator is the subject, the report goes to the governing body (GB-01).
Retaliation for reporting is prohibited. Any retaliation is grounds for discipline up to termination.
The Administrator reviews incident trends at least quarterly as part of the quality improvement program (SVC-10) and revises training or practices as needed.

responsibilities.duty: Provides training, equipment and a safe workplace, investigates reports, prevents retaliation and tracks trends.
Screen homes for hazards, respond to employee calls, document findings at home visits and communicate with clients.
Use safe practices and protective equipment, leave unsafe situations and report hazards, violence and injuries.
Provide a reasonably safe environment and cooperate with correction of hazards.

documentation: Orientation and in-service records covering home safety and safe lifting
Intake safety screening
Supervisory visit notes recording hazards
Incident reports and Administrator review
Employee injury records
Quality improvement trend reports

policies.title: Transporting Clients and Use of Vehicles
policies.applies_to: Employees who provide transport and escort, drivers, supervisors, the scheduler and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To make sure transport and escort is offered only when [AGENCY NAME] can reasonably deliver it safely, and that required waivers, insurance checks and authorizations are in place before an employee drives a client.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] offers transport and escort only if it is listed in the agency's scope of services (see ADM-01) and in the client's written service agreement. This policy meets Rule 111-8-65-.03(s) (transport and escort services): when the mode of transportation is not owned by the client and is operated by an employee of the agency, the agency either obtains a signed waiver by the client of any claims for damages arising out of the operation of the vehicle, or makes reasonable efforts to confirm that there is current motor vehicle insurance that will provide medical coverage for the client if the vehicle is involved in an accident causing injuries to the client. Use of the client's own vehicle requires written authorization in the service agreement (Rule 111-8-65-.09(2)(a)9). Employees who transport and escort must be trained or competent in transport and escort (Rule 111-8-65-.09(5)(d)). The agency does not offer services it cannot reasonably deliver (Rule 111-8-65-.09(2)).

definitions.definition: Accompanying or driving a client to appointments, errands or other activities, as defined in Rule 111-8-65-.03(s).

definitions.term: Vehicle not owned by the client
definitions.definition: Any vehicle that is the employee's own, the agency's, or belongs to another person, when an employee of the agency drives it.
A written statement signed by the client or responsible party giving up claims for damages arising out of the operation of the vehicle by the employee.
Liability coverage carried by the agency for employees driving their own or other vehicles on agency business.

procedures: The Administrator decides whether the agency offers transport and escort and states this in the written scope of services (ADM-01). If it is not offered, employees may not drive clients. A client who asks is told that the agency does not provide it.

At intake, the intake coordinator identifies whether the client needs transport and escort. The coordinator accepts the request only if a qualified driver is available and the service fits the agency's coverage.

The service agreement lists transport and escort as a service, with frequency and charges. It records whether the client authorizes use of the client's own vehicle or the employee's or agency's vehicle (service agreement element at Rule .09(2)(a)9; see ADM-02).

If the employee will drive the client's own vehicle, the client or responsible party signs the written authorization in the service agreement before any trip. The supervisor verifies that the client's vehicle is registered and insured.

If the employee will drive a vehicle that the client does not own, the supervisor obtains one of the following before the first trip: (a) a signed waiver of claims by the client or responsible party, or (b) documented reasonable efforts to confirm current motor vehicle insurance providing medical coverage for the client.

Reasonable efforts under item 5(b) mean obtaining a copy of the declarations page or insurance card, or calling the insurer or agent. The supervisor records who was contacted, the policy number, the coverage and the date.

Before an employee is assigned to drive, the Administrator checks that the employee holds a valid Georgia driver's license, reviews the driving record, and confirms that the employee's own insurance meets the agency's requirement. The check is filed in the personnel record (ADM-07) and repeated at least annually.
The agency carries hired and non-owned auto liability coverage for employees driving on agency business. The Administrator reviews certificates yearly and keeps them on file.

Employees who provide transport and escort are trained or competent in transport and escort, and the training is documented under ADM-12 and ADM-13. Training covers safe driving, seat belt use, assisting the client in and out of the vehicle, wheelchair securement if applicable, and what to do in a crash or medical emergency.
Employees do not drive when ill, impaired or fatigued, and do not use a phone while driving. They do not carry unauthorized passengers.

In a crash or medical emergency, the employee calls 911, gets help for the client, notifies the supervisor right away and completes an incident report (SAF-02). The supervisor notifies the responsible party and updates the file.
The scheduler confirms that the waiver or insurance verification is on file before scheduling any trip. A trip with missing documents is not scheduled.

The supervisor copies the signed waiver or the insurance proof into the client file (ADM-05). If the insurance, vehicle or driver changes, the check is repeated. The supervisor reviews the waiver and authorization at the supervisory home visit.
Mileage and travel are billed and paid as described in the service agreement and PER-02. Employees are not asked to pay vehicle costs for client trips.

responsibilities.duty: Decides whether transport is offered, maintains hired and non-owned auto coverage, and approves drivers.
Obtains and files the waiver or insurance verification and the vehicle authorization before the first trip.
Schedules trips only when documentation and a qualified driver are in place.
Drive safely with a valid license, follow training, and report crashes and incidents right away.
Sign the service agreement authorization and, when applicable, the waiver, and maintain the client's own vehicle insurance.

documentation: Written scope of services listing transport and escort
Service agreement with vehicle authorization
Signed waiver of claims or documentation of insurance verification
Driver's license and driving record checks
Hired and non-owned auto insurance certificates
Training records for transport and escort
Incident reports

policies.title: Change in Client Condition and Emergencies in the Home
policies.applies_to: Nurses, PCAs, companions and sitters, supervisors and the on-call representative
policies.purpose: To make sure that changes in a client's condition and emergencies are recognized, reported and acted on quickly, and that the responsible party, physician, service plan and record are updated.
policies.policy: PCAs, companions and sitters must report client needs, changes in condition and observed problems (Rule 111-8-65-.10(1)). For a life-threatening emergency, the employee calls 911 first and then the supervisor. The supervisor notifies the responsible party and the physician and updates the service plan. Employees are trained in reporting client progress and problems and in handling medical emergencies and incidents during orientation (Rule 111-8-65-.09(6)). Clients are informed in the written rights notice that they must report changes in their condition (Rule 111-8-65-.12). Unlicensed staff observe and report. They do not diagnose, change treatment or give medical advice.

definitions.definition: Any new or worsening sign, symptom, behavior, function, safety concern or need, such as a fall, new confusion, pain, breathing difficulty, skin breakdown, decreased eating or drinking, medication problem or change in mood.
A situation that may cause death or serious harm without immediate care, such as unresponsiveness, chest pain, trouble breathing, stroke signs, severe bleeding, choking, seizure or serious injury.
The person identified in the client record who acts for or is to be notified on behalf of the client.

procedures: During orientation the trainer teaches the signs of a change in condition, emergency response (including first aid and CPR as covered in the PCA training program), and how to report. Completion is documented in the personnel record (ADM-13).
Employees tell clients and families at the first visit that changes in condition must be reported to the agency, and clients are reminded in the written rights notice (CR-01).

For a life-threatening emergency, the employee calls 911 immediately, gives first aid within the limits of training, and stays with the client until help arrives. The employee then calls the supervisor or on-call representative.

For an urgent but non-life-threatening change, such as a fall without apparent injury or new symptoms, the employee calls the supervisor immediately and follows the supervisor's instructions. The supervisor may consult a nurse supervisor (see SVC-08).
For a minor change, such as slightly lower appetite or a new complaint, the employee reports it to the supervisor the same day and documents it in the daily note (SVC-09).

The employee does not give medications, adjust treatments, or advise the client about medical decisions. If the client refuses emergency care, the employee stays calm, tells the supervisor and documents the refusal.
The supervisor, or the nurse supervisor where nursing judgment is needed, assesses the report, decides on next steps and notifies the responsible party the same day, or immediately for emergencies.

The supervisor or nurse notifies the client's physician of significant changes, using the physician contact information in the client file, and documents the date, time, person reached and instructions.

The service supervisor reviews the service plan and updates it when the change affects functional limitations, services, frequency, goals or other plan content, with the client's agreement (PLN-01). Waiver clients' case managers are notified under OPS-04.

The employee who responded writes a factual note of the event, including time, observations, actions taken and persons notified, by the end of the shift. The supervisor adds follow-up and files it in the client record (ADM-05).

An incident report is completed under SAF-02 for falls, injuries, emergency calls, medication errors, or any event meeting the agency's incident criteria, and reports to the state are made if required under LIC-06.
If abuse, neglect or exploitation is suspected, the employee follows SAF-01 in addition to this policy.
The supervisor follows up with the client within one business day after an emergency or hospital visit to check status and determine whether services need to change.
If the client is hospitalized or the condition exceeds what the agency can safely manage, the Administrator follows OPS-03 on discharge or transfer.
The Administrator reviews emergency responses and changes in condition in the quality improvement program (SVC-10).

responsibilities.duty: Observe, call 911 for life-threatening emergencies, report all changes in condition promptly and document them.
Assess reports, notify the responsible party and physician, update the service plan and follow up.
Is available to employees to consult and reach a nurse supervisor.
Ensures training, incident review and required reporting.
Report changes in the client's condition to the agency.

documentation: Daily notes and shift notes on the change or emergency
Documentation of notification to the responsible party and physician
Updated service plan
Incident report
Orientation records on emergency training
Follow-up notes

policies.title: Medication Reminders and Self-Administration Assistance
policies.applies_to: PCAs, companions and sitters, supervisors, nurses and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To set clear limits on what unlicensed staff may do about medications, so that clients receive safe reminders and assistance without staff performing professional services.
policies.policy: Medically related activities include reminding clients to take medication and assisting with self-administration, and exclude professional services (Rule 111-8-65-.03(k)). [AGENCY NAME] allows trained non-licensed staff to remind clients to take medication and to assist with self-administration only. Non-licensed staff do not administer medications, draw up insulin, or make decisions about medications. Training in medically related activities is part of the 40-hour PCA training program (Rule 111-8-65-.09(5)(c)), and a PCA may not be assigned a task until training and a competency determination are complete. Significant medication errors are reported as incidents under SAF-02, and each reminder or assistance is recorded in the daily notes.

definitions.definition: Telling or prompting a client to take their own medication at the time ordered, without selecting, measuring or deciding on the dose.

Helping a client who is capable of directing their own care to take their own medication, for example by handing over the container the client chooses, or opening a container, with the client making and carrying out the decision.
Any act of giving a medication to a client, such as measuring or giving a dose, injecting, or drawing up insulin. This is not performed by non-licensed staff.
A missed dose, wrong medication, wrong time, wrong person, wrong amount or an unauthorized medication taken that the employee observes or learns of.

procedures: The service supervisor or nurse supervisor determines at intake and in the service plan whether the client needs medication reminders or self-administration assistance and records the medications, the schedule and what help is allowed (PLN-01).

The agency accepts a client whose needs require administration of medications by non-licensed staff only if the client or family provides that care or a licensed nurse is assigned under SVC-01 to the extent the agency's scope permits. Otherwise the agency does not accept the request (ADM-01).

Only PCAs who have completed training in medically related activities and have a documented competency determination perform reminders and assistance (ADM-11). Companions and sitters perform reminders only if so trained and listed in the service plan.
Employees remind clients at the times shown in the plan, using a verbal prompt or similar reminder. The client takes the medication.

When assisting with self-administration, the employee helps only if the client is able to direct the process. The client selects the medication, and the employee may do tasks such as handing over the client's own container, opening a container, or providing water. The employee does not decide the dose or the time.

Employees do not measure or pour doses, fill pill organizers except as the client directs and the plan allows, give injections, draw up insulin, crush medications, or give medication from an unmarked container.
