Employees never give advice about medications, never change or stop a medication, and never give medication that is not prescribed for the client. If a client asks, the employee refers the question to the client's physician or pharmacist and tells the supervisor.

If the client refuses a medication, the employee does not force or persuade beyond a polite reminder, documents the refusal and tells the supervisor the same day, or immediately if the missed medication could be serious.

If an employee suspects an error, an adverse reaction or confusion about medication, the employee calls the supervisor immediately and calls 911 for an emergency (SAF-07). The supervisor contacts the nurse supervisor, the physician or poison control as needed, and notifies the responsible party.
Each reminder or assistance given, refused or missed is recorded in the daily note with date, time, and the client's response (SVC-09).

The employee completes an incident report for any significant medication error or adverse event by the end of the shift or next business day, and the Administrator reviews it (SAF-02). Required state reports are made under LIC-06.
Supervisors review medication reminder entries during supervisory visits (SVC-06) and confirm that employees are working within these limits.
An employee who performs a task outside these limits is retrained, and discipline is applied as appropriate under PER-03.
The Administrator reviews medication-related incidents in the quality improvement program (SVC-10).

responsibilities.duty: Decides what medication assistance is allowed, records it in the service plan, and monitors compliance.
Perform only reminders and assistance with self-administration, document each one, and report refusals and errors.
Ensures training and competency, reviews incidents and enforces these limits.
Manage and store the client's medications and keep the agency informed of changes.

documentation: Service plan entry on medication reminders and assistance
40-hour training and competency records for medically related activities
Daily notes of reminders, refusals and assistance
Incident reports for medication errors
Supervisory visit notes

policies.title: Client Intake, Eligibility and Assessment
policies.applies_to: Intake staff, supervisors, nurses, the scheduler and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To provide a consistent process for receiving referrals, deciding whether the agency can reasonably serve a person, assessing needs, and completing the service agreement and service plan on time.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] accepts only clients whose services it can reasonably deliver (Rule 111-8-65-.09(2)). At first contact, the agency records the initial contact date, the referral date and the source of the referral, and screens for medical frailty. The agency collects the responsible party's information and the names and numbers of the client's physicians. A written service agreement is completed by the second visit, if that is on a different day from the first, or within 7 calendar days of the first service, whichever is earlier (Rule 111-8-65-.09(2)(b)). The service supervisor completes the written service plan within seven working days after services start (Rule 111-8-65-.11). Medicaid clients are referred through the Area Agency on Aging or the waiver case manager. A separate file is kept for each client (Rule 111-8-65-.09(4)(a)).

definitions.definition: The process from first inquiry or referral through the acceptance decision and the start of services.
The person or organization that referred the client, such as a family member, physician, hospital, Area Agency on Aging or waiver case manager.
A client who the agency's screening shows has medical needs that require nurse supervisor access and an on-call representative when personal care is provided (see SVC-05 and SVC-08).
The agency staff member designated to develop the service plan and supervise services under SVC-04.

procedures: The intake coordinator records the initial contact date, the referral date and the referral source on the intake form the day of contact, and opens a client file (ADM-05).

The coordinator collects identifying information, address and phone, the responsible party's name and contact information, the names and phone numbers of the client's physicians, emergency contacts, and payment source (private pay, long-term care insurance or Medicaid waiver).
The coordinator describes the agency's scope of services and the types of clients served (ADM-01), the services requested, schedule and hours, and any transport needs (SAF-06).

The coordinator screens for medical frailty or compromise and for special conditions that need additional training or nurse involvement, and flags the client for the nurse supervisor. Clients flagged as medically frail or compromised require an on-call representative and nurse supervisor access (SVC-08).

The nurse or service supervisor reviews the screening and the requested services and decides whether the agency can reasonably deliver them, including whether a qualified nurse, PCA, companion or sitter is available at the needed times and whether any assigned staff member has completed training and competency for the client's special conditions.

If the agency cannot reasonably deliver the services, it declines or defers the referral, tells the client or referral source promptly, and offers other resources where appropriate. The reason is recorded on the intake form.

If the client is a Medicaid waiver participant, the coordinator confirms that the client was referred through the Area Agency on Aging or the waiver case manager, verifies the authorization for the services and units, and follows OPS-04. A client who asks about Medicaid is directed to the Area Agency on Aging for access. The agency does not start waiver services without authorization.

A supervisor or nurse assesses the client in the home before or at the start of services, including functional limitations, safety, emergency needs (SAF-04), diet, equipment, medications to be reminded (SAF-08) and goals.

At or before the first visit, the supervisor reviews the service agreement with the client and responsible party. The agreement is completed and signed by the second visit if on a different day than the first, or within 7 calendar days of the first service, whichever is earlier (ADM-02, ADM-03). If completion is delayed for good cause, the supervisor documents the reason in the record.
The supervisor gives the client the written notice of rights and responsibilities when the service agreement is completed (CR-01).

The service supervisor develops the service plan with the client, the responsible party, and the physician if nursing is provided. The plan is completed within seven working days after services start (PLN-01).
The scheduler assigns qualified staff and confirms the first visit with the client (OPS-02). Supervisors orient the assigned staff on the client's plan and any safety concerns before the first visit.

The intake coordinator confirms that the file contains identifying information, the date and source of referral, physician contacts, the current service agreement and, when complete, the current service plan (ADM-05).
The Administrator reviews intake logs monthly for timeliness, declined referrals and missing documents, and reports findings to the quality improvement program (SVC-10).

responsibilities.duty: Records contact, referral and responsible party data, screens for frailty, and opens the client file.
Decides whether the agency can reasonably serve the client, assesses needs, and completes the service plan within seven working days.
Ensures the service agreement deadline is met, and reviews intake performance and compliance.
Assigns qualified staff and confirms the first visit.
Give accurate information and sign the service agreement.

documentation: Intake form with initial contact date, referral date and referral source
Medical frailty screening
Responsible party and physician contact information
Decline or deferral record and reason
Waiver authorization (for Medicaid clients)
Signed service agreement and good-cause delay note, if any
Rights notice receipt
Service plan

policies.title: Scheduling, Missed Visits and Continuity of Care
policies.applies_to: Administrator, service supervisors, schedulers, on-call representatives, nursing personnel, personal care assistants, companions and sitters
policies.purpose: To make sure each client receives the services and schedule in the service agreement, to respond promptly when a visit cannot be delivered, and to protect the client's right to be told, to be referred elsewhere, and to cancel at any time.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps enough qualified staff to deliver the services in every service agreement and does not offer services it cannot reasonably deliver (Rule 111-8-65-.09(2) and .09(5)). The agency keeps a current back-up caregiver list. If an unexpected staff shortage prevents delivery of scheduled services, the agency advises the client and refers the client to another provider if the client wishes. Every missed or late visit, the reason, and the notice to the client and the case manager (where one is involved) are documented. The agency does not use no-show or late-cancellation penalties that conflict with the client's right to cancel at any time and pay only for services rendered. The only permitted charge is a reasonable travel and staff-time charge when the staff member has already arrived. Late and missed visits are tracked and reviewed in the Quality Improvement program.

definitions.definition: A scheduled visit that is not delivered at all, or that is delivered so late or so short that the service plan tasks could not be completed, whether the cause is the agency, the caregiver or the client.
A visit that starts later than [LATE VISIT THRESHOLD, e.g., 30 minutes] after the scheduled start time.
A current list of qualified, oriented and cleared staff available to cover a visit on short notice, kept by the scheduler and the on-call representative.
A situation in which the agency cannot staff a scheduled visit because of illness, emergency, resignation, no-show or similar events it could not reasonably foresee.

procedures: The scheduler builds each client's schedule directly from the signed service agreement and service plan (services, days, times, frequency) and enters it in the scheduling system before the first visit.

Before assigning a caregiver, the scheduler confirms the caregiver is qualified for the tasks (nursing licensure, completed personal care training, orientation complete, background clearance on file) and is not already booked or in overtime.
The scheduler keeps the back-up caregiver list current, reviews it at least monthly, and records each person's qualifications, availability and service area.

A caregiver who cannot work a scheduled visit must notify the scheduler or the on-call representative at [PHONE] as early as possible, and at least [NUMBER] hours before the visit unless it is an emergency.
On receiving a call-out, the scheduler or on-call representative immediately contacts back-up caregivers in the order listed until the visit is covered, and records each attempt.
If a qualified replacement is found, the scheduler tells the client of the change and the replacement's name before the visit, whenever possible.

If no replacement can be found, the scheduler or service supervisor contacts the client without delay, explains the shortage, offers the earliest possible alternate visit time, and asks whether the client wants a referral to another provider.

If the client wants a referral, the service supervisor gives the client the names and contact information of at least [NUMBER] other licensed providers, helps arrange the transfer, and records the referral in the client record.

For a client who is medically frail or compromised, or who cannot safely be left without care, the service supervisor treats a shortage as urgent, contacts the family or responsible party, and escalates to the Administrator the same day.
If the client has a Medicaid waiver case manager, the service supervisor notifies the case manager of any missed visit and the plan to make it up, by the end of the next business day.

If a visit is missed because the client is not home or does not answer, the caregiver follows the safety steps in SAF-07 before leaving, including attempting to reach the client, the emergency contact and the supervisor.
The service supervisor documents each missed or late visit in the client record: date, scheduled time, reason, who was notified and when, and whether the visit was made up or the client was referred.

The agency honors a client's cancellation at any time. Charges are limited to services actually rendered and, only if the staff member has already arrived, a reasonable travel and staff-time charge as stated in the service agreement. No penalty or fee is assessed for a cancellation beyond that.
The service supervisor does not bill any visit that was not delivered. Billing staff check the missed-visit log against invoices and claims before they are submitted.

The QI Coordinator compiles the monthly log of late and missed visits (by cause, caregiver, client and day) and reports trends and corrective actions to the Administrator at least quarterly, as part of the Quality Improvement program.
The Administrator reviews staffing levels against the schedule at least quarterly. If missed visits show a pattern, the Administrator stops accepting new clients until staffing is sufficient.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures sufficient qualified staff, approves any pause in new admissions, and reviews missed-visit trends.
Builds schedules from service agreements, maintains the back-up caregiver list, arranges coverage and logs call-outs.
Contacts clients and case managers, arranges referrals, documents missed visits and follows up on urgent cases.
Receives after-hours call-outs and arranges coverage.
Report absences promptly and arrive on time.
Tracks late and missed visits and reports trends.

Missed or late visit report in the client record (reason, notices, make-up or referral)
Record of client referral to other providers
Notice to waiver case manager
Back-up caregiver list with review dates
Monthly late and missed visit tracking report and QI minutes

policies.title: Discharge, Transfer and Discontinuation of Services
policies.applies_to: Administrator, service supervisors, nursing personnel, billing staff, records staff
policies.purpose: To make sure services end in an orderly, documented and respectful way, whether the client cancels, the agency can no longer serve the client, or the client moves to another provider or level of care.
policies.policy: Every service plan includes a discharge plan (Rule 111-8-65-.11). A client may cancel services at any time and pays only for services rendered (Rule 111-8-65-.09(2)). If [AGENCY NAME] cannot continue to serve a client, it refers the client to another provider. When the agency itself initiates a discharge, it gives the client (and responsible party) written notice that states the reasons and the referral options. The agency notifies the payer or waiver case manager. The agency does not discharge a client in retaliation for a complaint or for exercising any right in the written notice of rights and responsibilities (Rule 111-8-65-.12). The client file is kept at least 5 years from the last service.

definitions.definition: The end of all services by [AGENCY NAME] to a client.
A discharge that the agency decides on, for example because it cannot meet the client's needs, the home is unsafe, or the client does not pay for private-pay services.
The client or responsible party cancels services, in whole or part, at any time and for any reason.
Movement of the client to another provider, program or level of care, with the agency's help and the transfer of needed information with the client's authorization.
The Medicaid waiver case manager, care coordinator, managed care contact, or other payer representative with authority over the client's authorized services.

procedures: At the time of the service plan (within seven working days after services start), the service supervisor writes the discharge plan with the client and responsible party. It states the circumstances in which services end and what the client will do afterward (e.g., return to family care, another provider, higher level of care). The plan is reviewed with the service plan at each review.

When a client or responsible party says they want to cancel or stop services, the service supervisor accepts the decision at once, confirms the effective date, and records it in the client record on the day it is received.
The service supervisor offers a referral to another provider if the client is changing providers or needs services the agency cannot provide, and records what was offered.

The service supervisor informs the client that charges are limited to services rendered (and, only if a staff member had already arrived, the reasonable travel and staff-time charge stated in the service agreement). Billing staff prepare a final statement on that basis.

If the agency is considering an agency-initiated discharge, the service supervisor first documents the problem and the steps taken to resolve it, such as a care conference, a service plan revision, or help from the family or case manager. The Administrator must approve every agency-initiated discharge.

Where the discharge is because the agency cannot reasonably continue or meet the client's needs, the service supervisor tells the client and responsible party by telephone first, then delivers a written discharge notice.

The written notice states the reasons for discharge, the last date of service, [NUMBER] days of notice where the circumstances allow, the names and contact information of other providers or referral sources (such as the Area Agency on Aging for waiver clients), the agency's telephone [PHONE], and how to make a complaint.

The agency continues services through the notice period unless there is an immediate threat to the safety of the client or staff. In that case the Administrator documents the reason and tells the client, the responsible party, and the case manager the same day.

If the client appears to be unable to care for themselves safely after discharge, the service supervisor notifies the responsible party, and if no safe arrangement exists, follows SAF-01 and SAF-07 and contacts the appropriate agencies.

The service supervisor notifies the payer or Medicaid waiver case manager of the discharge or discontinuation and its effective date, in writing, by the end of the next business day. The agency cooperates with any transition plan the case manager requires.
With the client's written authorization, the service supervisor gives the new provider the information it needs. Records are released only in accordance with ADM-06 and CR-03.

On the last day, the supervisor or caregiver retrieves any agency property, returns the client's keys and belongings, and ends any authorization for client funds or vehicle use. The supervisor records this in the file.
For nursing clients, the nurse writes a discharge summary of the client's condition, services provided, and recommendations, and sends a copy to the physician.

The service supervisor completes a discharge note in the client record with the date, reason, who initiated it, notices given, referrals offered, case manager contact, and the client's status at discharge.

Records staff close the file, remove the client from the schedule, EVV and billing systems, and keep the file at least 5 years from the last date of service. Records are then destroyed only as ADM-06 provides.
The QI Coordinator reviews all discharges quarterly for patterns, such as clients leaving because of missed visits or caregiver turnover, and reports them to the Administrator.

responsibilities.duty: Approves agency-initiated discharges and reviews discharge patterns.
Writes the discharge plan, gives notices and referrals, notifies the case manager, and documents the discharge.
Completes discharge summaries for nursing clients and communicates with the physician.
Prepare the final statement for services rendered only.
Close and retain the file for at least 5 years.

documentation: Discharge plan in the service plan
Cancellation or discontinuation note
Written discharge notice with reasons and referral options (for agency-initiated discharge)
Record of referrals offered
Notice to payer or waiver case manager
Nursing discharge summary, where applicable
Final billing statement

Return of property and funds record

policies.title: Coordination With Medicaid Waiver Programs (CCSP/SOURCE, ICWP, NOW/COMP)
policies.applies_to: Administrator, service supervisors, intake staff, billing staff, schedulers, caregivers serving waiver clients
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] serves and bills Georgia Medicaid waiver clients only as authorized, works with the case manager and the responsible state agencies, and keeps its license and enrollment in good standing.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] holds a current Georgia DCH private home care license before serving as an in-home waiver provider (DAS HCBS 5300 Manual § 208). Georgia's Elderly and Disabled Waiver (CCSP/SOURCE) operates under a Social Security Act § 1915(c) waiver. DCH handles reimbursement, enrollment and utilization review, and the Division of Aging Services (DAS) runs day-to-day CCSP operations. DBHDD manages NOW/COMP. The agency follows the waiver service plan and each case manager's authorizations and confirms for each client whether payment is fee-for-service or through a care management organization (CMO). It bills CCSP/SOURCE (waiver IDs 590/930) with code T1019 and the TF/UC modifiers, and ICWP (660) and NOW/COMP (680/681) with code T2025. It never bills private-pay rates for authorized waiver services.

definitions.definition: Georgia's Elderly and Disabled Waiver programs (waiver IDs 590/930), operated under a § 1915(c) waiver. CCSP is run by DAS day to day and DCH handles reimbursement, enrollment and utilization review.
Independent Care Waiver Program (waiver ID 660).

The New Options Waiver and Comprehensive Supports Waiver (waiver IDs 680/681), community living supports for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities; DBHDD manages the planning list and waiver slots.
The person who develops the client's waiver service plan and authorizes the services, units and dates.
The approved service, units and date range the agency must have before it delivers and bills a waiver service.
Care management organization. A client may be paid through a CMO rather than fee-for-service Medicaid.

procedures: Before accepting any waiver referral, the Administrator confirms the agency holds a current DCH private home care license for the location that will serve the client, and that the agency is enrolled with Georgia Medicaid and approved for the specific waiver program.
The Administrator keeps copies of the license, enrollment and provider agreements for each waiver program. The calendar for renewals and re-enrollments is reviewed every month.
Intake staff receive waiver referrals through the Area Agency on Aging, DBHDD, support coordination agency or other referral source, and record the date and source of the referral.

Intake staff identify the program (CCSP/SOURCE, ICWP or NOW/COMP), the client's Medicaid ID, the case manager's name and contact, and whether payment is fee-for-service or through a CMO. They document this on the intake form and verify eligibility before the first visit.
The agency obtains the waiver service plan and prior authorization (services, units, dates, rates) from the case manager before delivering services, and files them in the client record.

The service supervisor completes the agency service agreement (ADM-02) and service plan (PLN-01), which must be consistent with the waiver service plan. Differences are resolved with the case manager before services begin.

The scheduler schedules visits only within the authorized services, units and dates. The service supervisor notifies the case manager before authorized units run out so that reauthorization can be requested in time.
Caregivers perform only the tasks in the waiver service plan and the agency service plan. A request for additional or different tasks goes to the service supervisor, who contacts the case manager.
Visits for personal support services are verified through EVV (OPS-05). Billing staff bill only visits that were delivered, documented in the daily notes, and verified.

Billing staff use code T1019 with the TF/UC modifiers for CCSP/SOURCE (IDs 590/930) and code T2025 for ICWP (660) and NOW/COMP (680/681), and bill the payer indicated in the authorization (fee-for-service or the client's CMO).

The agency never bills a waiver client or family a private-pay rate, a co-payment, or a supplement for services that the waiver authorizes, except where the program expressly allows a client share. The Administrator approves any other charge in advance.

The service supervisor reports to the case manager any change in the client's condition, hospitalization, loss of eligibility, relocation, missed visits, or other event that affects the plan, promptly and no later than the next business day. Incidents and suspected abuse are also reported under SAF-01 and SAF-02.
The service supervisor participates in plan reviews and reassessments the case manager schedules, provides the agency's records requested, and records the contacts in the client record.
The Administrator and billing staff cooperate with utilization reviews, audits and record requests from DCH, DAS, DBHDD or a CMO, and provide records within the time requested.
Billing staff reconcile remittances monthly against claims, correct errors, and refund overpayments promptly. The Administrator reviews denials and reports patterns to QI under LIC-05.

The Administrator checks the DCH, DAS and DBHDD websites and provider notices at least quarterly for changes in waiver rules, rates, codes or modifiers, and updates this policy and billing procedures when they change.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the license and Medicaid enrollment, approves waiver referrals, oversees billing compliance and agency responses to audits.
Verify program, eligibility, case manager and payer for each referral.
Aligns the agency service plan with the waiver plan, monitors authorization, and communicates with the case manager.
Schedules only authorized services and units.
Bill with the correct code, modifiers and payer, reconcile payments, and refund overpayments.

documentation: DCH license and Medicaid and waiver enrollment records
Referral and intake record showing program, Medicaid ID, case manager and payer
Waiver service plan and prior authorizations
Agency service agreement and service plan aligned to the waiver plan
Case manager communications log
Daily service notes and EVV records
Claims, remittances and refund records
Audit and utilization review correspondence

policies.title: Electronic Visit Verification and Timekeeping
policies.applies_to: Administrator, schedulers, service supervisors, billing and payroll staff, personal care assistants and other caregivers
policies.purpose: To make sure every Medicaid-financed personal care visit is electronically verified as required by federal and state law, that billing is based on verified visits, and that employee pay matches the hours actually worked.
policies.policy: Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) is required for Medicaid-financed personal care services under Section 12006 of the 21st Century Cures Act and 42 USC 1396b(l). Georgia's EVV system is Netsmart Mobile Caregiver+. For every visit, [AGENCY NAME] records the service type, recipient, provider, date, location, and start and end times. Home health care services claims with dates of service on or after September 14, 2026 must be submitted through EVV; the agency confirms the current date and requirements on the DCH EVV page. Supervisors correct visit records before billing, and payroll hours must reconcile with EVV and the daily service notes. As a third-party employer, the agency does not claim the companionship exemption from overtime (29 CFR 552.109). See PER-02.

definitions.definition: Electronic Visit Verification: electronic capture of the details of each Medicaid personal care visit.
Georgia's EVV system and mobile application used to check in and out of visits.
A visit record that is missing or inconsistent, such as a missing clock-in or clock-out, a location mismatch, or a manual entry.
A supervisor's correction or addition to an EVV record, made with a documented reason.

procedures: Before the first visit, the Administrator confirms the agency's EVV registration and system access for each Medicaid program served, and keeps the Georgia EVV Customer Support number, (833) 483-5587, available to staff. The old EVV number was retired January 16, 2026.

Billing staff set up each Medicaid client in the EVV system with the correct recipient identifier, program, authorized service and caregiver assignment, using the authorization from the case manager (OPS-04).

Each caregiver is trained in EVV check-in and check-out, in the use of the mobile app, in correcting errors, and in the penalties for falsifying visit data. Training is completed before the caregiver's first Medicaid visit and documented in the personnel record.

At the start of each visit, the caregiver checks in at the client's home using the EVV system so that the service type, recipient, provider, date, location and start time are captured. The caregiver checks out at the end of the visit so that the end time is captured.

Caregivers record only the actual start and end time of the visit. They never check in or out for another person, from a different location, or before arriving or after leaving, and never share their login.

If the app, device or network fails, the caregiver calls the scheduler or on-call representative at once, writes down the actual times, and tells the supervisor. The supervisor enters the visit with a manual edit and a documented reason. Manual entries are reviewed by the Administrator.
The caregiver completes the daily service note (SVC-09) for every visit. The note's times must agree with the EVV record.
The scheduler or service supervisor reviews the EVV exception report at least daily. They contact the caregiver to correct each exception, and document the reason for any edit.

A supervisor corrects the visit record, with a reason, before any claim is created. Billing staff do not submit a claim for a visit that has an unresolved exception, a missing record, or a mismatch with the daily note.
Billing staff bill only visits that EVV verified, that match the authorized service and units, and that are documented in the client record, and use the codes and modifiers listed in OPS-04.

Before each payroll is processed, payroll staff reconcile each caregiver's paid hours against EVV records and daily notes. Differences are investigated and resolved before pay is issued. Travel time between clients is added separately according to PER-02.
The Administrator reviews a sample of visits each month, comparing EVV, daily notes, schedules and payroll, and reports findings to the QI program (SVC-10).

For claims with dates of service on or after September 14, 2026, billing staff confirm that each claim goes through EVV, and the Administrator checks the DCH EVV page at least quarterly for changes in dates, requirements or system instructions.

Suspected falsification of visit data is reported to the Administrator immediately. The Administrator investigates, takes corrective or disciplinary action, corrects or refunds any affected claims, and follows the reporting duties in LIC-05 and LIC-06.

EVV records, edit logs, exception reports, and timekeeping and payroll records are retained as long as the related billing and client records, and for at least the period required by DCH and by wage and hour law.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures EVV registration and compliance, reviews manual edits, audits samples monthly, and acts on suspected falsification.
Review exceptions daily, correct records with documented reasons, and support caregivers with system problems.
Set up clients in EVV, bill only verified visits, and keep claims consistent with EVV.
Reconcile payroll hours with EVV and daily notes.
Check in and out accurately at each visit and complete daily notes.

documentation: EVV registration and system access records
EVV training records
EVV visit records and exception reports
Manual edit log with reasons and approvals
Daily service notes

Monthly audit results

policies.title: Background Checks, Fingerprint Determinations and Employee Registries
policies.applies_to: Owner, Administrator, human resources staff, and all applicants and employees with direct access to clients
policies.purpose: To make sure that the owner, the Administrator and every employee with direct access to clients are screened before they serve clients, that no one with credible evidence of abuse, neglect or exploitation works for the agency, and that excluded individuals are never employed.
policies.policy: The owner complies with Chapter 111-8-12 (Rules and Regulations for Criminal Background Checks) before a new license is issued (Rule 111-8-65-.05(1)(b)). The Administrator must have no credible evidence of abuse, neglect, exploitation or deprivation, and the current Secretary of State text of Rule 111-8-65-.09(3)(a)1 also requires a satisfactory fingerprint records check determination. [AGENCY NAME] also requires a satisfactory fingerprint records check determination for each employee with direct access to clients before that employee serves any client. Employees must have no credible evidence of abuse, neglect or exploitation and must make no false statements about their qualifications (Rule 111-8-65-.09(5)). The agency checks the OIG exclusion list at hire and monthly. Because Chapter 111-8-12 does not clearly define which positions beyond the owner and administrator are covered, and the exact fingerprint process was not verified, the Administrator confirms the current requirements and process with the Healthcare Facility Regulation Division (HFRD) and updates this policy accordingly.

definitions.definition: The written result of a fingerprint-based criminal records check, showing whether the individual is satisfactory to work in the position under Chapter 111-8-12.

Any employee, including nursing personnel, personal care assistants, companions and sitters, who provides care or services to clients or who has unsupervised access to clients or their homes, property or records.
Information that a reasonable person would find to support that the individual abused, neglected, exploited or deprived a person, whether or not a conviction exists.
The federal HHS Office of Inspector General's List of Excluded Individuals and Entities (42 CFR 1001).
The state or federal registries and lists the agency checks as required, including the OIG exclusion list, and any others HFRD identifies.

procedures: Before filing the license application, the Administrator contacts HFRD to confirm the current Chapter 111-8-12 requirements, which positions must have a fingerprint determination, and the current process, forms and fees for obtaining one. The answers and the date are written in the compliance file.
The owner completes the Chapter 111-8-12 requirements before the license is issued. Human resources keeps the owner's determination in the compliance file.

The governing body does not appoint an Administrator until the candidate has a satisfactory fingerprint determination, has no credible evidence of abuse, neglect, exploitation or deprivation, and has made no false statements. The determination is filed in the Administrator's personnel record.

Every job posting and application states that employment depends on a satisfactory fingerprint determination, a background check, and registry checks, and that false statements will lead to rejection or termination.
Before any offer becomes final, human resources has the applicant sign a consent and disclosure form, which includes any history of abuse, neglect, exploitation or deprivation.
Human resources starts the fingerprint records check process with the approved vendor or agency as HFRD directs, and records the date requested.

No direct access employee may be scheduled to work with a client, shadow a visit alone with a client, or receive client information until a satisfactory determination is on file. Where HFRD allows work pending results, that exception is written into this policy by the Administrator first and conditions are documented.

Human resources reviews each determination on receipt. An unsatisfactory or incomplete determination, or any credible evidence of abuse, neglect or exploitation, means the person is not hired or is removed from client contact immediately. The Administrator decides any appeal rights and documents the decision.

Human resources checks the OIG exclusion list for each applicant before hire, and for every employee, the Administrator and the owner at least monthly. Each check is logged with the date, the name checked and the result.
Human resources also checks every other registry or list that HFRD, DCH or a Medicaid program requires and documents the result.

If any person is found on the OIG exclusion list, the Administrator removes the person from all duties immediately, stops billing any federal program for their services, reviews past claims, and reports as LIC-05 and LIC-06 require.

Human resources verifies licensure for nursing personnel (ADM-10), training and credentials (ADM-09, ADM-11) and checks professional references. Statements on the application that prove false are cause for refusal to hire or termination.

Each employee must tell the Administrator immediately if they are arrested for, charged with or convicted of a crime, or are the subject of an abuse, neglect or exploitation allegation. The Administrator reviews each report, and takes action, which may include removal from client contact.
If the agency receives credible information about an employee, it follows the investigation and reporting steps in SAF-01 while the employee is removed from client contact.

Human resources keeps the fingerprint determination, consent forms and registry check logs in a confidential section of the personnel record (ADM-07), apart from the general personnel file, and limits access to authorized staff.

The Administrator audits all personnel records at least annually to verify that every direct access employee has a satisfactory determination and monthly OIG checks, and reports results to the governing body.

responsibilities.duty: Completes Chapter 111-8-12 requirements before licensure and appoints only a qualified Administrator.
Confirms requirements with HFRD, makes final decisions on determinations, and audits compliance annually.
Initiates checks, reviews results, runs OIG checks at hire and monthly, and maintains logs.
Provide truthful information and report arrests, charges, convictions and allegations immediately.

documentation: HFRD confirmation of requirements (date, name and contact)
Owner's Chapter 111-8-12 compliance record
Administrator and employee fingerprint determinations
Signed consent and disclosure forms
OIG exclusion check log (at hire and monthly)
Other registry check results
Reports of arrests, charges and allegations and the Administrator's decisions
Annual personnel record audit

policies.title: Wage, Hour, Overtime and Travel Time Compliance
policies.applies_to: Owner, Administrator, payroll and human resources staff, schedulers, supervisors, and all hourly employees
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] pays all employees correctly under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), including minimum wage, overtime, training time, and travel time between clients.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] employs its aides and other caregivers as W-2 employees. As a third-party employer of home care workers, the agency does not claim the companionship exemption from overtime (29 CFR 552.109(a)). Because the current status of 29 CFR 552.109 must be confirmed before this policy is finalized, the Administrator verifies it with the U.S. Department of Labor or legal counsel and records the result. Until then the agency pays overtime. The agency pays at least the federal minimum wage of $7.25 per hour for all hours worked, or a higher rate set by the agency or a Medicaid program. It pays for travel between clients during the workday and for time spent in orientation and in the 40-hour personal care training program.

definitions.definition: All time an employee is required or allowed to work, including client visits, travel between clients during the workday, orientation, training, required meetings, charting, and waiting time that is for the agency's benefit.
A fixed, recurring period of 168 hours (seven consecutive 24-hour days) set by the agency as [WORKWEEK START DAY AND TIME].
Hours worked beyond 40 in a workweek, paid at not less than one and one-half times the employee's regular rate.
A worker the agency treats as an employee for tax and wage purposes, with taxes withheld and employer taxes paid.
An agency or other employer that is not the individual, family or household employing the worker directly.

procedures: Before the agency hires its first employee, the Administrator verifies the current status of 29 CFR 552.109(a) and the FLSA rules for home care workers with the U.S. Department of Labor or counsel, and records the answer, date and source in the compliance file. This is re-checked at least annually.

The agency classifies every aide, nurse (as the FLSA allows), companion and sitter who works for the agency as a W-2 employee and does not treat aides as independent contractors. The Administrator reviews any exception with counsel before the worker begins.
Human resources gives each new employee a written notice of pay rate, pay day, workweek definition, and how time is recorded. The employee signs it.
Payroll sets each hourly employee's rate at or above $7.25 per hour and at or above the rate required by any Medicaid program or contract the agency serves.

The agency pays for all orientation time (ADM-13), the 40-hour personal care training (ADM-11) including the first 20 hours before serving clients, annual in-service hours (ADM-14), required meetings, and competency evaluations as hours worked.

Employees record all hours worked. For Medicaid personal care visits, time comes from EVV (OPS-05). For other time such as travel, training and charting, employees submit a time record by [DEADLINE] each pay period, and the supervisor reviews it.

The agency pays for travel time between clients during the workday as hours worked, from the end of one visit to the start of the next. Schedulers plan routes to keep travel time reasonable and record the travel time on the schedule.

Travel from home to the first client and from the last client to home is handled according to FLSA rules, and payroll applies the rule the Administrator has confirmed. Mileage reimbursement for use of an employee's own vehicle is stated in the pay notice. See SAF-06 for vehicle use.
Payroll adds up total hours worked in each workweek, including client visits, travel, training and other work, and pays one and one-half times the regular rate for all hours over 40.
Where an employee has more than one rate in a week, payroll calculates overtime using the weighted-average regular rate as the FLSA requires.

Schedulers check projected weekly hours when scheduling. They notify the Administrator before an employee is scheduled over 40 hours so that overtime is approved in advance, but overtime that is worked is always paid whether or not it was approved.

The agency does not permit off-the-clock work. Supervisors may not tell employees to skip clock-in, work through breaks without pay, or complete charting off the clock. Employees who feel pressured to do so should tell the Administrator.
Payroll reconciles paid hours against EVV records and daily service notes every pay period (OPS-05), investigates differences, and corrects underpayments in the next payroll.

The agency pays wages on regular paydays at least [PAY FREQUENCY], gives itemized pay statements, withholds required taxes, and registers with the Georgia Department of Labor for state unemployment insurance.
Payroll keeps time and payroll records for each employee for at least the period required by the FLSA and state law and keeps them available for inspection.

The Administrator audits payroll quarterly for minimum wage, overtime, travel time and training pay, and corrects any error promptly with back pay. Employees may raise a pay question with the Administrator without retaliation.

responsibilities.duty: Budgets for compliant wages and overtime and supports the classification of aides as W-2 employees.
Verifies the current legal status, approves rates, audits payroll quarterly, and corrects errors.
Calculate hours, overtime and travel time, reconcile against EVV, and keep records.
Plan routes and schedules to manage travel time and overtime.
Record all hours accurately and report any pay problem.

documentation: Record of verification of 29 CFR 552.109 status (date, source)
Worker classification records (W-2) and pay notices
Time records, EVV records and travel time records
Training and orientation attendance and pay records
Payroll registers and itemized pay statements
Payroll to EVV reconciliation
Quarterly payroll audits and corrections

policies.title: Staff Conduct and Professional Boundaries
policies.applies_to: All employees and contracted personnel of [AGENCY NAME]: nurses, personal care assistants (PCAs), companions/sitters, supervisors, office staff and the Administrator, while working or when representing the agency.
policies.purpose: To make sure every caregiver treats clients, their property and their information with respect, stays within the tasks assigned and the training received, keeps a professional relationship with the client, and promptly reports boundary violations, abuse, neglect or exploitation. These expectations follow the client rights notice required by Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. R. 111-8-65-.12 (C28), the personnel record and evaluation requirements of R. 111-8-65-.09(4)(c) (C13), and the reporting duty in O.C.G.A. § 30-5-4 (C34).
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires professional conduct from all staff at all times. (1) Caregivers perform only the tasks listed in the client's service plan and only those tasks for which they have been trained and are qualified. They decline or refer to the supervisor any request that falls outside the plan or their training. (2) Caregivers may not accept gifts, cash, loans or other valuables from clients or families, and may not lend or borrow money or property. Caregivers may not handle client money, cards, checks or financial accounts unless the service plan or service agreement authorizes it in writing. Any employee with unlimited access to client funds must be bonded, and the bond is documented in the personnel record (a universal bond is acceptable) as required by C13. (3) Caregivers keep all client information confidential and respect the client's property and residence, consistent with the client rights notice given to every client under C28. (4) Caregivers report any boundary violation, whether their own, a coworker's or a client's, to the supervisor. Retaliation against anyone who reports in good faith is prohibited. (5) Every caregiver is a reporter of suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation of a disabled adult or elder person. Reports go to the designated adult protection agency (DHS-DAS Adult Protective Services) and to law enforcement as required by O.C.G.A. § 30-5-4 (C34). The agency treats every caregiver as a reporter, and staff must also notify the person in charge so the agency can make or confirm the report. Good-faith reporters are immune under the statute. (6) Conduct and professional boundaries are evaluated in each employee's annual performance review, which is kept in the personnel record (C13). Violations lead to corrective action up to and including termination.

definitions.definition: The limit that separates a caregiver's professional role from personal, financial or social involvement with a client or family, so that the relationship stays focused on the client's service plan.

Any act that crosses that limit, such as accepting gifts or loans, financial dealings, personal or romantic relationships, sharing personal problems in a way that burdens the client, undisclosed social media contact, or performing tasks outside the service plan.
The written plan that lists the tasks a caregiver is assigned to perform for a client.
Improper use of a client's money, property or resources for another person's benefit, including by a caregiver, coworker, family member or other person.
Authority or practical ability to withdraw, spend or transfer a client's money without a transaction-by-transaction limit or direct client approval. An employee with such access must be bonded.

procedures: At hire, the Administrator or designee gives each employee a copy of this policy during orientation, reviews it with the employee, and obtains a signed acknowledgment placed in the personnel record.
Before a caregiver's first visit, the supervisor gives the caregiver the client's service plan and explains the assigned tasks. The supervisor confirms the caregiver is trained for each task.

Caregivers perform only the tasks in the service plan. If a client or family member asks for something outside the plan or beyond the caregiver's training, the caregiver politely declines and contacts the supervisor the same day. The supervisor decides whether to revise the plan (through the service plan review process) or refer the request elsewhere.

Caregivers do not accept gifts, cash, tips, loans, or items of value from clients or families, and do not give gifts or loans to clients. A thank-you card or verbal thanks is acceptable. The caregiver tells the supervisor the same day if a gift is offered or left behind, and the supervisor documents it and arranges for it to be returned or declined.

Caregivers may not be named as a client's agent, executor or beneficiary through any document they helped prepare, may not witness or influence the signing of wills, powers of attorney or financial documents, and may not sell to, buy from, or borrow property from a client.

Handling of client money occurs only when the Administrator or supervisor has authorized it in writing in the service plan or service agreement. The authorization states the purpose, any dollar limit, and receipt requirements. Without written authorization, the caregiver declines and notifies the supervisor.

Before any employee is given unlimited access to client funds, the Administrator confirms the employee is covered by a bond (a universal bond is acceptable) and places the bond documentation in the personnel record.

When authorized to spend client money (for example, for groceries), the caregiver keeps the client's money separate from personal funds, obtains and keeps receipts, returns change to the client, and records the transaction in the daily documentation. The supervisor reviews the receipts and documentation during home visits or record review.

Caregivers keep client information confidential. They do not discuss clients with anyone outside the care team, do not post about clients or the client's home on social media or messaging apps, and do not photograph clients or their homes without written permission from the client and the agency.

Caregivers respect the client's residence and property. They use only the items and areas needed to perform the service plan, report any damage or loss immediately to the supervisor, and do not remove client property for any reason.

Caregivers do not engage in personal, romantic or sexual relationships with clients, do not bring family or friends to the client's home, and do not use the client's phone, car or other property for personal purposes.

Any employee who observes or learns of a boundary violation tells the supervisor within 24 hours. If the supervisor is involved, the employee reports directly to the Administrator at [PHONE]. The person receiving the report completes an incident or conduct report the same day.

If the situation involves suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation of a client, the caregiver reports immediately to the supervisor or Administrator and, with the agency, makes a report to DHS-DAS Adult Protective Services at [DHS-DAS APS REPORTING PHONE] and to law enforcement. A caregiver who has reasonable cause to report may not wait for agency approval. The agency follows policy SAF-01 for the full process.

The Administrator investigates each reported boundary violation promptly, interviews involved parties, and decides on corrective action (coaching, written warning, retraining, suspension, reassignment or termination). The outcome is documented in the personnel record and conduct file.

Clients receive the written notice of rights and responsibilities, which includes the supervisor's name and contact information and the complaint procedure. If a client complains about caregiver conduct, the supervisor handles it under policy CR-02. The agency does not retaliate against clients or staff who complain or report.

Reassignment: when a boundary violation has occurred, the Administrator removes the caregiver from the client's case as needed to protect the client while the matter is reviewed, and arranges replacement coverage so services are not interrupted.

Annual review: the supervisor includes conduct and professional boundaries (task limits, handling of money and gifts, confidentiality, respect for property, and reporting) in each employee's annual performance evaluation. The employee and supervisor sign it and it is filed in the personnel record.

The Administrator reviews boundary-related incidents, complaints and reports at least annually, identifies trends, and updates training or this policy as needed through the governing body review process.

responsibilities.duty: Approves this policy and reviews it annually. Ensures resources for orientation, bonding and enforcement.

Ensures staff are oriented to this policy, confirms bonding where required, investigates reported violations, directs corrective action, and makes or confirms required reports to Adult Protective Services and law enforcement.

Explains service plan tasks to caregivers, authorizes any handling of client money in writing, reviews receipts and documentation, receives boundary reports, documents gifts offered, and evaluates conduct in annual reviews.

Perform only assigned and trained tasks, refuse gifts and loans, handle money only as authorized, keep information confidential, respect the client's property and home, and report violations and suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation immediately.
Maintain personnel files (acknowledgments, bonding documents, evaluations) and route conduct reports and client complaints to the Administrator the same day.

documentation: Signed acknowledgment of this policy in each personnel record
Bonding documentation for employees with unlimited access to client funds, in the personnel record
Written authorization for handling client money, with receipts and daily documentation entries
Gift-offered and boundary-violation reports with investigation notes and corrective action
Reports made to DHS-DAS Adult Protective Services and law enforcement, kept in a confidential file
Annual performance evaluation, including conduct and professional boundaries, in the personnel record
Orientation and training records covering conduct, boundaries and reporting

required_items.text: Each private home care provider shall have a governing body empowered and responsible to determine all policies and procedures and to ensure compliance with these rules.

Services Description. A provider shall establish and implement written policies and procedures that define the scope of private home care services it offers and the types of clients it serves. No provider shall provide services that are prohibited by these rules, the applicable legal authority, or other laws.
Service Agreements. No provider shall offer to provide a client any private home care services that it cannot reasonably expect to deliver in accordance with these rules.

A provider shall establish and implement policies and procedures for service agreements. All services provided to a client shall be based on a written service agreement entered into with the client or the client's responsible party, if applicable. The service agreement must include the following:
Date that provider makes initial contact with client for services;
Date of referral, i.e. the date on which the provider received a specific request to deliver private home care services to a particular client;
Description of services needed as stated by client or responsible party, if applicable;
Description of services to be provided and expected frequency and duration of services;
Charges for such services, and mechanisms for billing and payment of such charges;
Acknowledgment of receipt of a copy of client's rights and responsibilities as outlined at rule .12;
A telephone number of the provider that a client can call for information, questions, or complaints about services supplied by the provider;

The telephone number of the state licensing authority, i.e. the department, to call for information or questions about the provider concerning a violation of licensing requirements that was not resolved to the client's satisfaction by complaining to the provider;

Authorization from client or responsible party, if applicable, for access to client's personal funds when home management services are to be provided and when those services include assistance with bill paying or any activities, such as shopping, that involve access to or use of such funds; similarly approved authorization for use of client's motor vehicle when services to be provided include transport and escort services and when the client's personal vehicle will be used;

Signatures for the provider's representative and the client or responsible party, if applicable, and date signed; if a client or responsible party refuses to sign the agreement, such refusal shall be noted on the agreement with an explanation from the provider's representative.

For new clients, such initial service agreements shall be completed not later than the second visit to the client's residence to provide services if the second visit occurs on a different day from the first visit or not later than seven calendar days after services are initially provided in the residence, whichever is earlier.
If the provider is unable to complete the service agreement for good cause, the provider will document such reason(s) in the client's file.

Subsequent revisions to the initial service agreement may be handled by the provider noting in the client's record the specific changes in service (e.g. addition or deletion of service, changes in frequency, or duration, or charge for services, etc.) that will occur and that the change was discussed with and agreed to by the client and/or responsible party, as appropriate, who signed the initial agreement prior to the change in services occurring.

A client has the right to cancel any service agreement at any time and shall only be charged for services actually rendered prior to the time that the provider is notified of the cancellation. The provider may assess a reasonable charge for travel and staff time if notice of the cancellation of the service agreement is not provided in time to cancel the service prior to the provider's staff member arriving at the client's house to perform the service.
Administrator. The governing body shall appoint an administrator who shall have full authority and responsibility for the operation of the private home care provider.

Any administrator employed by the provider must meet the following minimum qualifications: 1. Obtain a satisfactory fingerprint records check determination in compliance with the Rules and Regulations for Criminal Background Checks, Chapter 111-8-12; 2. Participate in the orientation and training required by these rules; 3. Not have made any material false statements concerning qualifications requirements either to the department or the provider.

Client Records. A provider shall maintain a separate file containing all written records pertaining to the services provided for each client that it serves and the file shall contain the following: 1. Identifying information including name, address, telephone number, and responsible party, if any; 2. Current service agreement as described at rule .09(2); 3. Current service plan as described at rule .11; 4. Clinical and/or progress notes if the client is receiving nursing services that have been signed and dated by the staff providing the direct care; 5. Documentation of personal care tasks and companion or sitter tasks actually performed for the client; 6. Documentation of findings of home supervisory visits by the supervisor unless entered in service plan; 7. Any material reports from or about the client that relate to the care being provided to the client including items such as progress notes and problems reported by employees of the provider, communications with personal physicians or other health care providers, communications with family members or responsible parties, or similar items; 8. The names, addresses, and telephone numbers of the client's personal physicians, if any; and 9. Date and source of referral.

Retention and Confidentiality of Client Records. Written policies and procedures shall be established and implemented for the maintenance and security of client records specifying who shall supervise the maintenance of records, who shall have custody of records, to whom records may be released and for what purposes and how long the records will be retained.
At a minimum, all client records shall be retained for five years from the date of last service provided. The provider shall maintain the confidentiality of client records.

Employees of the provider shall not disclose or knowingly permit the disclosure of any information in a client record except to appropriate provider staff, the client, responsible party (if applicable), the client's physician or other health care provider, the department, other individuals authorized by the client in writing or by subpoena.

Personnel Records. A provider shall maintain separate written records for each employee and the records shall include the following: 1. Identifying information such as name, address, telephone number, and emergency contact person(s); 2. A five year employment history or a complete employment history if the person has not been employed five years; 3. Records of qualifications; 4. Records of health screenings, demonstrating compliance with the following: (i) Each provider shall have in place a health screening program designed to identify conditions that may place clients at risk for infection, injury, or improper care. The program shall include requirements and processes for initial, routine, and targeted health screenings of employees and contractors who interact with clients or conduct other activities with environmental impact. (ii) Screening for Tuberculosis (TB). Prior to starting work, all employees must be screened for TB in accordance with CDC guidance for baseline screening and testing for health care personnel. 5. Date of employment; 6. The person's job description or statements of the person's duties and responsibilities; 7. Documentation of orientation and training required by these rules; 8. Documentation of at least an annual performance evaluation; 9. Documentation of bonding if the employee performs home management services which permit unlimited access to the client's personal funds. (If bonding is provided through a universal coverage bond, evidence of bonding need not be maintained separately in each personnel folder.)

Reports of Complaints and Incidents. The provider shall maintain files of all documentation of complaints submitted pursuant to rule .12(2). A provider shall also maintain on file for a minimum of five years all incident reports or reports of unusual occurrences (e.g. falls, accidents, significant medication errors, etc.) that affect the health, safety, and welfare of its clients. Documentation required to be maintained shall include what actions, if any, the provider took to resolve clients' complaints and to address any incident reports or unusual occurrences required to be retained.

Staffing. The provider shall have sufficient numbers of qualified staff as required by these rules to provide the services specified in the service agreements with its clients. In the event that the provider becomes aware that it is unable to deliver the specified services to the client because of an unexpected staff shortage, the provider shall advise the client and refer the client to another provider if the client so desires.

All staff employed by a provider shall have included in their personnel records or files maintained by the particular provider a written evaluation that was performed within one year before or after the effective date of these rules. The written evaluation must reflect that the employee's performance of required job tasks was observed personally by a supervisor either by demonstration or observation and such performance was determined to be competent for all job tasks required to be performed. All staff hired by the provider must meet the following minimum qualifications: 1. Prior to serving as a direct access employee, obtain a satisfactory fingerprint records check determination in compliance with the Rules and Regulations for Criminal Background Checks, Chapter 111-8-12; 2. Participate in the orientation and training required by these rules; 3. Not have made any material false statements concerning qualifications requirements either to the department or the provider.

Nursing Personnel. Any persons employed by the provider to provide nursing services shall be licensed in Georgia in accordance with professional licensing laws and associated rules. Such persons may also provide any other types of private home care services offered by the provider.

Personal Care Assistant (PCA). The provider may have PCAs perform personal care tasks for clients. Such persons may also perform companion or sitter tasks for clients, but shall not provide nursing services unless qualified as stated in rule .09(5)(b) above.

Any PCA hired after the effective date of these rules shall have the following training and/or experience: (i) successful completion of a nurse aide training and competency evaluation program pursuant to the requirements of 42 CFR Part 483, Subpart D, as revised or recodified, if applicable; or (ii) successful completion of a competency examination for nurse aides recognized by the department; or (iii) successful completion of a health care or personal care credentialing program recognized and approved by the department; or (iv) successful completion or progress in the completion of a 40 hour training program provided by a private home care provider, which addresses at least the following areas: (I) Ambulation and transfer of clients, including positioning; (II) Assistance with bathing, toileting, grooming, shaving, dental care, dressing, and eating; (III) Basic first aide and CPR; (IV) Caring for clients with special conditions and needs so long as the services are within the scope of the tasks authorized to be performed by demonstration; (V) Home management; (VI) Home safety and sanitation; (VII) Infection control in the home; (VIII) Medically related activities to include the taking of vital signs; and (IX) Proper nutrition.
